papers.abstract: Perceived algorithmic bias is defined as users' comprehensive subjective cognitive judgment, grounded in a cognitive attribution perspective, regarding whether an algorithmic system engages in differential treatment, whether its outcomes exhibit systematic deviations, and whether such differential treatment is justified. This study develops a theoretical model of perceived algorithmic bias and systematically elucidates the construct through three dimensions: perceived differential treatment, perceived outcome skew, and perceived lack of justification. The paper examines the mechanisms through which perceived algorithmic bias influences human-AI collaborative decision-making performance across three levels: cognitive processing, affect and morality, and human-AI interaction. It also analyzes the moderating roles of individual characteristics, algorithmic characteristics, and task characteristics. By systematically reviewing the conceptualizations of algorithmic bias and perceived algorithmic bias and clarifying their effects on and theoretical mechanisms underlying human-AI collaborative decision-making performance, this study offers theoretical implications for advancing research on perceived algorithmic bias. Future research may further develop a measurement scale for perceived algorithmic bias, enrich empirical investigations, test its underlying mechanisms, and explore its impact on human-AI collaborative decision-making performance across diverse application contexts.

papers.title: The Impact of GenAI Literacy on Consumer Decision-Making: A Moderated Mediation Model of Information Overload and Consumer Involvement
papers.authors: He-Ran Wen, Yi-Ming Guo, Ze-Long Feng
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of consumer decision-making by providing unprecedented levels of personalized information. However, the inherent complexity and potential for AI hallucinations introduce significant cognitive challenges that may undermine decision quality. Grounded in Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study investigates the mechanism through which GenAI literacy influences consumer decision quality, specifically focusing on the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Through a structured survey of 401 Chinese college students and subsequent structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis, the empirical results demonstrate that GenAI literacy is directly and positively associated with decision quality. Furthermore, perceived information overload serves as a critical mediator, indicating that high levels of GenAI literacy could reduce cognitive friction and prevent decision paralysis. Notably, the continuous latent interaction analysis reveals that consumer involvement significantly moderates the relationship between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload, with the inhibitory effect of literacy being more pronounced in high-involvement scenarios. These findings extend the application of IPT to the era of human-AI symbiosis and offer actionable insights for policymakers and enterprises to optimize the digital consumption ecosystem.

papers.title: How AI Is Transforming Education: Toward a Symbiotic Relationship among AI, Teachers, and Students
papers.authors: Xu Fang, Zhiyi Liu, Hanshuo Yang, Yongqiang Luo
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping education by reorganizing interactions among teaching, learning, and instructional decision-making. Existing research has largely focused on isolated tools or specific learning outcomes, providing limited insight into how AI operates within integrated educational systems. This study examines an AI-enabled educational environment to explore how interactions among AI systems, teachers, and students relate to changes in instructional organization and student performance. Drawing on multi-source data generated from routine teaching activities, the findings suggest overall improvements in learning outcomes and indicate three interconnected mechanisms: improved instructional efficiency through reduced routine workload, stronger alignment between diagnosis and feedback, and a complementary division of roles between human teachers and AI systems. By linking learning outcomes with underlying instructional processes, the study provides system-level evidence on how integrated AI-enabled environments reshape educational practice and contribute to the emerging symbiotic relationship among AI, teachers, and students.

papers.title: How “AI Info” Labels Influence Social Media Posting Behavior? Evidence from Instagram
papers.authors: Pengkun Wu, Yuanxi Liu, Yuanyuan Wu, Yang Liu
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: AI-generated content (AIGC) has reshaped content creation on social media, prompting platforms to adopt “AI Info” labels as transparency mechanisms. Drawing on signaling theory, this study examines how such labels influence content creators’ posting frequency. Using a propensity score matched difference-in-differences (PSM-DiD) design applied to a panel dataset of 237 Instagram creators observed from January 2023 to December 2025, we find that mandatory AI labeling significantly reduces creators’ weekly posting frequency. This study contributes to AI transparency research by demonstrating unintended behavioral consequences of disclosure policies for content creators, and offers implications for platform governance design.

papers.title: Anthropomorphism and Relational Ontology of Purchase Intention in Generative AI Use: Insights from Mind Perception Theory and the Computers as Social Actors Paradigm
papers.authors: Jao-Hong Cheng, Li-Ming Wang
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: A human-centric understanding of purchase intention in generative AI contexts requires attention to how users interpret and experience AI systems under conditions of algorithmic opacity. Rather than treating AI adoption as the outcome of attribute evaluation, we argue that anthropomorphic cues shape how users construe the system itself. When AI is experienced as socially responsive rather than purely instrumental, evaluative emphasis shifts toward trust beliefs and interactional arousal. Drawing on Computers as Social Actors (CASA) and Mind Perception Theory, we theorize that anthropomorphism restructures the experiential architecture through which intention is formed. Using structural equation modeling with data from 526 generative AI users, results show that anthropomorphism influences purchase intention both directly and indirectly through trust and arousal, with relational mechanisms exerting stronger effects. By foregrounding user construal and experiential engagement, this research advances a human-centric framework for understanding AI adoption in opaque, interactive environments.

papers.title: The Impact of AI-Generated Content on Brand Image: A Dual Perspective of Algorithm Appreciation and Aversion
papers.authors: Mingxin Sun, Beiping Tan, Congyu Niu, Xinyu Guo
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technologies such as ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL-E, brands are increasingly leveraging AI to create marketing content. However, systematic research on how AI-generated content affects brand image remains scarce in academia, creating a critical knowledge gap for marketing practitioners. This study addresses this gap by investigating consumer attitudes toward brand use of AI-generated content and the underlying psychological mechanisms. Grounded in Algorithm Aversion theory and AI Technological Image Transfer theory, we examine whether brands should disclose AI involvement in their marketing content and how different AI participation approaches influence brand perception through three experimental studies (N=940). Results show that 100% AI-generated content significantly enhances brand image across all dimensions, with innovativeness showing the largest improvement. AI involvement approach significantly affects brand perception, with 100% AI producing the strongest effect. AI social identity emerges as the key psychological driver, while AI aversion paradoxically benefits 100% AI strategies through an “honesty effect.” This research challenges traditional algorithm aversion assumptions and provides guidance for brand AI marketing strategies.

papers.title: Color and Spatial Cue Modulation of Emotional Word Processing: Evidence from ERPs
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Luo, Chao LI, Yi Sun
papers.abstract: Emotional word processing is shaped by lexical meaning and concurrent perceptual context. This study investigated when red and green color cues and symbolic upward and downward direction cues modulate the processing of positive and negative Chinese emotional words. Thirty-four native Chinese speakers were recruited, and 27 remained in the final ERP sample after behavioral and EEG-quality exclusions. The experiment used a 2 (color: red vs. green) × 2 (direction: up vs. down) × 2 (word valence: positive vs. negative) within-subject design. Positive words elicited larger P1 amplitudes, and negative words elicited more negative-going N1 and N400 amplitudes. A significant Color × Valence interaction emerged in the late positive complex (LPC) window. The positive-minus-negative LPC difference was descriptively larger under green cues than under red cues, and neither within-color comparison reached significance after Bonferroni correction. Interactions involving spatial direction were not significant across the four components. These findings trace emotional word processing from early valence-sensitive visual attention through semantic processing to late color-dependent evaluation. The temporal pattern supports a context-sensitive account in which perceptual cues, lexical valence, and learned cultural associations contribute to emotional meaning at different processing stages.

papers.title: Institutional digitalization and digital stress: a four-wave observational study of teacher-reported AI-collaborative teaching in physical education
papers.authors: Xiangyu Wang, Xiangyu Wang, Wang Xiaoyun, Wang Xiaoyun
papers.abstract: Introduction How institutional digitalization relates to teachers’ experience of work and subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-supported practice remains unclear. Methods Drawing on job demands-resources principles, we examined these relationships in a four-wave observational cohort of 961 physical education teachers from 120 Chinese institutions. We linked an organizational-source digitalization proxy to teacher questionnaires and a study-specific teacher-reported score of AI involvement in teaching tasks. Analyses adjusted for baseline practice and separated between-institution from teacher-relative associations. Results Two of five primary tests met the Holm-adjusted criterion. The stress-related product of between-institution coefficients was negative (−0.099; pointwise 95% confidence interval [−0.184, −0.033]). The positive digitalization–stress association was weaker among teachers with higher digital self-efficacy relative to colleagues (interaction coefficient −0.101; [−0.168, −0.037]) but remained positive at the low, average, and high self-efficacy levels examined. The adjusted digitalization–practice association, appraisal-related coefficient product, and appraisal interaction did not meet the corrected criterion. Discussion The findings connect the organization and experience of work with reported AI practice, emphasizing perceived digital work pressure and relative self-efficacy while complementing accounts centered on technology acceptance.

papers.title: Authenticity across human and synthetic influencers: a configurational review of source evaluation and social influence
papers.authors: Xiao-Rui Lin, Amily Binti Fikry, Wei-Guo Zhang, Kai Ding
papers.abstract: Introduction Authenticity has become a central concern in social media influencer research, yet its construction is examined differently across human, virtual, and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated sources. This study examines how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across these influencer contexts. Methods This study conducted a corpus-based review of 1,676 English-language research articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between July 2017 and March 2026. BERTopic modeling was employed to identify recurring semantic topics, followed by an abductive, theory-informed synthesis organized around source ontology and the dominant basis of authenticity construction. Temporal changes in relative topic prevalence were examined across the eight complete calendar years from 2018 to 2025. Results The synthesis identified four configurations: relational human authenticity, curated human authenticity, humanized synthetic authenticity, and governed synthetic authenticity. Human-influencer research emphasizes biography, accumulated interaction, commercial congruence, and motive transparency, whereas synthetic-influencer research places greater weight on persona coherence, humanization, identity disclosure, ownership, automation, and accountability. Credibility, trust, parasocial interaction, social presence, and engagement emerge as closely associated evaluative processes. Temporal analysis revealed selective changes in relative topic prevalence, particularly concerning virtual-influencer credibility, humanization, and tourism-related applications, while most topics showed no clear linear trend. Discussion The findings provide a corpus- and method-dependent framework for understanding how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across human and synthetic influencer contexts. The framework highlights distinct evidential foundations underlying authenticity judgments and offers a basis for further research on source evaluation and social influence.

papers.title: Feeling or thinking? User aversion to AI customer service in online education
papers.authors: Yuan He, Lin Huang
papers.abstract: Introduction AI customer service is increasingly integrated into online education, yet users may not always respond favorably to AI-assisted service interactions. Drawing on robotic role theory, this study examines how thinking and feeling AI customer service influence user aversion in online educational service encounters. Methods Three experiments were conducted to examine the effect of AI customer service type on user aversion (Study 1, N = 120), the mediating role of perceived intelligence (Study 2, N = 120), and the moderating role of AI identity disclosure timing (Study 3, N = 120). Across the three between-subjects experiments, thinking AI was operationalized through analytical, information-processing, and task-oriented communication, whereas feeling AI emphasized emotional recognition and relational support. Results The results show that feeling AI generates greater user aversion than thinking AI. Perceived intelligence mediated this effect, such that feeling AI is perceived as less intelligent, which in turn increases user aversion. Further, AI identity disclosure timing moderates the indirect effect through perceived intelligence. Early disclosure of AI identity attenuates the negative effect of feeling AI. Discussion These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of different AI customer service types depends on the service context and highlight the importance of aligning AI communication with users’ task-oriented service needs.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and its influence on student engagement in higher education
papers.authors: Yongsheng Chen, Jing Dong, 冀国娟
papers.abstract: Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η 2 p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η 2 p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η 2 p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η 2 p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.

papers.title: Intelligent scaffolding for musical practice: a systematic review of AI and digital support for the self-regulated learning cycle
papers.authors: Xiuran Li, Mar Galera-Núñez, Yao Zhang
papers.abstract: Introduction Independent music practice depends on learners’ self-regulated learning (SRL), yet how digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) support the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of the SRL cycle, and when such support may undermine learner autonomy, remains unclear. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO through March 2026. Sixteen empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Because of methodological heterogeneity, we conducted a thematic synthesis rather than a meta-analysis. Results Three categories emerged: traditional digital tools, discriminative AI, and generative AI. Traditional tools supported planning and reflection; discriminative AI enabled real-time error detection; and generative AI may help learners manage task difficulty and translate expert feedback into actionable steps. Study quality was uneven, and several findings came from small-sample or cross-sectional designs, which limits causal inference. Two potential risks, over-scaffolding that may diminish autonomy and visual feedback that may divert attention from sound, were insufficiently studied. Discussion Digital and AI tools appear to scaffold different phases of SRL, but learner autonomy should remain at the core. Fading explicit support and pedagogical guidance may help reduce dependence. Longitudinal studies are required to test these mechanisms.

papers.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
papers.authors: Yan Liu
papers.abstract: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

papers.title: Motor action observation evaluation questionnaire: development and initial validity evidence for the scores in people with and without chronic low back pain
papers.authors: Roy La Touche, Prado Silván‐Ferrero, Encarnación Nouvilas-Pallejà, Alba Paris‐Alemany, Alfonso J. López-Rivero, Miguel Ángel Sorrel
papers.abstract: Introduction Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is highly prevalent and associated with functional limitations. Although action observation is increasingly used as a cognitive–motor rehabilitation strategy, no brief instrument exists to assess how individuals appraise and understand movements during observation. Methods The Questionnaire for the Assessment of Motor Action Observation (CENOAM) was developed using a sequential mixed-methods design. Phase 1 involved item generation based on literature review and qualitative analysis, followed by expert content validation using Aiken’s V . Phase 2 consisted of a cross-sectional study including 280 participants (140 with CLBP and 140 asymptomatic). Dimensionality and psychometric properties of the CENOAM scores were examined using exploratory factor analysis, complementary dimensionality methods, internal consistency ( α , ω ), floor and ceiling effects, concurrent associations, and known-groups comparisons, following COSMIN recommendations. Results The final seven-item instrument showed a parsimonious two-dimensional structure, comprising Familiarity and Competence–Demand, supported by converging evidence across multiple methods. Internal consistency was high for both total and subscale scores, and no floor or ceiling effects were observed. CENOAM scores were positively associated with motor imagery ability, physical activity, and pain self-efficacy, and negatively associated with fear of movement. Participants with CLBP showed significantly lower scores than asymptomatic individuals across all dimensions, with large effect sizes. Conclusion The CENOAM provides a brief and interpretable measure of movement appraisal during action observation. Its scores show initial evidence of validity and may support the individualization of action-observation–based rehabilitation in musculoskeletal conditions.

papers.title: Dynamic adaptation of attentional control across bilingual interactional contexts
papers.authors: Min Li, Xiangyu Shi, Qinghong Xu, Jie Li
papers.abstract: Background/objectives Bilingual experience is thought to shape cognitive control via adaptive attentional reorganization, yet the neural mechanisms by which different interactional contexts dynamically modulate attentional control remain unclear. This study used EEG to examine how Chinese monolingual, English monolingual, bilingual, and voluntary naming contexts influence attentional control in Chinese–English bilinguals. Methods Thirty-five bilinguals completed picture-naming tasks in different contexts, followed by an antisaccade task with concurrent EEG. We analyzed reaction time, ERPs, frontal and parietal delta/theta power, and frontoparietal functional connectivity (wPLI). Results Bilingual and voluntary naming contexts shortened antisaccade reaction times (all p < 0.01). No significant main effect of context was found on N2 amplitudes ( p = 0.615). Both contexts reduced parietal delta and theta power relative to the English monolingual context (all p < 0.05). Exploratory connectivity analysis initially suggested bilingual-context effects, but this finding did not survive homologous ROI validation. These preliminary sensor-level findings await validation by source-localized EEG or fMRI. Conclusions These findings suggest that bilingual and voluntary naming contexts may facilitate attentional control through adaptive reorganization of the attentional system rather than through enhancing a specific inhibitory process. This pattern is consistent with the adaptationist perspective on bilingual cognition and provides preliminary neural evidence for the language mode theory.

papers.title: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation
papers.authors: Jiayi Xia, Song Pei, Song ZHOU, Yulong Bai
papers.abstract: Advances in naturalistic language assessment, portable neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and brain-network modeling are creating new opportunities to evaluate post-stroke aphasia under conditions closer to real-world communication. Conventional aphasia batteries and isolated linguistic tasks remain essential for diagnosis, severity classification, and treatment planning, but they provide limited information about how language-network activity supports communication in dynamic, naturalistic contexts. This integrative review, informed by a structured literature search and descriptive thematic mapping, synthesizes evidence on connected speech, discourse production, narrative comprehension, interactive communication, and contextual reading after stroke. We examine how multilevel features from these behaviors can be organized into graded, interacting dimensions of lexical-semantic access, phonological encoding, grammatical organization, discourse processing, executive-predictive control, and speech-motor output. We further review multimodal evidence from fNIRS, fMRI, EEG/ERP, lesion-symptom mapping, structural connectivity, and functional connectivity, highlighting residual left-hemisphere language networks, conditional right-hemisphere support, bilateral reorganization, domain-general control systems, and longitudinal recovery. Portable EEG and fNIRS are considered complementary approaches for repeated assessment during less constrained language tasks, with distinct temporal, spatial, and practical trade-offs. Building on this evidence, we propose an operational ecological biomarker framework that links task choice, multilevel feature extraction, multivariate behavioral profiles, neural measures, prespecified clinical questions, and longitudinal outcomes. This framework may support recovery prediction, rehabilitation stratification, neuromodulation target selection, individualized therapy planning, and monitoring of functional communication.

papers.title: Post-traumatic headache as a window into persistent brain dysfunction after traumatic brain injury: an opinion article
papers.authors: Denise Franco de Almeida Duarte, Jader Vinicius Da Silva Rocha, Fernanda Moura Vargas Dias, Micheline Henrique Araújo da Luz Koerich, Vitória Caroline Reinoso de Almeida, Rodrigo Freire de Almeida, Walter Gomes da Silva Filho, Fernando Zanela da Silva Arêas
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide, particularly among young adults and individuals of working age (1,2). Advances in prehospital care, neurosurgery, and intensive care have improved survival after TBI, increasing attention to the persistent symptoms and functional limitations that may affect long-term recovery and quality of life (1,2).Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is a secondary headache attributed to traumatic injury to the head, including TBI, and is among the most frequent neurological symptoms reported after TBI (3)(4)(5)(6). In this article, we specifically address PTH occurring in the context of TBI rather than the broader category of headache attributed to head injury without established TBI. Consistent with the International Classification of Headache Disorders, PTH that persists for more than three months is referred to here as persistent PTH (3). Persistent PTH may coexist with fatigue, cognitive complaints, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and limitations in daily activities (4)(5)(6), contributing to the complexity of long-term clinical recovery.Conventional measures of initial TBI severity, including the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupillary reactivity, and structural imaging findings, remain essential for acute assessment and prognosis.However, the relationship between the extent and characteristics of the initial injury and persistent symptoms is not straightforward, and individuals with apparently similar acute injury characteristics may follow different long-term recovery trajectories (4-6, 11, 12). This variability has increased interest in biological and functional processes that may persist or evolve after the acute injury (7)(8)(9).Against this background, we propose the hypothesis that persistent PTH may serve as a clinical window into persistent brain dysfunction after TBI. This concept does not imply that persistent PTH is itself a biomarker or that it demonstrates the presence of a specific underlying mechanism. Rather, we propose that its persistence may serve as a clinical signal warranting investigation of functional or biological abnormalities that are not fully characterized by conventional structural assessment. This hypothesis is considered across the TBI severity spectrum. However, the evidence discussed in this article derives from heterogeneous populations, including mild TBI and moderate-to-severe TBI, and findings from one severity group should not be assumed to generalize to another. Furthermore, evidence directly obtained from patients with persistent PTH remains more limited than evidence derived from broader TBI populations. Throughout this article, we therefore distinguish PTH-specific findings from mechanisms that remain biologically plausible on the basis of the broader TBI literature.Acute TBI severity remains a major determinant of early clinical outcomes. Measures such as the GCS, pupillary reactivity, and structural imaging findings are strongly associated with mortality and functional disability and remain fundamental for clinical decision-making and prognostic assessment (1,2,10). However, these measures were primarily developed to characterize the initial injury and estimate acute outcomes, and their ability to account for persistent symptoms and heterogeneous longterm recovery trajectories is more limited (11,12).Patients with apparently similar initial injury characteristics may experience markedly different longterm outcomes, including persistent headache, fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, emotional symptoms, and reduced quality of life (11,12). This variability suggests that the extent and characteristics of the initial injury alone do not fully capture the processes associated with long-term recovery.TBI initiates a cascade of biological events that may extend beyond the acute phase (7-9). Among these processes, neuroinflammation has been extensively investigated. Acute activation of microglia and astrocytes contributes to tissue responses following injury, whereas sustained or dysregulated inflammatory activity has been associated with blood-brain barrier alterations, persistent inflammatory signaling, and changes in neuronal function (7)(8)(9)(17)(18)(19). Importantly, evidence of persistent neuroinflammation after TBI derives predominantly from experimental studies and broader TBI populations and should not be interpreted as evidence that neuroinflammation directly causes persistent PTH. Rather, it provides a biologically plausible framework that requires specific validation in patients with persistent PTH.Altered nociceptive processing may represent another relevant mechanism. Central sensitization should be distinguished from nociplastic pain and other forms of altered nociceptive signaling because these concepts are related but not interchangeable (20,21). PTH-specific studies have identified sensory abnormalities, including cephalic allodynia, hyperalgesia, and altered pain modulatory responses, supporting abnormal nociceptive processing in at least a subset of patients with persistent PTH (22). Experimental evidence of hypersensitivity to calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) further supports the involvement of CGRP-related nociceptive pathways (23). However, these findings neither establish central sensitization as a universal mechanism nor demonstrate a single pathophysiological pathway underlying persistent PTH.A complementary perspective is provided by network neuroscience, which conceptualizes neurological dysfunction as potentially arising from disturbances in interactions among distributed brain networks rather than exclusively from focal structural damage (13)(14)(15). TBI studies have demonstrated persistent structural network abnormalities during recovery (24), while PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have identified alterations in resting-state functional connectivity involving pain-processing, painmodulatory, and affective networks (25,26). These findings provide more direct, although still limited, evidence that persistent PTH may be associated with alterations in brain network function.Persistent PTH also frequently co-occurs with fatigue, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbances, emotional symptoms, and reduced quality of life (4)(5)(6). Rather than representing different expressions of a single persistent biological condition, these manifestations may arise from partially overlapping, independent, or mutually reinforcing mechanisms. Their co-occurrence therefore underscores the heterogeneity of post-traumatic recovery and the need to investigate how different biological and functional processes contribute to individual symptom profiles.Within the framework proposed here, persistent PTH is considered a potential clinical window into persistent brain dysfunction rather than a validated biomarker, prognostic indicator, or surrogate measure of an underlying biological process. We use the term clinical window to describe an observable clinical feature whose persistence may signal the need to investigate ongoing functional or biological abnormalities that are not fully captured by conventional structural assessment. Thus, persistent PTH is proposed primarily as a clinical signal for further investigation, not as evidence that a specific pathophysiological process is present.We use the term persistent brain dysfunction as an umbrella concept encompassing ongoing abnormalities in neural function or biological processes after TBI, including altered nociceptive processing, disturbances in brain network function, and potentially persistent inflammatory activity. This definition does not imply a single mechanism, nor does it assume that these abnormalities are present in all individuals with persistent PTH or that persistent PTH is caused by any one of them.The distinction is important because the evidence supporting these potential mechanisms varies substantially. PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have demonstrated alterations in resting-state functional connectivity involving pain-processing and pain-modulatory networks, including periaqueductal gray-related connectivity, with some alterations associated with headache burden or the subsequent development of persistent PTH (25,26). By contrast, evidence for persistent neuroinflammation and several other chronic neurobiological abnormalities derives predominantly from broader TBI populations. These mechanisms should therefore be regarded as biologically plausible contributors requiring direct investigation in persistent PTH rather than as established pathophysiological correlates of the condition.Persistent PTH may also reflect greater overall symptom burden rather than a distinct biological state.Headache commonly co-occurs with sleep disturbance, fatigue, cognitive complaints, anxiety, depression, and other post-traumatic symptoms (4-6), and these factors may independently influence both headache persistence and measures of brain function. Pre-existing headache disorders, injury severity, medication use, cervical or extracranial pain generators, and psychological and behavioral factors may further contribute to clinical heterogeneity. Consequently, the presence or severity of persistent PTH cannot currently be assumed to indicate the presence, type, or magnitude of persistent brain dysfunction.Testing the proposed clinical-window hypothesis will therefore require prospective studies that combine detailed headache phenotyping with objective measures of brain function and biology while accounting for relevant confounding factors. Quantitative electroencephalography, neuroimagingderived connectivity measures, and molecular or inflammatory measures are candidate approaches that could be evaluated in this context (24,27,28,31). Artificial intelligence and machine-learning methods may complement these measures as analytical approaches for identifying multidimensional patterns or patient phenotypes, rather than representing biological or functional measures themselves (29,30).At present, none of these candidate approaches can be considered a validated biomarker of persistent PTH. Their value lies in testing whether persistent PTH is systematically associated with measurable patterns of post-traumatic dysfunction beyond headache severity and overall symptom burden.The hypothesis proposed in this article should be interpreted within several important limitations. First, evidence directly linking persistent PTH to measurable ongoing brain dysfunction remains limited.Although PTH-specific neuroimaging studies have identified alterations in functional connectivity (25,26), much of the evidence supporting persistent neuroinflammation, neurophysiological abnormalities, and other chronic biological processes derives from broader TBI populations. Extrapolation of these findings to persistent PTH therefore requires caution, and associations observed after TBI should not be assumed to represent mechanisms of persistent PTH.Second, persistent PTH is clinically and biologically heterogeneous. Headache phenotype, pre-existing headache disorders, TBI severity, sleep disturbance, fatigue, psychological symptoms, medication use, cervical or extracranial pain generators, and other post-traumatic symptoms may influence both headache persistence and measures of brain function. These factors provide alternative or complementary explanations for associations between persistent PTH and biological or functional abnormalities. Consequently, future studies should determine whether such associations remain after appropriate characterization and adjustment for relevant confounding factors.The proposed clinical-window hypothesis also generates testable predictions. If persistent PTH is associated with ongoing post-traumatic dysfunction beyond overall symptom burden, individuals with persistent PTH should demonstrate reproducible functional or biological abnormalities when compared with appropriately matched TBI survivors without persistent PTH. These associations should remain detectable after accounting for injury severity, pre-existing headache, headache phenotype, psychological symptoms, sleep disturbance, medication use, and other relevant clinical factors.Longitudinal studies should further determine whether changes in headache frequency, intensity, or disability are accompanied by changes in candidate neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or molecular measures.Conversely, failure to identify reproducible associations between persistent PTH and objective measures of post-traumatic dysfunction, particularly after controlling for symptom burden and relevant confounders, would argue against the proposed clinical-window hypothesis or restrict its applicability to specific patient subgroups. This possibility is important because the framework proposed here should be considered a testable hypothesis rather than an assumption that persistent headache necessarily reflects ongoing brain dysfunction.Future research should therefore prioritize prospective longitudinal designs with detailed headache phenotyping and appropriate comparison groups. Studies comparing TBI survivors with persistent PTH, TBI survivors without persistent PTH, and, where appropriate, individuals with primary headache disorders may help determine which findings are related specifically to persistent PTH, to TBI more broadly, or to chronic headache irrespective of trauma. Stratification by mild TBI and moderate-to-severe TBI will also be necessary because mechanisms and recovery trajectories may differ across injury severity.Multimodal studies integrating clinical phenotyping with neuroimaging, quantitative electroencephalography, and molecular measures may help determine whether reproducible patterns of dysfunction can be identified in specific persistent PTH subgroups. Artificial intelligence and machine-learning approaches may support the analysis of these multidimensional datasets and the identification of patient phenotypes, but their role is analytical and depends on the quality and validation of the underlying clinical and biological measures (24,(27)(28)(29)(30)(31). Candidate measures should not be considered biomarkers until their reproducibility, specificity, longitudinal behavior, and clinical relevance have been established in persistent PTH populations.Ultimately, the value of the proposed framework will depend on whether persistent PTH provides clinically meaningful information beyond established measures of injury severity and overall posttraumatic symptom burden. Prospective validation is therefore required before persistent PTH can be used to identify individuals for additional biological assessment, prognostic stratification, or mechanism-based interventions. Persistent PTH may provide a clinically accessible signal for investigating ongoing functional or biological abnormalities after TBI, but this relationship remains hypothetical and should not be interpreted as evidence that persistent headache is itself a biomarker of brain dysfunction.Distinguishing PTH-specific findings from abnormalities associated with TBI more broadly, controlling for alternative explanations and confounding factors, and prospectively testing the proposed associations will be essential to determine the validity and clinical relevance of this framework.

papers.title: Functional brain activity in cancer-related cognitive impairment: a scoping review of EEG studies
papers.authors: Barbara Johanne Thomas Nordhjem, Laura Maria Toftekær Rothschild, Clotilde Rose Honoré, Anders Thyge Steen Larsen, Martin Kaj Fridh, Lisa Lyngsie Hjalgrim
papers.abstract: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) is reported across the cancer trajectory, yet its neurobiological basis remains incompletely understood. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a temporally precise method for assessing brain activity at rest and during cognitive processing, but its application in CRCI research has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review characterized how EEG has been used to study cognitive functioning in people with cancer, including populations studied, EEG paradigms and analytic approaches employed, and cognitive outcomes assessed. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to February 2025 for studies using EEG to examine cognitive functioning. Sixty articles were included. Most were small and cross-sectional, with publication output increasing markedly after 2015. Task-based event-related potentials, particularly from oddball and attention tasks, were used most frequently, whereas quantitative EEG approaches, including spectral power and connectivity analyses, were less common. In populations with cancers outside the central nervous system (CNS), longer P300 latency and lower amplitude were common, but opposite and null findings also occurred. Evidence from primary CNS and other intracranial tumor populations was sparse. Across cancer contexts, quantitative EEG findings showed limited convergence across articles. Associations between EEG measures and cognitive outcomes were inconsistent and often not tested directly. Overall, EEG provides a complementary approach to investigating cognition in people with cancer, but the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. Larger longitudinal studies, more consistent cognitive outcome selection, and closer integration of neural and cognitive measures are needed to establish reproducible findings and evaluate their potential clinical utility. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251084951 .

papers.title: Mapping generative AI in higher education teaching and learning: a scoping review
papers.authors: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel Chang, Philip H. Winne, Gervase Michael Bowen, Jeeho Ryoo
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered higher education, but empirical research on its roles in teaching and learning remains fragmented across instructional activities, outcomes, assessment approaches, and stakeholder perspectives. This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map 394 empirical studies of GenAI use in higher education published from November 2022 through December 2025. The review examined how GenAI tools were integrated into authentic teaching and learning activities, what outcomes or skills were targeted, how studies assessed those outcomes, and how students and instructors perceived GenAI use. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI was most often used to support existing academic tasks, especially feedback, tutoring, and writing. The most frequently targeted outcomes included engagement, usability and acceptance, critical thinking, disciplinary knowledge, academic performance, writing quality, and AI literacy. Self-regulated learning, ethics, creativity, feedback quality, and equity received less attention. Assessment practices relied mainly on surveys, tests or rubrics, artifact analysis, and interviews, suggesting that much of the evidence base is shaped by short-term and readily implemented methods. Student and instructor perceptions were predominantly mixed, reflecting perceived benefits alongside concerns about pedagogy, integrity, workload, and governance. The review highlights the need for stronger alignment between learning constructs and assessment methods, more process-sensitive evidence, clearer reporting of governance practices, and greater attention to equity in GenAI-supported higher education. Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00630-9.

papers.title: Individualized Theta Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation Modulates Mnemonic Discrimination and ERP Responses to Positive Information in Individuals With Elevated Depressive Symptoms
papers.authors: Xinyu Huang, Min Zhou, Chun Wang, Yuxin Huang, Wenchang Wang, Jianfei Shao, Junyu Mao, Jiaqi Li, Zhang Lei, Rong Ye, Chunyan Zhu, Yanghua Tian, Kongliang He, 余凤琼, Kai Wang
papers.abstract: Individuals with elevated depressive symptoms often show impairments in positive memory processing. This randomized, double-blind study investigated whether individualized theta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) using an OFC-oriented montage modulates mnemonic discrimination and ERP responses to positive information. Sixty-one individuals with elevated depressive symptoms received either real or sham stimulation before completing an emotional mnemonic discrimination task. Behavioral results showed that lure discrimination increased following real stimulation but not sham stimulation. EEG results showed that real stimulation modulated ERP responses during positive memory encoding and retrieval, as reflected by increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes during encoding and altered early retrieval-related ERP amplitudes. These findings suggest that individualized theta-tACS may influence both mnemonic discrimination performance and neural responses to positive information.

papers.title: From digital interaction to social connection: AI virtual humans as interactive learning partners for older adults
papers.authors: WeiCheng Pan, WanQing Zhang, Hong Chen, Qi Guo, Shuyi Wang, Hesen Li
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational and social interaction systems, its potential to alleviate digital exclusion and digital loneliness among older adults has attracted growing attention. Across two independent experiments, this study examined the association between AI-assisted interaction and digital loneliness among older adults, as well as the underlying psychological mechanisms. In Experiment 1, 90 older adults participated in a four-week randomized longitudinal experiment. A 2 (group) × 5 (time) mixed-design repeated-measures analysis of variance was conducted to compare changes in digital loneliness between an AI-assisted interaction group and a conventional interaction control group. The results showed that participants in the AI-assisted interaction group exhibited a more pronounced reduction in digital loneliness over the intervention period. Experiment 2 involved an independent sample of 210 participants and used PROCESS analyses to examine further the roles of perceived social support, evaluative emotional fulfillment, and technology acceptance. After controlling for baseline digital loneliness, perceived social support constituted a significant indirect pathway linking AI-assisted interaction to post-intervention digital loneliness, whereas the indirect effect through evaluative emotional fulfillment did not reach statistical significance. Technology acceptance further moderated the association between AI-assisted interaction and perceived social support. Taken together, these findings suggest that the association between AI-assisted interaction and reduced digital loneliness among older adults is primarily related to the perceived social support pathway. In contrast, evidence supporting the mediating role of evaluative emotional fulfillment remains insufficient. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding older adults’ experiences of social connectedness in inclusive AI-enabled environments. It underscores the importance of enhancing both the acceptability of AI-mediated interaction and its capacity to provide social support within educational and digital learning ecosystems.

papers.title: The Blurring of Reality in the Age of AI: Development of the AI-Induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale and Its Association with Generative AI Literacy and AI Anxiety
papers.authors: BİLAL KAYA, Sezen Ateş Yaman
papers.abstract: This study sought to develop the AI-induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale (AI-RPCS) and investigate the mediating role of AI-induced reality perception confusion in the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. In Study I (N = 355), exploratory factor analysis revealed a single-factor structure, and item response theory indicated that the items displayed high discrimination and suitable difficulty. In Study II (N = 332), confirmatory factor analysis indicated satisfactory model fit indices for the single-factor structure. Significant relationships among the variables supported criterion validity. In Study III (N = 408), structural equation modelling indicated that AI-induced reality perception confusion mediated the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. These results demonstrate the AI-RPCS's initial psychometric validity. Furthermore, this study suggests that GenAI literacy may be associated with lower levels of AI-induced reality perception confusion, which may, in turn, be associated with lower levels of AI anxiety.

papers.title: Measuring Successful Cooperation in Human-AI Teamwork: Development and Validation of the Perceived Cooperativity and Teaming Perception Scales
papers.authors: Christiane Attig, Christiane B. Wiebel-Herboth, Patricia Wollstadt, Tim Schrills, Mourad Zoubir, Thomas Franke
papers.abstract: As human–AI cooperation becomes increasingly prevalent, reliable instruments for assessing the subjective quality of cooperative human–AI interaction are needed. We introduce two theoretically grounded scales: the Perceived Cooperativity Scale (PCS), grounded in joint activity theory, and the Teaming Perception Scale (TPS), grounded in evolutionary cooperation theory. The PCS captures an agent’s perceived cooperative capability and practice within a single interaction sequence; the TPS captures the emergent sense of teaming arising from mutual contribution and support. Both scales were adapted for human–human cooperation to enable cross-agent comparisons. Across three studies (complete N=409) encompassing a cooperative card game (N1=94), LLM interaction (N2=182), and a decision-support system (N3=133), analyses of dimensionality, reliability, and validity indicated that both scales successfully differentiated between cooperation partners of varying cooperative quality and showed construct validity in line with expectations. The scales provide a basis for empirical investigation and system evaluation across a wide range of human–AI cooperation contexts.

papers.title: Social robots in the real world: an analysis of social robot use based on consumer reviews
papers.authors: Katarzyna Kabacińska, Gabriella K. Guerra, Mallorie T. Tam, Julie M. Robillard
papers.abstract: Social robots (SR) are increasingly developed to support users’ mental health needs. Previous research suggests that potential benefits of interacting with SR include reduction in depressive symptoms, loneliness and improved quality of life. Despite the promising impact of short-term robot use, little is known about how SRs are used beyond short interaction in the research environment, and what spontaneous robot adoption looks like. Thus, in this study we set out to address this gap through an analysis of user-generated robot reviews. We analysed online reviews of commercially available SRs to characterise their impact and user experience. We used qualitative content analysis to extract salient themes from 1350 user-generated reviews, supplemented by sentiment analysis of the full sample of 9333 reviews. The content analysis revealed a list of SR use cases, user circumstances and characteristics, the impact of using the robots and ethical challenges experienced by users. The results suggest that self-reported benefits, such as improved mood, reduced depression and loneliness, are maintained through long-term robot use. This study provides a novel qualitative insight into user experiences and SR use in the real world that will inform future robotic development and implementation efforts.

papers.title: Beyond accuracy: How humans evaluate legally correct but socially controversial legal advice from machines.
papers.authors: Benjamin Minhao Chen, Zhiyu Li
papers.abstract: AI systems are increasingly used to provide legal advice, raising questions about whether laypeople accept guidance from algorithms-especially when that advice is legally correct but socially controversial.We report a preregistered survey experiment with 3,348 adults in mainland China examining how people evaluate identical legal advice when it is attributed either to an AI system or to a human lawyer and when it is accompanied by reasoning or not.Contrary to expectations of algorithm aversion, attribution to an AI system has no net effect on perceived reasonableness.However, mediation analyses reveal opposing psychological pathways underlying this null result.AI-attributed advice is perceived as more objective, which increases perceived reasonableness, but also as less comprehensive and less attentive to special circumstances, which decreases perceived reasonableness.By contrast, providing legal reasoning substantially increases perceived reasonableness regardless of source, largely by enhancing perceptions of objectivity.Qualitative responses corroborate this tension between objectivity and contextual sensitivity in evaluations of legal advice.Together, these findings suggest that public responses to AI legal advisors are shaped not by rigid attitudes toward automation but by the balancing of competing normative expectations.The results have implications for theories of algorithm aversion and the design of AI recommendation systems in normatively salient domains.

papers.title: Task-evoked brain network dynamics underlying executive function in preadolescent children
papers.authors: Alfia Parvez, Shreya Verma, Ruyu Liu, Ginger E. Reeser, Sean Patrick Mullen, Lauren B. Raine, Lisa M. Renzi‐Hammond, Charles H. Hillman, Naiman A. Khan
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Executive function (EF) has been studied using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) based functional connectivity (FC); however, electroencephalography (EEG) based dynamic FC interactions supporting EF in children and explaining behavioral performance remain underexplored. We used EEG to examine FC within and between seven core brain networks: Default Mode (DMN), Dorsal Attention (DAN), Ventral Attention (VAN), Somatomotor (SMN), Frontoparietal (FPN), Visual (VIN), and Limbic (LIN), during a modified Eriksen flanker task. We aimed to identify dynamic network configurations linked to EF, specifically selective attention and inhibitory control in preadolescent children (8-10 years). METHODS: Secondary analyses of source-localized EEG data from 84 children (mean age 8.89 ± 0.82 years; 51.2% female) were conducted. A Hidden Markov model extracted spatiotemporal dynamics, quantifying within- and between-network FC correlations. Support vector regression (SVR) with an interpretable kernel identified connectivity patterns predicting behavioral outcomes, including accuracy and reaction time (RT) interference. RESULTS: = 0.26). Behavioral performance indices were most strongly associated with interference within VAN, DMN, SMN, and VIN. Notably, within-VAN FC explained between-subject variability in both Accuracy Interference (ρ = -0.28, p = 0.012) and RT Interference (r = 0.26, p = 0.017). CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic, task-based FC, particularly within-VAN, underpins individual differences in EF among preadolescent children. Stronger within-VAN reconfiguration during high cognitive demand trials supported accuracy but at the cost of slower responses, highlighting a trade-off between stability and efficiency in developing EF.

papers.title: Investigating secondary school students’ shared epistemic agency with GAI in online scientific explanation writing
papers.authors: Hsin‐Yi Chang, Bo-Ren Mau, Jyh-Chong Liang, Chin‐Chung Tsai
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used as a pedagogical assistant in online learning; yet how young students, such as secondary school students, enact epistemic agency (EA) when learning with GAI remains underexplored. In this study, we examined the types and levels of EA demonstrated by secondary school students with scaffolded GAI and investigated the relation among students’ prior academic proficiency, self-efficacy in learning, and EA demonstrated. Participants were 122 seventh graders who engaged in an online bilingual inquiry unit on photosynthesis. The unit supports students in Taiwan in learning science inquiry and English as a foreign language, with GAI prompted and integrated to support students’ scientific explanation writing in English. Data collected and analyzed included students’ prior academic proficiency through assessments, self-efficacy in learning through questionnaires, and student–GAI conversation turns through textual conversation logs. Results identified seven types of student–GAI shared epistemic agency (SEA), with over 80% of students demonstrating such agency at least once. Correlation results indicated that the frequency of EA demonstrated by students was associated with their prior language proficiency. Cluster analysis with the retained four-profile solution further suggested that student–GAI SEA was likely to be activity-specific. The identified SEA categories provide a framework for examining student–GAI SEA, and the instruction design illustrates how GAI can be prompted to preserve opportunities for student contribution. Design implications for supporting students with different needs are discussed.

papers.title: Bridging accuracy and interpretability in predictive learning analytics: A human-centered grey-box approach
papers.authors: Ángel Hernández-García, Julián Chaparro-Peláez, Carlos Cuenca-Enrique, Carlos Salcedo-Valverde
papers.abstract: Learning analytics has been increasingly using predictive models to support educational decision-making. However, the trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability remains a central challenge that limits how these models can be understood and used by educators. This study examines grey-box approaches to performance prediction by comparing two strategies: a theory-driven approach that groups interaction data into pedagogically meaningful categories, and a data-driven approach based on raw clickstream events followed by post hoc eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques. Using clickstream data from three educational contexts with different scales and instructional formats, we empirically compare the predictive performance, interpretability, and pedagogical relevance of both strategies. The results show that raw-event models achieve higher predictive performance in the large-scale online context with rich interaction data, where XAI methods provide relatively stable and consistent explanatory patterns. In the smaller-scale blended setting, where platform data capture only part of the learning activity, theory-driven aggregation provides a predictive advantage, although results become inconclusive in very small cohorts. The findings indicate that there is no single optimal approach, and that modeling strategies should be selected according to data characteristics, instructional design, and analytic goals. From a human-centered learning analytics perspective, the study highlights the importance of methodological alignment for the meaningful and responsible use of predictive models in education.

papers.title: Does AI encourage lax thinking, or does the human preference for validation make it that way?
papers.authors: Braden T. Hall, William Hart

papers.title: Writing Motivation and Self‐Efficacy in AI ‐Chatbot‐Supported EFL Writing: Exploratory Insights Across Proficiency Levels
papers.authors: Thi-Ngoc-Anh Duong, Hsiu‐Ling Chen
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Writing motivation and self‐efficacy are critical factors of success in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts, yet they are frequently undermined by learner anxiety and limited teacher feedback. While artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots offer potential for adaptive writing support, limited research has examined these affective constructs in parallel across learner proficiency levels. Objectives This study investigated changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy among high school EFL learners at higher‐ and lower‐proficiency levels following chatbot‐supported writing and examined whether these changes differed across proficiency levels. Methods Using an exploratory mixed‐methods design, the study involved 47 Vietnamese high school students divided into higher‐ and lower‐proficiency level groups. Over the 11‐week study, participants completed 8 weeks of AI‐supported writing activities using a chatbot designed in accordance with principles of Self‐Determination Theory, Self‐Regulated Learning Theory and Self‐Efficacy Theory. Changes in intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy were examined using pre‐ and post‐questionnaires and semi‐structured interviews. Results and Conclusions The quantitative findings revealed that intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and writing self‐efficacy increased over time in both proficiency groups, with no significant differences in the magnitude of change between higher‐ and lower‐proficiency learners. This suggests that the affective changes observed during AI‐supported writing were not confined to one proficiency group. The qualitative findings indicated that learners linked their positive experiences to reduced anxiety, clearer guidance, and supportive interaction, although the types of support they valued differed by proficiency level. Overall, the findings suggest that when positioned as a supportive writing partner rather than an answer generator, AI chatbot feedback may be associated with positive motivational and self‐efficacy development in mixed‐ability EFL writing classrooms.

papers.title: Frustrative nonreward engages midfrontal theta power and modulates effort expenditure
papers.authors: Nellia Bellaert, Federico Cassioli, Wan-Ling Tseng, Mandy Rossignol
papers.abstract: Irritability is characterized by a propensity to experience frustration and has been associated with reduced self-reported willingness to expend effort for rewards. Frustration may be relevant to effortful reward pursuit, but its effects on effort expenditure have rarely been experimentally tested in humans. To address this gap, this study introduced a frustration induction in the Effort-Doors task to elicit frustrative nonreward (FNR), a negative emotional state triggered by unexpected reward loss, and examined its effects on physical effort expenditure and feedback-related electroencephalographic (EEG) activity. We also tested whether these effects vary as a function of state and trait measures of motivation and affect. Linear mixed-effects models tested the effects of FNR induction on self-reported, behavioral, and EEG measures in young adults (N = 83) completing the Frustrative Effort-Doors task. Models tested manipulation effects, trial-level post-feedback adjustment, and moderation by state and trait measures. Midfrontal theta power (MFθ) extracted using multivariate spatial filtering was examined as a function of feedback (win vs. FNR), effort (low vs. high), and subsequent behavioral adjustments. The frustration condition was associated with decreased self-reported state motivation and increased frustration, arousal, and response speed. Midfrontal theta power was larger following FNR feedback and increased with state frustration during high-effort trials. Higher state frustration was associated with reduced response vigor during effort execution following FNR feedback. MFθ did not predict trial-to-trial behavioral adjustments. These findings indicate that FNR recruits MFθ, a neural marker of cognitive control, while state frustration modulates physical effort execution following unexpected reward loss.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence literacy profiles differ in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being among adolescents
papers.authors: Ja-Yeoung Lee
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly important for adolescents, yet variation in literacy across multiple dimensions and its associations with educational and psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study identified generative AI literacy profiles among Korean adolescents with generative AI experience ( N = 3,959) using K-means cluster analysis based on information evaluation, communication, creative use, and ethical use. Two profiles were identified: Higher AI Literacy and Lower AI Literacy. The profiles differed primarily in their overall literacy levels rather than in qualitatively distinct patterns across the four dimensions. Adolescents in the Higher AI Literacy profile reported greater generative AI education experience and higher academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being than those in the Lower AI Literacy profile. Differences in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being remained significant after adjustment for gender, school level, academic achievement, and economic status. These findings demonstrate meaningful level-based variation in generative AI literacy among adolescents with generative AI experience and suggest that such variation is associated with educational experience and academic and psychological outcomes. A person-centred perspective may complement variable-centred approaches and inform future research and educational approaches that consider differences in students’ generative AI literacy levels.

papers.title: How generative AI becomes embedded in design learning: a 14-instructional-day intensive longitudinal study of reciprocal dynamics between AI use and self-efficacy
papers.authors: Yang Li, Yi Yang, Silu Bao
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design education, yet little is known about how students’ daily engagement with generative AI is dynamically associated with their learning-related capability beliefs across successive instructional days. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examined the reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between daily generative AI use in design learning and daily design-learning self-efficacy, and further investigated whether baseline hassles were associated with individual differences in these dynamics. A 14-instructional-day diary study was conducted with 260 Chinese undergraduate design students, yielding 3,558 observed person-day assessments out of 3,640 possible assessments. Daily generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy were assessed throughout the diary period, whereas hassles were measured at baseline. The data were analyzed using bivariate dynamic structural equation modeling within a Bayesian estimation framework. The results showed significant autoregressive effects for daily generative AI use ( β = 0.198, 95% CrI [0.154, 0.237]) and daily design-learning self-efficacy ( β = 0.138, 95% CrI [0.100, 0.175]). At the within-person level, higher-than-usual generative AI use on one instructional day positively predicted design-learning self-efficacy on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.043, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.077]), while higher-than-usual design-learning self-efficacy also positively predicted generative AI use on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.059, 95% CrI [0.023, 0.095]). At the between-person level, greater baseline hassles were associated with higher average generative AI use ( β = 0.135), lower average design-learning self-efficacy ( β = −0.254), and a stronger cross-lagged association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy ( β = 0.458). Gender did not significantly predict the main random effects. These findings indicate modest reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy, suggesting that the two may reinforce one another across instructional days. The stronger association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy among students reporting greater baseline hassles further suggests that contextual demands may shape how generative AI becomes integrated into students’ day-to-day design learning.

papers.title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
papers.authors: Usman Rehman
papers.abstract: Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

papers.title: Academic emotions and perceived learning outcomes in GenAI-supported learning: the serial mediating roles of AI acceptance and learning behaviors
papers.authors: Huaruo Chen, Gefan Wang, Zhentao Peng, Wanru Song, Jie Xu
papers.abstract: Objective With the widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, academic emotions play a vital role in students’ learning processes. This study aims to examine the associations between positive and negative academic emotions and college students’ perceived learning outcomes, and analyze the serial mediating roles of AI acceptance and learning behaviors within GenAI-supported learning environments. Methods A total of 526 college students with GenAI learning experience were recruited via convenience sampling. All participants completed four standardized scales measuring academic emotions, AI acceptance, learning behaviors and perceived learning outcomes. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, confirmatory factor analysis and bias-corrected Bootstrap mediation tests were conducted using SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 27.0. Results All variables were significantly correlated ( p < 0.01). Positive academic emotions exerted a significant direct association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.176), whereas the direct association of negative academic emotions was non-significant ( β = −0.098, p = 0.049, 95% CI [−0.205, 0.007]). AI acceptance and learning behaviors had significant independent mediating effects. The serial mediation effect value was 0.020 for positive emotions and −0.037 for negative emotions, with all 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Indirect pathways dominated the influence of negative academic emotions. Conclusion This study identifies a pattern of associations consistent with the hypothesized emotion-cognition-behavior-outcome pathway in GenAI-supported learning. The findings offer empirical evidence for developing targeted academic-emotion-informed intervention strategies, improving students’ AI acceptance and learning engagement, and promoting the high-quality development of intelligent education.

papers.title: Needs and current status of generative artificial intelligence use among college students: a cross-sectional survey based in China
papers.authors: Rong Zeng, 雷春涛, Qian Jiang, Xueqin Gan, Xiaoguo Zhang, Yu Feng, Qin Xu, Yan Huang, Yang Qian
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the current status of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) usage needs among vocational college students from China, explore their relationships with learning engagement and academic resilience, and identify variables associated with GAI usage demand. Methods Using convenience sampling, 3,876 students from five vocational colleges in Sichuan Province were enrolled. Surveys were conducted using the Generative Artificial Intelligence Application Status and Usage Demand Scale, the Learning Engagement Scale, and the Academic Resilience Scale. Results The average GAI needs score among vocational college students was 58.23 ± 12.77. Correlation analysis revealed positive relationships between GAI needs and both learning engagement and academic resilience ( p < 0.01). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that gender, academic year, availability of GAI learning devices at home, level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, frequency of active GAI use, student-reported frequency of teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, learning engagement, and academic resilience were independently associated with GAI usage demand (all p < 0.05). The model explained 24.4% of the variance in GAI usage demand [ R 2 = 0.244, adjusted R 2 = 0.241, F (14, 3,861) = 88.932, p < 0.001]. Conclusion Vocational college students’ GAI usage demand was slightly above the theoretical midpoint of the scale.
