Greater GAI usage demand was independently associated with male gender, earlier academic year, better availability of GAI learning devices at home, a higher level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, more frequent active GAI use, more frequent student-reported teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, higher learning engagement, and greater academic resilience. Because of the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships.

papers.title: Comprehensive artificial intelligence-assisted mental health program for university students in China (CAMPUS): study protocol for a multi-center prospective cohort with planned embedded randomized intervention trials
papers.authors: Guang Yang, Rongxun Liu, Chuansheng Wang, Rongxin Zhu, Shisen Qin, Jinnan Yan, Yan Wang, Hongbo Pei, Lijuan Liang, Yingying Su, Shuai Wang, Weidong Wu, Guangjun Ji, Fei Wang, Wei Yange
papers.abstract: University students face a rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal ideation that exceeds the capacity of conventional, resource-constrained campus support services. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools have emerged, many have evaluated selected modalities or isolated prediction tasks, and their integration with prospectively evaluated intervention pathways remains limited. This protocol describes the Comprehensive Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mental Health Program for University Students in China (CAMPUS), a multi-center research program comprising a five-year prospective cohort, eight planned embedded randomized controlled trials, and exploratory multimodal AI and multi-omics studies across seven Chinese universities. Longitudinal cohort enrolment commenced at Henan Medical University in September 2025 and is planned to expand across seven participating universities. Multidimensional screening integrates psychological self-report (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, BSI-CV, and others), physiological measurements (EEG, MRI, fNIRS, HRV, eye tracking, facial-expression analysis, ERP, voice acoustics), and an exploratory biospecimen component for multi-omics profiling, potentially including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome analyses, subject to the finalization and approval of layer-specific protocols. Students identified through cohort screening as potentially eligible for an intervention trial will undergo trial-specific eligibility assessment. Those who meet the eligibility criteria and provide trial-specific informed consent will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or its comparator within one of eight separate two-arm, multi-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trials. A Transformer-based multimodal AI framework with SHAP-based feature attribution will be developed and internally evaluated for questionnaire-defined risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. The initial Henan Medical University cohort recruitment and university-student mental-health assessment were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Henan Medical University (XYLL-20250484), and written informed consent is obtained from participants before enrolment. Each additional participating center will obtain local ethics approval before study activation. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences, and policy briefs, providing evidence that may inform the design and prospective evaluation of youth mental-health programs in other university settings. Clinical trial registration The two clinical trials were registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR). The registration details and URLs are as follows: ChiCTR2500113527: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298271 ; ChiCTR2500113613: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298268 .

papers.title: The study of Chinese EFL teachers' emotions in the digital transformation of education
papers.authors: Feng Wu, Youjie Hua
papers.abstract: Introduction The rapid and continuing development of digital technologies has significantly reshaped the educational landscape, generating diverse emotional experiences among teachers. This study examined the emotional experiences of Chinese EFL teachers and the major antecedents of those emotions. Methods This study employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. First, questionnaire data collected from 296 university EFL teachers identified five primary emotions (love, joy, anger, sadness, and fear). Secondly, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 participants to explore the antecedents underlying these emotional experiences. The qualitative findings were subsequently integrated with the quantitative results and presented through a joint display. Results The findings showed that EFL teachers experienced positive emotions more frequently than negative emotions. Of the five primary emotions, joy and love had the highest mean scores, followed by fear, anger, and sadness, respectively. The findings further showed that teachers' emotions were closely associated with their professional goals and students' performance. Several antecedents were found to shape these emotional experiences. The flexibility, interactivity, and innovative opportunities introduced by digital transformation enhanced EFL teachers' sense of love for their work. Likewise, the efficiency and abundance of resources provided by digital tools and platforms contributed to their sense of joy. In contrast, students' misconduct and dishonest behaviors often provoked feelings of anger. Teachers experienced sadness when confronted with students' lack of critical thinking and when they felt inadequately supported in their work. Fear was primarily driven by peer pressure, time constraints, and the threat of being replaced by artificial intelligence. Discussion The study discussed the implications of these findings and proposed recommendations for emotion regulation and emotional support for EFL teachers in China and comparable educational contexts.

papers.title: Can large language models reproduce humans’ perspective-dependent judgements of gratitude? Evidence from Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Doubao
papers.authors: Wenjun Chen, Yujie Chu, Xiaoming Jiang, Yan Li
papers.abstract: Human social interaction is full of episodes of help, and the person giving it and the person receiving it may not interpret the same episode in the same way. Against a background of reports that large language models match or exceed human performance on social reasoning tasks, this study asks whether they reproduce this asymmetry between the two sides. Forty-eight Chinese university students read 24 everyday helping scenarios, each in four situational versions, from either the beneficiary’s or the benefactor’s side, and rated the helper’s willingness, the recipient’s need, the difficulty of helping, and the recipient’s gratitude. The identical Chinese materials were then given to 12 models, the flagship and the light model of three providers based in English-speaking countries and three based in China, with 30 independent runs per text, followed by two further prompt conditions: the same scenarios in English for the six models of the Chinese providers and a stated identity prepended to the prompt for all 12. Bayesian mixed models showed a dissociation. On what the situation called for, the models mostly matched the humans or exceeded them: the contrast between a pressing need and one already met was 1.325 scale points in the humans and 1.159 to 1.825 across models, above the human value in 11 of 12. On which side the episode was judged from, most fell short: the humans rated gratitude 0.756 points higher from the beneficiary’s side, the models 0.047 to 0.727, with 11 of 12 credibly below the human estimate. Only Doubao-2.1-Pro matched the humans on gratitude, and it departed from them on willingness and difficulty. Capability tier ordered the 12, though the contrast did not exclude zero, while the provider’s country did not order them at all. Among the six models of the Chinese providers, writing the scenarios in English raised the effect in five, though not to the human estimate. Likewise, across all 12, stating an identity raised it in 10, by 0.10 on average against a mean shortfall of 0.44, and 11 of 12 still sat below the human estimate. Our results suggest that large language models, at least those surveyed here, read what a situation calls for at a level comparable to human readers, but that they show markedly less sensitivity to perspective, namely to the asymmetry with which benefactors and beneficiaries evaluate one and the same act of help.

papers.title: Stress-related helplessness is independently associated with reward-driven eating in adults with BMI-defined normal weight and obesity
papers.authors: Imke Schamarek, Peter Louis Kovacs, Michael Stümvoll, Matthias Blüher, Anke Tönjes, Kerstin Rohde‐Zimmermann
papers.abstract: Background Accumulating evidence indicates that stress is associated with reward-driven eating, yet the stress dimensions underlying this relationship remain insufficiently understood. Inconsistent findings may partly reflect conceptualizing stress as a unitary construct and insufficient consideration of weight status. This study examined the independent associations of perceived stress dimensions (Helplessness, Self-Efficacy) with hedonic hunger, trait food craving, and uncontrolled eating in adults with BMI-defined normal weight and obesity. Methods Ninety adults were enrolled, 47 with normal weight, 18 with overweight, and 25 with obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ). Primary inferential analyses included participants with normal weight and obesity ( N = 72); participants with overweight were excluded. Participants completed questionnaires assessing perceived stress (Perceived Stress Scale, PSS), hedonic hunger (Power of Food Scale), trait food craving (Food Craving Questionnaire-Trait reduced), and uncontrolled eating (Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire). PSS Helplessness and Self-Efficacy subscales were derived. Associations were examined using Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and current hunger. Helplessness and Self-Efficacy were entered simultaneously to estimate independent associations with reward-driven eating outcomes. PROCESS moderation analyses tested whether BMI or BMI-defined weight status influenced the association. Results In the primary analysis sample, PSS Total was not independently associated with any reward-driven eating outcome after correction for multiple testing. In contrast, Helplessness was independently associated with greater hedonic hunger, food craving, and uncontrolled eating after FDR correction, whereas Self-Efficacy was not independently associated with any outcome after accounting for Helplessness. In subgroup analyses, associations were descriptively more consistent among participants with obesity than those with normal weight. However, no interaction effect remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Conclusion These findings highlight Helplessness, reflecting, perceived uncontrollability, as the perceived stress dimension most consistently associated with reward-driven eating and underscore the importance of distinguishing between stress dimensions rather than relying solely on overall perceived stress. There was no robust evidence in the present study that BMI or BMI-defined weight status modified these associations. Perceived uncontrollability may represent a potential target for interventions aimed at reducing maladaptive reward-driven eating behavior.

papers.title: Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review
papers.authors: Batyrkhan Omarov
papers.abstract: Background Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. Objective This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. Methods The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. Results MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. Conclusion The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain–computer interfaces
papers.authors: Shouvik Paul, Garima Bajwa
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.

papers.title: A two-stage RAG-LLM pipeline for roadmapping neuroscience research in operational environments
papers.authors: Cara A. Spencer
papers.abstract: Introduction Neuroscientific research and applications in real world environments are often constrained by limited access, equipment limitations, and high costs. Consequently, robustly selecting constructs to focus effort on is a high-impact task. Method This study introduces a two-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline that generates research roadmaps from existing real-world data to inform research priorities in the field, given the state of the art. Stage 1 uses retrieval-augmented generation on operational logs to identify candidate psychological, social, and neurocognitive constructs and map their co-occurrence. Stage 2 evaluates how well these constructs are represented in the literature across four dimensions that commonly inform prioritization: ecological validity, neural correlates, biosensor protocols, and brain computer interface readiness, producing an evidence gap matrix. Pipeline evaluation combined human review, deterministic computations, and human-LLM alignment analysis. Results Applying the pipeline to Mars Desert Research Station logs, Stage 1 identified 19 constructs. Stage 2 highlighted critical gaps in neuroimaging and measurement protocols, particularly for social domains, thereby identifying potential research priorities and risks. Discussion This methodology offers a generalizable starting point for synthesizing operational logs into actionable research roadmaps, but the evaluation showed it still required human scrutiny.

papers.title: Use of Generative AI in Scholarly Research: Challenges and Opportunities
papers.authors: Marco Marabelli, Robert M. Davison, Giovanni Gatti, Ankita Srivastava, Monideepa Tarafdar
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: The focus of this panel report is to present evidence of a panel discussion that took place in October 2025 on the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in academic research and publishing. The panel included publishers (Elsevier, Emerald, Galiot Press, MIT Press, Nature/Springer, Wiley) and editors-in-chief (representing the Information Systems Journal, Journal of the AIS, Journal of Data Science and ICES Journal of Marine Science). Key outcomes of the panel are the following: (1) publishers and editors have some disagreements regarding GAI use; (2) besides disagreements, all recognize that GAI is here to stay, and therefore, outstanding issues (e.g., training for PhD students and junior faculty and consequences for unallowed uses of GAI) need to be addressed jointly; (3) GAI is in constant flux, and this is a challenge for publisher and journal policies; and (4) it is unclear the extent to which GAI will affect future scholarship outcomes, especially having in mind the potential for scholarly deskilling.

papers.title: ChatGPT’s feedback credibility and students’ perceived learning: the role of agent-related social perceptions
papers.authors: Raúl Pérez‐López, Rubén González-Vallejo, Laura Lucia‐Palacios, Iguácel Melero‐Polo, Andreea Trifu
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether students’ agent-related social perceptions of ChatGPT are associated with the perceived credibility of its feedback in academic tasks and whether such credibility, in turn, is related to students’ perceived learning. It also investigates whether the relationship between feedback credibility and perceived learning varies according to students’ sensitivity to the quality of their academic work and their sensitivity to grade-based rewards. To address this, we develop a theoretical model grounded in social perception theory and prior research on students’ experiences with AI-based tools. The model is tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on data collected from 230 students who completed an academic writing task. The findings reveal that students’ agent-related social perceptions—particularly perceived competence and human-like empathy—are positively connected to the credibility students attribute to its feedback. In turn, perceived feedback credibility is interestingly related to students’ perceived learning in the context of academic writing. Furthermore, the positive link between credibility and perceived learning is weaker among students with higher grade-based reward sensitivity. This research contributes to the educational technology literature by advancing understanding of how students evaluate the credibility of ChatGPT-generated feedback and how such evaluations are associated with learning perceptions. It also shows that agent-related social perceptions play a significant role in students’ credibility judgements. Finally, the findings offer practical implications for educators and students seeking to integrate ChatGPT effectively into academic activities.

papers.title: Latent profiles of academic stress and exercise motivation among college students: A latent profile analysis
papers.authors: Pukui Wang, Zihao Li, Wang Xiangyu, Gao Xiang
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the latent profile structure of academic stress and exercise motivation among Chinese college students and to examine the predictive effects of demographic variables, including gender, body mass index (BMI), grade, and household registration background, on profile membership. From May 14 to June 3, 2025, convenience cluster sampling was employed to recruit 1,346 first- to third-year undergraduate students. The participants completed the Academic Sub-Scale and the Chinese-translated Behavioral Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire-2. Latent profile analysis was performed using Mplus 8.3 to identify distinct combined patterns of academic stress and exercise motivation, and the R3STEP method was applied to test the predictive utility of demographic variables on profile assignment. Four latent profiles were identified as the best-fitting solution. Profile 1, the High stress-low motivation profile (9.0%), was characterized by elevated academic stress and low scores across all exercise motivation dimensions. Profile 2, the High stress-high motivation profile (7.4%), exhibited the highest academic stress and the highest levels of external, introjected, and identified regulation. Profile 3, the Low stress-high autonomy profile (22.1%), demonstrated the lowest academic stress and the highest intrinsic motivation. Profile 4, the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile (61.6%), was marked by moderate scores on all variables and represented the most prevalent pattern. Students with normal weight showed a significantly stronger probability association with the High stress–high motivation profile, the Low stress–high autonomy profile, and the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile compared to their overweight and obese counterparts. Female students and third-year students demonstrated a lower probability of belonging to the High stress–low motivation profile. Rural students exhibited a stronger probability association with the Low stress–high autonomy profile, whereas urban students showed a stronger probability association with the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile. Four heterogeneous combined patterns of academic stress and exercise motivation exist among Chinese college students. Normal weight, female gender, higher grade level, and rural background were positively associated with autonomous exercise motivation and may have a potential protective role in the present sample. These findings provide empirical support for the application of self-determination theory and the strength model of self-control in the context of academic stress and offer targeted references for the implementation of differentiated mental health and physical exercise interventions in higher education settings. However, due to the sampling limitations of this study, caution is warranted when extrapolating the present conclusions to the entire population of Chinese college students.

papers.title: Fairness in the Eye of the Beholder: How Gender Bias Alignment Influences Fairness Perceptions and Reliance in Human–AI Teams
papers.authors: Domenique Zipperling, Luca Deck, Julia Lanzl, Niklas Kühl
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems
papers.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly relevant in consequential areas where AI recommendations support human discretion. However, human-AI teams’ effectiveness, capability, and fairness highly depend on human perceptions of AI. Positive fairness perceptions have been shown to foster trust and acceptance of AI recommendations. Yet, work on confirmation bias highlights that humans selectively adhere to AI recommendations that align with their expectations and beliefs—despite those recommendations not being necessarily correct or fair. This raises the question of whether confirmation bias also transfers to the alignment of gender bias between human and AI decisions. In our study, we examine how gender bias alignment and the presence of explanations accompanying the AI recommendation influence fairness perceptions, human self-confidence, and reliance on the AI system. Findings from two 2 \(\times\) 2 between-subjects studies underscore the relationship between gender-bias alignment, fairness perceptions, and reliance, demonstrating that merely constructing a “formally fair” AI system is insufficient for optimal human–AI collaboration. Ultimately, AI recommendations are likely to be overridden when the system's biases do not align with those of its users.

papers.title: Algorithm or Assembly? An Experimental Study of Recommendations by AI Versus Deliberative Mini-Publics in Democratic Decision-Making
papers.authors: Nuri Kim, Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Sangwon Lee, Jihyang Choi
papers.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) renewed debates about who—or what—can legitimately contribute to democratic processes. While both AI and deliberative mini-publics can supplement citizens’ efforts to form judgments about issues, little is known about how citizens evaluate policy advice from these sources. In an online survey experiment with U.S. adults (N = 502), participants read a mock news story reporting a policy recommendation, attributed either to an AI system or a deliberative citizens’ assembly. Opinion climate was orthogonally varied to assess contextual influences. Results were split: citizens’ assemblies were rated fairer and more satisfying, but AI was perceived to be more useful. Opinion climate cues had no moderating effects. Further analysis indicated that acceptance of AI versus citizens’ assembly recommendations depends on individual factors, such as prior attitudes toward the issue and trust in AI. Findings offer theoretical and practical implications for designing democratic decision support systems.

papers.title: Why this AI app? The impact of generative artificial intelligence on educators’ choices in educational apps
papers.authors: Emma Liptrot, Adam Kenneth Dubé
papers.abstract: In elementary education, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being incorporated into educational applications, despite still-emerging evidence of its effects on children’s learning and development. Educators, who are already overwhelmed with choice in the commercial app space, may increasincly have to decide whether to incorporate GenAI-enabled apps for their classrooms. Thus, the present study investigates how mentioning GenAI in app store descriptions impacts K-6 educators’ selection of educational apps. Over two studies, K-6 educators (each n = 101) from Canada, the US, and the UK viewed and evaluated eight researcher-created educational math apps with and without GenAI. Study 1 tested whether mentioning GenAI in app descriptions affected educators’ app evaluations but found no effect. In Study 2, results from a repeated measures MANOVA revealed that educators rated apps without AI higher than those mentioning GenAI, but there were no significant effects of GenAI on likelihood to download or willingness to pay for apps. A hierarchical cluster analysis identified three distinct groups of educators: 1) selectors (n = 28), who exhibited a preference for downloading, rating, and paying for apps including GenAI; 2) agnostics (n = 59), who exhibit minimal preferences; and 3) avoiders (n = 14), who prefer apps without AI. Most educators were agnostic to the use of GenAI in educational apps, highlighting the need to support educators’ informed decisions about when to adopt GenAI tools and encourage critical evaluation of GenAI’s role in education. More research is needed to understand how educators’ GenAI preferences relate to their attitudes, knowledge, and use of GenAI.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Growth: Adaptive Human Intelligence, Emotional Dynamics, and Willingness to Write in Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English (AI-IDLE)
papers.authors: Chenghao Wang, Lanfang Sun, Bin Zou, Yunyan Zhang
papers.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is expanding AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) from predominantly receptive and conversational activities to cognitively demanding productive tasks such as academic writing. Yet little is known about how learners’ motivation and technology-related emotions develop over time, or how sustained interaction with GenAI may engage human capacities for evaluation and adaptation. Grounded in Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), this study investigated the longitudinal development of willingness to write (WTW), technology-related enjoyment (ENY), and technology-related anxiety (ANX) among Chinese undergraduates learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in teacher-supported AI-IDLE embedded within an 11-week English for Academic Purposes writing course. Twenty-six participants with complete records across 11 measurement occasions were included in the longitudinal analysis. Trajectory analysis, change-point analysis, and exploratory moving-window correlation analysis were combined with thematic analysis of learners’ reflections. WTW followed a nonlinear trajectory, declining during the middle period before a potential late-stage transition and subsequent increase, whereas ENY remained comparatively stable and ANX generally declined. The relationships of WTW with ENY and ANX also varied over time. Learners’ reflections revealed increasing recognition of human–AI complementarity and more selective, critical, and strategic engagement with GenAI. From a human-intelligence perspective, these patterns illustrate adaptive and metacognitive capacities involved in evaluating AI-generated information, adjusting strategies, and coordinating human and artificial resources. Rather than treating WTW or emotions as measures of intelligence, the findings position AI-IDLE as a context in which such human intellectual capacities may be exercised and expressed.

papers.title: Empathetic responses by AI legal assistants and user over-disclosure: evidence from an online survey experiment
papers.authors: 思媛 王
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative AI legal assistants rely on users to describe events, evidence, and transaction histories, yet the same accounts may contain private information that is unnecessary for legal guidance. Empathetic language may affect how selectively users decide what to provide. Methods A one-factor between-subjects online survey experiment on Wenjuanxing randomly assigned 360 participants to rational, mildly empathetic, or highly empathetic AI legal responses (n = 120 per condition). Participants completed 1-5 Likert-type measures of parasocial response, privacy boundary judgment, and over-disclosure intention, together with related relational measures, and then answered an open-ended disclosure task. Results The empathy manipulation was successful, F (2,357) = 524.170, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.746. Stronger empathetic responses increased parasocial response (η 2 = 0.428), reduced privacy boundary judgment (η 2 = 0.242), and increased over-disclosure intention (η 2 = 0.406). The coded non-essential disclosure score rose from 0.994 in the rational condition to 6.132 in the highly empathetic condition, F (2,357) = 170.795, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.489. Necessary case facts remained stable, F (2,357) = 0.245, p = 0.783. Bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect effect through parasocial response of 0.214, 95% CI [0.151, 0.283], and a sequential indirect effect through parasocial response and privacy boundary judgment of 0.063, 95% CI [0.033, 0.098]. Discussion Within this consumer-dispute scenario, stronger empathetic cues reduced users' selectivity about which information was appropriate to provide. Data-minimization prompts and evidence-oriented questioning may help retain limited emotional support without encouraging unnecessary disclosure.

papers.title: Exploration or exploitation? The double-edged effects of AI use modes on radical creativity: evidence from AI-enabled drug discovery
papers.authors: Hao Wang, Zhi Xu, Zhihong Huang, Huaihong Pan, Guanbin Zheng
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

papers.title: When loneliness amplifies the risk of problematic emotional dependence: perceived anthropomorphism and basic psychological need satisfaction in AI companion use
papers.authors: Ting Liu, Ruey-ming Shih, Tingyun LUO, Shining Jin
papers.abstract: Background Companion-oriented conversational AI can be experienced as socially responsive, yet evidence about problematic reliance requires construct clarity and noncausal interpretation. This study examined whether perceived anthropomorphism was associated with problematic AI-companion dependence directly and indirectly through basic psychological need satisfaction. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 666 adults in China who reported using a listed AI companion or conversational AI product during the preceding month. The nonclinical outcome was operationalized with six indicators spanning impaired control, distress, continued use, perceived understanding, emotion-regulation reliance, and displacement of offline communication. Measurement evidence was examined using reliability estimates, one-factor confirmatory models, and HTMT. Standardized composite-score regressions used HC3 robust standard errors, and the indirect association was evaluated with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Perceived anthropomorphism was positively associated with need satisfaction ( β = 0.569, p < 0.001). In the outcome model, need satisfaction ( β = 0.317, p < 0.001) and perceived anthropomorphism ( β = 0.385, p < 0.001) were both positively associated with problematic dependence. The standardized indirect association was 0.180 (95% bootstrap CI [0.137, 0.229]); R 2 was 0.323 for need satisfaction and 0.389 for problematic dependence. Conclusion The pattern is consistent with a need-satisfaction account of companion-oriented AI use, but the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering, substitution, or causality. Design and policy implications should therefore focus on transparency, user agency, and safeguards against escalating reliance rather than treating anthropomorphism itself as inherently harmful.

papers.title: ChatGPT as cognitive scaffold: computational thinking and metacognition in AI-embedded instruction
papers.authors: Tanya Chichekian, Joel Trudeau
papers.abstract: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

papers.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
papers.authors: Quanyi Zhao, Xiangming Mu, Xun Zhu
papers.abstract: This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

papers.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
papers.authors: NICOLE DSILVA
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

papers.title: Design Implications for Teacher-Configurable Generative AI Writing Tools: A Participatory Design Study with StoryBot
papers.authors: Ariel Han, Shenshen Han, Zhenyao Cai, Joey Huang, Franceli L. Cibrian, Kylie Peppler
papers.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools become accessible, their integration into K–12 writing presents opportunities and challenges. This study partnered with 21 primary school teachers in a participatory co-design process to develop StoryBot, a teacher-configurable GenAI story-authoring platform. Teachers identified instructional needs and learning outcomes that informed system features, including genre-specific writing scaffolds, configurable prompts, and constraints on full-text generation to preserve student voice. The platform positions educators as co-designers of AI behavior rather than passive users. We conducted a pilot writing workshop with 13 youth (ages 8–12) and a focus group with six educators to examine how the platform influenced students’ writing behaviors and classroom integration. Findings demonstrate the value of teacher co-design and configurable AI systems in aligning GenAI tools with pedagogical priorities and practices. We present design implications for teacher-configurable GenAI writing systems that support student agency, ethical safeguards, and instructional alignment in human–AI coauthoring environments.

papers.title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
papers.authors: Zhuoying Li, Sikai Wang
papers.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

papers.title: The power of framing AI: preliminary evidence on hybrid intelligence and future work perceptions
papers.authors: Lau Holgersen, Janet Frances Rafner, Patrycja Julia Rogozińska, Michail J. Beliatis, Dominik Dellermann, Jacob Friis Sherson
papers.abstract: As generative AI diffuses across organisations, individuals encounter competing frames of AI as autonomous automation or human–AI collaboration. We examine framing as an early interpretive condition that may shape whether people understand AI as a replacement for human labour or as a collaborative system supporting human co-adaptation. Two exploratory experiments tested whether competing AI frames influence master's students' perceived automation risk and sensemaking about AI's role in future work. In Study 1, a randomised repeated-measures experiment with Business Intelligence students (N = 35), introducing a hybrid intelligence (HI) counter-frame after an AI-capability frame was associated with lower perceived job displacement expectations than in the control condition. In Study 2, a randomised framing-primacy workshop with Digital Design students, numeric automation estimates did not differ significantly (N = 31), but in the written-response sample (N = 35), participants exposed to an HI-first frame expressed significantly more augmentation-oriented interpretations of AI's role. The studies suggest that AI frames may influence perceived automation risk and the language used to make sense of human–AI collaboration. We discuss implications for managers and educators and position HI-TAM2 as a preliminary theoretical agenda for research on framing and contextual antecedents in HI acceptance rather than a validated model extension.

papers.title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
papers.authors: Susana Sánchez Castro, María Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines post-intervention self-reported outcomes associated with a short intervention designed to introduce coding, educational robotics, and introductory concepts of machine learning into initial teacher education for Primary Education. The proposal is grounded in Papert’s principles and the Creative and Computational Problem Solving model, combining active learning methodologies with accessible technologies. A quasi-experimental design with a non-equivalent control group was employed. A total of 144 first-year students from three Spanish universities participated (105 in the experimental group and 39 in the control group). The intervention consisted of a two-hour workshop with hands-on stations and technological challenges, designed as a feasible microintervention within regular teacher education contexts. Assessment was carried out through an ad hoc questionnaire focused on three dimensions: knowledge of programming and machine learning, block-based programming and game engines, and active learning, all assessed through self-reported perceptions. The results showed statistically significant post-intervention differences in favor of the experimental group, with a small effect size for knowledge of programming and machine learning and large effect sizes for block-based programming and game engines and active learning. Item-level analyses revealed that favorable overall perceptions coexisted with lower self-reported familiarity in specific technical areas, particularly machine learning, prior experience with block-based programming, and programming in game engines. Three exploratory response profiles were also identified: reluctant, intermediate, and enthusiastic. The findings suggest that well-structured microinterventions may support higher self-reported knowledge of programming and machine learning, greater familiarity with block-based programming and game engines, and more positive perceptions of active learning in teacher education.

papers.title: When AI Is—and Is Not—Needed: AI Literacy and Computational Thinking in Primary STEM
papers.authors: Ahmet Akif ERBAŞ, Tolga Topçubaşı
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in children’s lives, yet exposure does not necessarily lead to an accurate understanding of how AI works. This study examined whether a LEGO-based integrated STEM intervention could improve third-grade students’ AI literacy and computational thinking, particularly their ability to distinguish machine learning from rule-based automation and reason about training data, model error, and technology choice. An embedded mixed-methods, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was conducted with 93 students from four intact classrooms. The experimental group (n = 46) completed eight weeks of authentic design problems, while the control group (n = 47) continued regular Life Studies instruction. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in AI literacy, F(1, 90) = 152.51, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.629, and computational thinking, F(1, 90) = 22.18, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.198. Qualitative evidence showed a shift from viewing AI through robots and automatic actions toward reasoning about learning from examples, data diversity, limitations, human oversight, accessibility, and problem–technology fit. Integrated STEM instruction can foster critical AI literacy by making AI mechanisms visible and inviting students to judge whether AI is needed at all.

papers.title: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC image generation waiting period: effects on creativity in conceptual design
papers.authors: Ziliang Zhu, Jiang Xu
papers.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

papers.title: A new spiral model of AI literacy and competency in higher education developed through a systematic literature review
papers.authors: Zubair Ahmad, Nafilah Abdul Latheef, Almaas Sultana, Nitha Siby, Thomas K. F. Chiu
papers.abstract: This study introduces a new spiral model of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and competency in higher education. It conceptualizes AI competency as a recursive and multidimensional developmental process that evolves from foundational AI literacy. The model addresses persistent conceptual ambiguity between AI literacy and competency and extends existing static and fragmented frameworks by explaining how competency progressively develops through iterative learning. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature review and thematic synthesis of 18 studies identified three major gaps, including conceptual overlap between AI literacy and competency, fragmented framework structures, and limited developmental progression. In response, the proposed model integrates three interdependent dimensions, reflective, dispositional, and practical, within interactive learning environments. Repeated cycles progressively deepen students' critical, ethical, and applied engagement with AI. The model is theoretically grounded in Piaget's Cognitive Development Theory, Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, and Bruner's Spiral Curriculum Theory. Its developmental mechanism is further formalized through the Multiplicative Spiral Gain Function (MSGF), which represents how balanced growth across these dimensions strengthens the transformation of AI literacy into competency. The model provides a foundation for curriculum design, competency assessment, learning analytics, and future empirical validation.

papers.title: Assessing AI-Supported Problem-Solving in Young Adults Reporting Previous Learning-Disorder Diagnoses: Adaptation and Validation of the PS-AIRES and Preliminary Evaluation of a Claude-Based Training Program
papers.authors: Norah Alkhateeb
papers.abstract: AI-supported problem-solving environments increasingly require users to formulate effective prompts, iteratively refine interactions, critically evaluate outputs, and integrate AI assistance into coherent, self-directed solutions. Using a mixed-methods design, this two-phase study involved 672 participants across developmental, validation, and intervention stages. Study 1 included 12 participants in qualitative and cognitive interviewing, 40 independent participants in pilot testing, and 500 participants in the main validation sample. The study developed and psychometrically validated the Problem-Solving Skills in AI-Rich Environments Scale (PS-AIRES) and conducted a preliminary evaluation of a brief Claude-based training program. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor model comprising Strategic Task Framing and AI Instruction Design, Iterative Prompting and Response Refinement, and Verification, Critical Evaluation, and Integration. The model demonstrated satisfactory fit, high internal consistency, and acceptable temporal stability (ICC = 0.713, 95% CI [0.479, 0.852]). Measurement invariance across gender supported structural stability. A subsequent randomized pretest–posttest study involving an independent sample of 120 young adults reporting a previous specialist diagnosis of a learning disorder preliminarily evaluated the brief Claude-based training program. The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of PS-AIRES and suggest the short-term usefulness of structured, dyslexia-sensitive AI literacy training for enhancing problem-solving in AI-rich environments.

papers.title: Logic or Emotion? The Impact of Persuasion Strategies on Human-AI Trust
papers.authors: Tianhao Li, Yue QI
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

papers.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Fostering Inclusive and Culturally Responsive Education for Multilingual and Multicultural Learners
papers.authors: Salma Gehad Waly
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background of the Study Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the way teaching and learning occur in formal and informal settings. Simultaneously, classrooms across global contexts continue to welcome students from various linguistic and cultural backgrounds due to the shifting global dynamics around us. With a wide range of AI platforms currently utilised worldwide, the question of whether AI is creating inclusive spaces for multilingual and multicultural students remains unanswered. AI tools can support multilingual and multicultural students by personalising learning journeys, enhancing efficiency and access to resources and differentiating instruction. Despite that, AI tools are influenced by social, cultural and institutional factors, and there is growing concern that AI might cause further inequalities among traditionally marginalised students, especially when dominant languages and cultures are privileged and algorithmic bias is embedded. Objectives This study critically examines the extent to which AI supports or undermines equity, diversity and inclusion in multilingual and multicultural educational settings, grounded in culturally responsive pedagogy, translanguaging theory and critical digital pedagogy. Methods Utilising a systematic literature review informed by PRISMA guidelines, the study examines how AI use overlaps with issues of equity, diversity and inclusion in multilingual and multicultural settings. Results Findings identified recurring concerns across literature related to monolingual design bias, cultural misrepresentation in AI‐generated content, algorithmic representational harm and constraints on learner agency and access. These findings informed the development of the IHSAN Framework (Identity, Humanity, Safety, Access and Nuance), presented as a conceptual model in the Discussion. Conclusions The study recommends shared accountability among educators, AI developers, educational institutions and policymakers through culturally responsive AI design, equitable implementation practises and governance structures that protect linguistic diversity and learner access.

papers.title: Human–AI collaborative patterns in GenAI-supported instructional design among pre-service teachers: an analysis of interaction sequences and cognitive load
papers.authors: Xu Fang, Junci Feng, Bianyu Yan, Binbin Zhou
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

papers.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
papers.authors: Guoqing Lu, Huimin Zhang, Shen Ba, Lan Yang
papers.abstract: Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants ( n = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

papers.title: Between Human and Machine: University Teachers’ Accounts of Judgment, Metacognitive Defense, and Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI Use
papers.authors: Zhen Qiang, Zhuo Wang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

papers.title: Socratic, Artifact-Gated Generative AI Scaffolding in a 6E Inquiry Unit: A Clustered Quasi-Experiment in Elementary Students’ Computational Thinking
papers.authors: Yu-Chih Huang, Cheng‐Hsuan Li
papers.abstract: Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer ( B = 4.05, SE = 1.58, Wald 95% CI [0.94, 7.15], p = .011; sensitivity p = .034; Hedges’ g = 0.52). Class-clustered analyses found no Holm-adjusted difference on any Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscale; Perceived Choice had the largest positive estimate ( B = 0.27, cluster-adjusted SE = 0.12, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.55], p = .061, pHolm = .306; Hedges’ g = 0.38). The Condition × Pretest interaction was nonsignificant ( B = −0.109, SE = 0.125, 95% CI [-0.354, 0.137], p = .385). Descriptive coding of 101 matched responses showed different distributions of expected and planned AI-use orientations; no inferential transition test was conducted. Findings provide preliminary evidence concerning the bundled intervention but do not isolate component contributions.

papers.title: Message scrutiny and claim verification: Changes in preadolescent reasoning about disinformation across AI-supported instruction
papers.authors: Layda Lopez-Lora, Esteban Vázquez Cano
papers.abstract: Digital information environments expose preadolescents to misleading content before verification routines are fully developed. This study examined pre–post patterns in disinformation evaluation across a two-session instructional sequence combining media-literacy orientation, guided news-analysis activities, researcher supervision, and interaction with Pimpoyo, a generative-AI chatbot using Socratic questioning and a ZPD-inspired rationale. The sample comprised 152 Spanish students aged 10–14 years. Longitudinal evidence came only from the pre–post group (n = 80); a baseline-only reference group (n = 72) contributed baseline information. The primary outcome comprised 24 measurement-equivalent indicators expressed on a 0–25 scale. Indicator-level changes were differentiated: the clearest increases clustered around cues available within the focal message, including sensationalism, alarmist format, writing quality, tone/style, and timeliness, whereas triangulation/lateral reading did not change reliably and externally oriented verification remained mixed. The overall composite increased from M = 11.90 to M = 15.90, t(79) = 6.18, p < .001, d_z = 0.69. These indicator-level patterns are exploratory and are not formal comparisons between psychometric reasoning domains. Self-perceived competence changed, whereas perceived task difficulty did not; these secondary findings do not demonstrate metacognitive recalibration. Because only one group was followed longitudinally and the sequence bundled several instructional components, observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI, Socratic prompting, or any single component. The findings identify a potentially important distinction between focal-message scrutiny and external verification for future controlled research.

papers.title: From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
papers.authors: Shijun Cindy Chen, Conrad Borchers, Christian Dieter Schunn
papers.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.

papers.title: AI attitudes and organizational learning in distance education: interpreting an AI learning gap through structural equation modeling
papers.authors: Merve Gevher, Sefa Emre Öncü, Serpil Koçdar, Erdem Erdoğdu

papers.title: The dynamic bodily self across lifespan: Agency, ownership, and the plasticity of internal body models
papers.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi, Matthew R. Longo, Roman Liepelt
papers.abstract: Two fundamental aspects of research on bodily self-consciousness, agency and body ownership, have recently seen exponential growth. The seminal paper of Botvinick and Cohen in 1998 provided a vital psychophysical tool for studying the bodily self - the rubber hand illusion, in which one feels as if an external object becomes a part of one's body. Recent motor control views of ownership highlight the influence of agency, the sense that one is in control of one's movements. Technological advancements have facilitated more ecologically valid experimental paradigms, such as virtual versions of the rubber hand illusion, furthering our understanding of the mechanisms through which the brain generates agency and ownership sensations. Recent findings suggest that agency and ownership can interact while remaining dissociable, as one may experience agency over an object that is not embodied or ownership of an object that cannot be controlled. Understanding the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying agency and ownership is critical for addressing the challenges of healthy aging. As sensory-motor precision declines across the lifespan, maintaining a coherent sense of body and control becomes essential for mobility, the successful adoption of assistive technologies, and overall cognitive resilience. This review synthesizes current findings on the agency-ownership interaction, discusses its neurobiological substrates, and explores its transformative potential for the design of "self-inclusive" prosthetics and brain-machine interfaces. We conclude by outlining a framework showing how optimization of these processes can support functional independence and psychological well-being in an aging population.

papers.title: The impact of human-AI co-creation on perceived creativity in generative AI art: a serial mediation mechanism of psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow
papers.authors: Chenyang Wang, 陈苗, Wen Yang
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is shifting digital art from one-step generation toward interactive human-AI co-creation. Across two between-subject experiments ( N = 600), we examined how creation mode and prespecified AI-involvement workflows related to perceived creativity. Methods In Study 1, participants completed digital art tasks under human-only creation, AI-only generation, or human-AI co-creation conditions. In Study 2, three workflows differing in AI involvement (low, moderate, high) were evaluated. Psychological ownership, perceived agency, creative flow, and perceived creativity were measured. Results In Study 1, human-AI co-creation produced higher perceived-creativity ratings than AI-only generation, with indirect effects consistent with a serial pathway through psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow. In Study 2, the moderate-involvement workflow yielded higher perceived-creativity ratings and psychological states than the low- and high-involvement workflows. Discussion Perceived creativity in generative-AI art depends on how users experience contribution, control, and engagement during creation. Within the workflows tested, balancing generative assistance with consequential user choice fosters the most favorable subjective creativity evaluations.

papers.title: GAI hallucinations and user dependence: cognitive-affective responses and individual differences
papers.authors: Rongqin Liu, Hui Jiang, Fangying Pang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) hallucinations raise questions about how users respond to unreliable outputs from a technology on which they depend. Drawing on the cognitive–affective components of the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) framework, this study examines the roles of GAI trust, cognitive dissonance, perceived controllability, and frustration in the relationship between perceived hallucinations and GAI dependence, with GAI literacy and self-efficacy as individual-difference moderators. A between-subjects experiment involved 546 participants who viewed the same GAI dialogue labelled as either containing fabricated information or verified as accurate. Participants in the former condition reported lower trust and perceived controllability, greater cognitive dissonance and frustration, and lower dependence scores. In the parallel model, the indirect associations through trust, controllability, and frustration were negative, whereas the indirect association through cognitive dissonance was positive. Higher GAI literacy weakened the positive controllability–dependence association. The remaining moderation hypotheses were not supported under the directional and multiplicity-adjusted criteria. The findings connect users’ evaluations of unreliable GAI responses with the difficulties they report in regulating their use. They underscore the importance of examining dependence alongside reliability judgements, cognitive conflict, and emotional reactions when assessing the human consequences of GAI hallucinations.

papers.title: How human–AI collaboration event strength shapes information security behavior: evidence from a University in Shanghai
papers.authors: Wei Jin, Yuhui Ge
papers.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into higher education learning contexts, university students receive technological support while also facing new information security risks.
