However, existing research has paid limited attention to how the event characteristics of human-AI collaboration are associated with university students' information security behavior and to the psychological processes underlying these relationships. Drawing on event system theory, this study develops a dual pathway model to examine how human-AI collaboration event strength, reflected in event novelty, event disruption, and event criticality, is associated with information security behavior among university students through security vigilance and cognitive overload. Methods Data were collected from students at a university in Shanghai using a three-wave time-lagged survey design, yielding 351 valid responses. Results The results show that event novelty, event disruption, and event criticality are positively associated with security vigilance and cognitive overload. Security vigilance is positively associated with information security behavior, whereas cognitive overload is negatively associated with information security behavior. Further analyses indicate that these event strength attributes generate positive indirect effects through security vigilance and negative indirect effects through cognitive overload. Discussion This study explains information security behavior during university students' use of artificial intelligence from an event-strength perspective and provides a more nuanced understanding of the underlying psychological processes. The findings provide a theoretical basis for universities to refine guidelines for artificial intelligence use, strengthen information security education, and optimize the design of human-AI collaborative learning.

papers.title: Latent profiles of AI teaching self-efficacy and their associations with occupational well-being among vocational education teachers in China: the moderating role of AI anxiety
papers.authors: 嘉苗 胡, Sheng Zhou
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) tools has placed Chinese vocational education teachers at the frontline of a transition combining instructional, practical-training, and emotional demands. Although prior variable-centered research has linked teachers’ AI-related self-efficacy to occupational outcomes, heterogeneity in the multidimensional structure of AI teaching self-efficacy has not been systematically examined in vocational education, and the moderating role of AI anxiety in linking such configurations to occupational well-being remains untested. A regionally stratified online survey was conducted with 768 in-service teachers (378 from secondary vocational schools, 390 from higher vocational colleges) across eastern, central, and western mainland China. AI teaching self-efficacy was measured with the six-dimensional Teacher Artificial Intelligence Competence Self-Efficacy Scale (TAICS), AI anxiety with a teaching-contextualized adaptation of the AI Anxiety Scale, and occupational well-being with the Teacher Subjective Well-Being Questionnaire (TSWQ). Latent profile analysis was conducted in Mplus alongside multi-group confirmatory factor analysis, covariate (R3STEP) analysis, and posterior-probability-weighted (BCH) distal-outcome analysis. Full scalar measurement invariance of the TAICS held across school levels. Four distinct profiles emerged: Foundational Stage (21.4%), Technically Skilled but Ethically Cautious (21.4%), Pedagogically Engaged but Technically Constrained (25.7%), and Holistic Competence (31.6%). Occupational well-being rose monotonically across profiles (TSWQ M = 2.74, 3.04, 3.17, 3.43), with pairwise Cohen’s d (pooled within-class SD) from 0.39 to 2.06. AI anxiety moderated the profile-to-well-being association only for the Holistic Competence profile (B = − 0.13, p < .001); the interaction did not reach significance for the Technically Skilled (B = − 0.07, p = .062) or Pedagogically Engaged profiles, and it accounted for a small share of variance overall (ΔR² = 0.012). The Holistic-over-Foundational well-being advantage was correspondingly smaller, by roughly one third, across the observed range of AI anxiety, an association we interpret cautiously given the cross-sectional design. Chinese vocational education teachers organize into meaningful configurations of AI teaching self-efficacy, with broadly balanced configurations conferring the largest well-being benefits but showing the steepest anxiety-related attenuation of that advantage. The findings apply the Job Demands–Resources framework to AI-in-education research and support differentiated development and support strategies matching competence-building and anxiety-mitigation interventions to teachers’ profiles.

papers.title: Relational Role Attribution: A Unifying Construct in Human–AI Interaction
papers.authors: Michael J Gazzanigo, Xiao Yang
papers.abstract: How users come to perceive an AI not merely as capable but as intentionally oriented toward them in a specific relational capacity remains undertheorized. We propose relational role attribution (RRA) as a discrete psychological construct addressing this gap, positioned as a precursor to downstream relational outcomes rather than a reframing of trust. A PRISMA-ScR scoping review charted 1223 reports at full text against a registered protocol, including 466. Of 179 records excluded for establishing no relational or social role for the agent, 122 (68.2%) nonetheless manipulated or measured anthropomorphism: the field reaches the cue and stops short of the attribution. RRA comprises two concurrent components, a relational inference of social orientation and a role assignment drawn from contextual and communicative cues, checked against the expectancy the user brings. Naming the attribution allows findings accumulated separately across marketing, teaming, and communication literatures to constrain one another, and scaffolds role-specific design principles.

papers.title: Distinguishing AI and human work in green digital advertising: authorship disclosure, claim specificity, and greenwashing suspicion
papers.authors: Stefanos Balaskas
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to create digital advertising, but its effects on perceived sustainability communication remain unclear. This research examines whether AI authorship disclosure increases greenwashing suspicion and whether specific evidence-based claims mitigate this effect. Across three studies using promotional messages for a fictional sustainable delivery service, GreenDrop, we tested authorship disclosure, claim specificity, perceived authenticity, claim diagnosticity, visual attention, and physiological arousal. Study 1 showed that AI-labelled green advertisements elicited higher greenwashing suspicion and lower perceived authenticity than human-labelled advertisements, with a significant indirect association through perceived authenticity. Study 2 showed that specific evidence-based claims reduced greenwashing suspicion, increased claim diagnosticity, and attenuated—but did not eliminate—the AI-disclosure penalty. Study 3 replicated this interaction in a laboratory setting and added eye-tracking and GSR evidence: AI-labelled advertisements increased attention to the authorship label, specific claims altered visual allocation toward claim-related information, and AI-labelled vague claims elicited higher physiological arousal. Overall, AI disclosure operates as a source-attribution cue that can undermine authenticity and heighten greenwashing suspicion, especially when sustainability claims are vague.

papers.title: Lateralized amyloid PET uptake and beta-band connectivity in relation to cognition in temporal lobe epilepsy
papers.authors: Jooheon Kong, Hyun Joo Kim, Mingyeong So, 이인영, Hayom Kim, Young-Tak Kim, Hyun-Ji Kim, Synho Do, Dong-Kwon Lim, Jae-Ho Han, Sung Hoon Kang, Kisoo Pahk, Jung Bin Kim
papers.abstract: We examined focus-relative amyloid PET asymmetry and its associations with resting-state EEG connectivity and processing speed in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Thirty adults with clinically assigned MTLE (19 right-focus, 11 left-focus) underwent 18 F-florapronol PET and resting-state EEG. Regional standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) and sensor-level weighted phase lag index (wPLI) were evaluated using paired comparisons, rank correlations and exploratory bootstrap indirect-association models. Cognitive data were available for 26 participants, including Digit Symbol Coding (DSC) for 25. Under the original analytical convention, mean medial temporal SUVR was 1.066 ipsilaterally and 1.013 contralaterally (difference 0.053, 95% CI [0.013, 0.093]; p = 0.011; Cohen’s d z = 0.500). The contrast differed by focus side (interaction p = 0.002) and was 0.038 under source-table reconstruction ( p = 0.075). Ipsilateral SUVR correlated with inter-hemispheric beta wPLI ( ρ = 0.617, q = 0.034 across 240 tests). The intra-contralateral association ( ρ = 0.536) did not survive this broader correction. Indirect estimates for Trail Making Test A (0.279, 95% bootstrap CI [0.043, 0.761]) and DSC (0.151, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.114, 0.476]) did not survive correction across 136 models. Regional medial temporal PET uptake was associated with beta-band scalp connectivity in this small cohort, while focus-side heterogeneity and labeling sensitivity limit a uniform ipsilateral interpretation. Processing-speed indirect associations were exploratory and did not establish compensation or causality. Replication with structural correction, longer EEG sampling and longitudinal cognitive follow-up is required.

papers.title: How trust shapes human reliance on AI decision support in healthcare: A simulation-based behavioral study
papers.authors: Han Qing
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based decision support systems are increasingly used in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, making it important to understand how trust relates to the use of AI recommendations. Although trust can support effective human–AI collaboration, miscalibrated trust may contribute to inappropriate recommendation acceptance and reduced decision performance. This study examined associations among perceived AI performance, trust, AI recommendation acceptance, and decision accuracy under different levels of AI reliability. In a simulation-based experiment, 100 medical students completed clinical decision-making tasks with AI assistance under high- and low-reliability conditions. Perceived AI performance and trust were measured after each block, while recommendation acceptance and decision accuracy were recorded at the trial level. Mixed-effects models showed that perceived AI performance was positively associated with trust. Higher trust was associated with greater overall acceptance of AI recommendations and greater acceptance of incorrect recommendations. Conversely, higher trust was associated with lower odds of rejecting correct recommendations, indicating more frequent rejection at lower trust. Greater misalignment between normalized trust and objective AI reliability was associated with lower decision accuracy. These findings indicate that calibrated trust is important for effective AI-assisted decision making. They also support the development and evaluation of AI interfaces that communicate reliability and uncertainty to help users align trust with system capability.

papers.title: Informing users about LLMs' environmental costs encourages ethical consumption
papers.authors: Hagai Rabinovitch, Isabel Kashi, Shaul Shalvi
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming deeply embedded in everyday human-AI interaction. However, the environmental costs associated with using those tools remain elusive. Here, we address the question of whether providing users with information about the environmental costs of using LLMs tempers their use. Such information highlights an ethical tension: acting pro-environmentally requires people to forgo some of the benefits AI tools provide. We study how people solve this trade-off in tasks that are relatively easy to tackle without using LLMs and further assess if the impact of providing such information has a stronger effect on people who have stronger environmental concerns. In two preregistered experiments (total N = 1,200), we studied participants’ use of ChatGPT in a text-editing task after they learned about the tool’s environmental costs. Results revealed that (i) raising awareness of ChatGPT’s environmental costs reduced its use and usage volume; (ii) interacting with a sycophantic model, one that encourages continuous use, did not attenuate the awareness effect, although it led to greater overall use; and (iii) raising awareness was especially effective among people with high environmental concerns. The findings highlight how raising awareness concerning LLM’s environmental costs can encourage responsible consumption.

papers.title: Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature
papers.authors: Rebecca Yvonne Bayeck
papers.abstract: Abstract A growing body of research on board games demonstrates that these games can function as learning environments and provide opportunities for learning across diverse contexts. Although learning is often conceptualized contextually within this literature, studies increasingly demonstrate that meaningful learning can occur through participation in board game environments. However, the relationship between board games and learning has been examined predominantly through the study of modern board games, with comparatively limited attention given to classic African board games. This literature review explores learning in classic African board games. This study serves two purposes as it highlights the state of research on classic African board games and the relationship of these games with learning. The fi ndings show that classic African board games are spaces where learning occurs and players engage in a constellation of literacies. The studies analyzed indicate that playing these games can facilitate mathematical learning, engage players in computational thinking and songoputation, and foster the development of skills related to science, engineering, and technology (i.e. STEM). These board games also allow for the exploration of artificial intelligence (AI), which results in the learning of new AI techniques. Classic African board games have the potential to simplify the learning of various subjects and the acquisition of skills relevant to the 21st century. As such, more empirical studies should be conducted to further investigate the connection between playing thesegames, their game mechanics and learning; and particularly the link between their gameplay and the learning of specific subjects such as mathematics, science, and engineering.

papers.title: Ethical Generative AI Use in Higher Education: An Action Research Study Using the Think Aloud Method
papers.authors: Suha Karaki, Sandra Baroudi
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, it presents significant challenges related to ethical use, academic integrity and students' potential over‐reliance on AI‐generated outputs. The Think Aloud method offers a pedagogical approach for making students' reasoning visible as they interact with generative AI tools. Objective This mixed‐methods action research study explored the role of the Think Aloud method as a pedagogical intervention in supporting students' metacognitive awareness and ethical engagement with generative AI tools in a first‐year entrepreneurship course. Method Data were collected through reflective journals, classroom observations and a post‐intervention survey. The study involved 44 first‐year undergraduate students, with 38 students completing the post‐intervention survey. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, while survey responses were examined using descriptive statistics and an exploratory correlation analysis. Results and Conclusions Findings suggested that Think Aloud supported students' emerging awareness of prompt construction, verification practices and ethical decision‐making when using generative AI. However, students' critical evaluation of AI‐generated content often remained at a surface level, particularly among students requiring additional support. The study indicates that Think Aloud can make students' AI‐related reasoning more visible and can support more intentional engagement with generative AI, but it should not be viewed as a stand‐alone solution. Rather, it appears most effective when embedded within a broader pedagogical framework that includes AI literacy, prompt engineering, verification strategies and evaluative judgement. The study contributes classroom‐based evidence on process‐oriented approaches to ethical generative AI use in higher education and highlights the need for sustained instructional scaffolding to support deeper critical engagement with AI tools.

papers.title: Retrieval‐Augmented Lesson Generation With Large Language Models for Scenario‐Based Tutor Training
papers.authors: Jionghao Lin, Sandy Yiyang Zhao, Ashish Gurung, xianghui meng, Kenneth R. Koedinger
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background High‐impact tutoring can improve student learning, but scaling tutoring programmes requires large numbers of novice tutors. Developing high‐quality tutor‐training lessons remains a key bottleneck. Objectives This study compared post‐test performance after participants studied human‐created or LLM‐created tutor‐training materials and examined whether immediate explanatory feedback moderated differences by lesson creation source (human‐created vs. LLM‐created). Methods We conducted a randomized eight‐condition between‐subjects experiment. Participants completed a source‐matched pre‐instruction practice assessment, studied a tutor‐training lesson created by the same source, and then completed two fixed‐order post‐lesson assessments. The design compared lesson creation source, manipulated immediate explanatory feedback and counterbalanced the pre‐instruction scenario form. Post‐test performance was the mean proportion correct across the human‐created and LLM‐created post‐lesson assessments. Results and Conclusions Average post‐test performance was higher after the human‐created lesson than after the LLM‐created lesson, but this difference depended on feedback. The human‐created advantage appeared in the no‐feedback condition, whereas no statistically reliable lesson creation source difference was detected when feedback was provided. Feedback had no statistically significant overall main effect. The human‐created lesson condition performed better on the human‐created post‐lesson assessment, while the LLM‐created post‐lesson assessment showed a small descriptive difference favouring the LLM‐created lesson condition. Because pre‐instruction performance differed by lesson creation source and scenario form, and because assessment source was confounded with fixed assessment order, the results do not isolate pure learning gains or establish a general transfer advantage.

papers.title: The Social Intelligence Reliance Halo: Perceived Social Understanding, Epistemic Trust, and Reliance Quality in Human–AI Decision Making
papers.authors: Filiz Mızrak, Ayça Can Kırgız, Hatice Gokce Demirel
papers.abstract: As generative AI systems become more socially responsive, personalized, and perspective-aware, a central question is whether such features improve human–AI decision quality or simply make AI advice more influential. This study introduces the Social Intelligence Reliance Halo as a proposed social-to-epistemic spillover pattern in which perceived social understanding functions as a non-diagnostic cue for epistemic evaluation: an AI that appears to understand the user may also be granted greater epistemic authority or reliability even when the relational cue provides no evidence of factual accuracy. A randomized two-condition experiment was conducted with 462 working adults with recent generative-AI experience. Participants interacted with either a High Social-Intelligence (High-SI) relational framing package or a Neutral AI across six repeated decision trials. Post-interaction measures assessed perceived social intelligence, epistemic authority, epistemic reliability, suspension of critical judgment, verification behavior, and AI literacy; trial-level behavioral reliance was analyzed with generalized estimating equations. The randomized High-SI package increased perceived social intelligence and increased advice-taking both when participants were initially correct and the contingent AI recommendation was wrong (OR = 1.507, p < .001) and when participants were initially incorrect and the recommendation was correct (OR = 1.800, p < .001). The Condition × participant-dependent advice-correctness interaction was nonsignificant (OR = 1.195, p = .289), providing no reliable evidence that the randomized treatment effect differed across these two states. Because recommendation correctness was mechanically determined by participants’ initial accuracy rather than independently randomized, this interaction is interpreted as exploratory treatment heterogeneity across participant-dependent correctness states rather than evidence that the High-SI package altered sensitivity to AI accuracy. Post-interaction perceived social intelligence was positively associated with epistemic authority and reliability, and AI literacy was associated with lower suspension of critical judgment and greater verification; these associations do not establish temporal or causal mediation. The study therefore provides experimental evidence that a bundled relational framing package can amplify both beneficial and harmful reliance, while the proposed social-to-epistemic pathway and accuracy-sensitive reliance remain questions for stronger future designs.

papers.title: Cognitive flexibility, technostress, and mathematics teachers' acceptance of ChatGPT: a cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis
papers.authors: Baris Demir, Rümeysa Beyazhançer
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

papers.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
papers.authors: Xuming Shang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

papers.title: The structural pathways from AI attitude to AI literacy among university students: considering the serial mediators of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation
papers.authors: Xu Wang, Jinpeng Niu
papers.abstract: Background In the digital era, university students' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has increasingly received considerable scholarly attention. However, the existing literature predominantly focused on extrinsic supportive conditions that influence AI literacy development, and very rare research has examined how subjective AI attitudes relate to AI literacy acquisition. In view of this, the current study aims to explore the structural relations between AI attitude, AI self-efficacy, AI motivation, and AI literacy among contemporary university students. Methods A chain mediation model was employed as the statistical technique, and the participants were 1,323 college students selected from two universities in Shandong, China. Results The results demonstrated that AI attitude is positively associated with AI literacy both directly and indirectly through the single mediation of AI self-efficacy, the single mediation of AI motivation, and the serial mediations of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation. Nevertheless, due to the limitations of unrecorded classroom-level clustering, the statistical findings should be treated as exploratory associations. Conclusion The research underscores the importance of addressing AI-related psychological factors, rather than solely focusing on external supports, in order to effectively promote students' AI literacy in higher education system. Additionally, this exploratory study suggests that the preliminary associations among AI attitude, AI self-efficacy, AI motivation, and AI literacy may require more rigorous replication using hierarchically structured data with recorded cluster identifiers in the future.

papers.title: The association between generative AI acceptance and college students’ career preparation: the serial mediating role of AI trust and career confidence and the moderating role of intrinsic motivation
papers.authors: Juan Jiang, Shuang Liang, Jiachun Chen
papers.abstract: Against the backdrop that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market and occupational ecosystem, how college students build career preparation amid technological uncertainty has become a pressing question. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study constructs a research model in which AI acceptance is associated with career goal setting through AI trust and career confidence, and it examines the moderating role of intrinsic motivation. This study surveys undergraduate students in Chinese universities, obtaining 539 valid responses. The results show that (1) both performance expectancy and effort expectancy are positively associated with AI trust, with a stronger association for performance expectancy; (2) AI trust is positively associated with career confidence; (3) career confidence is positively associated with career goal setting; (4) AI trust and career confidence play a serial mediating role between performance expectancy, effort expectancy and career goal setting; (5) intrinsic motivation positively moderates the relationship between AI trust and career confidence, such that this association is stronger at higher levels of intrinsic motivation. These findings reveal how AI acceptance relates to college students’ career preparation and offer evidence for universities to implement AI literacy education and career counseling.

papers.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on students’ metacognition: a systematic review
papers.authors: Chunyu Ji, Qi Tan
papers.abstract: Given the critical role of metacognition in academic achievement and the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings, understanding the interplay between the two has become essential. In recent years, a growing number of studies have examined their relationship, creating a pressing need for a systematic review to synthesize the accumulating evidence. This review adhered to the PRISMA guidelines, involving the search and screening of papers from three major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost). A total of 22 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. Data extraction and thematic analysis were employed to identify key impacts and underlying interaction patterns. This review distinguishes between Learning-Oriented AI (LAI) and General-Purpose AI (GAI) to organize the evidence. The findings suggest that LAI was more often associated with Guided Interaction, in which AI provides guiding feedback without directly supplying answers, whereas GAI was more commonly associated with Direct Feedback Interaction, in which AI provides answers or explicitly corrects errors. Across both categories, positive findings were reported for several metacognitive outcomes, including regulation, awareness, and shared metacognition. However, some GAI studies also reported that students relied excessively on AI, particularly when they accepted direct answers from AI without sufficient reflection. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of interaction design and teacher guidance in shaping how AI supports students’ metacognitive development.

papers.title: Validity and reliability of the Turkish version of the weight-related eating questionnaire in young adults
papers.authors: Elif Çelik, Emine Koçyiğit, Özge Cemali
papers.abstract: This study aimed to adapt the Weight-Related Eating Questionnaire (WREQ) into Turkish and to evaluate its validity and reliability among young adults. The WREQ is a brief instrument assessing weight-related eating behaviors, including routine and compensatory restraint, susceptibility to external cues, and emotional eating. A total of 301 young adults aged 19–35 years from three regions of Türkiye participated. Translation and cultural adaptation of the WREQ followed International Test Commission guidelines. Construct validity was assessed using exploration factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Convergent validity was examined through correlations with the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (TFEQ-R21) and the Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ). Reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha, McDonald’s omega, and test–retest intraclass correlation coefficients. The sample consisted of 301 participants (85% female), with a mean age of 20.65 years (± 2.08) and a mean BMI of 22.33 kg/m² (± 3.67). EFA indicated adequate sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.88; Bartlett’s χ² = 2424.6, p < 0.001) and revealed a three-factor structure that explained 62.15% of the variance. The factors included Emotional Eating (33.96%), Dietary Restraint (19.32%), and Susceptibility to External Cues (8.87%), with communalities varying from 0.335 to 0.814. CFA indicated that the original four-factor model fit the data better than the three-factor model (Δχ²(3) = 41.025, p < 0.001; ΔCFI = 0.016), as shown by the following fit indices: χ ²/df = 2.46, RMSEA = 0.070, SRMR = 0.068, CFI = 0.940, and TLI = 0.920. Measurement invariance by sex was partially supported (ΔCFI ≤ 0.002). Convergent validity was evidenced by moderate to significant correlations with the TFEQ-R21 and DEBQ subscales ( r = 0.401–0.690, p < 0.001). BMI showed minor positive correlations with most subscales in the whole group. The overall scale exhibited strong internal consistency (α = 0.864), whereas subscales demonstrated acceptable to exceptional reliability (α = 0.708–0.924; ω = 0.725–0.927), HTMT readings below 0.85 corroborated discriminant validity. The Turkish version of the WREQ is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing weight-related eating behaviors among young adults and may serve as a useful tool in both research and clinical practice.

papers.title: When Classification Errors Preserve Correct Recommendations: The Structural Mechanism and Effects of Inadvertent Safeguards in AI Decision Support
papers.authors: Jin Yong Kim, X. Jessie Yang
papers.journal: Human Factors The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
papers.abstract: can occur. An inadvertent safeguard refers to a counterintuitive scenario in which an AI error at the diagnosis/classification stage nevertheless produces a correct downstream decision recommendation. In this paper, we analyze the structural relationship between the AI's classification space and its recommendation outputs. We formalize the conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise and compare the performance implications of Stage 3 action-selection support versus Stage 2 information-analysis support.BackgroundRecent research in human-automation and human-AI interaction has allowed for the structural possibility of inadvertent safeguards. However, this phenomenon has not been explicitly theorized or systematically examined.MethodWe first characterized the structural conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise. We then conducted an experiment in which 90 participants completed a mental rotation task with a simulated AI decision aid that provided either Stage 2 information-analysis support or Stage 3 action-selection support.ResultsWhen inadvertent safeguards occur, Stage 3 action-selection support produced better performance, faster responses, and more positive trust adjustment than Stage 2 information-analysis support. Overall, Stage 3 action-selection support also produced higher perceived reliability, post-condition trust, and usability ratings.ConclusionThe impact of AI errors depends not only on classification accuracy but also on the mapping structure between classifications and actions. Many-to-one mappings, together with misclassifications between recommendation-equivalent states, can preserve correct downstream recommendations despite classification errors.ApplicationDesigners should distinguish classification accuracy from recommendation accuracy when evaluating Stage 3 action-selection support, especially in domains where multiple states can map to the same action.

papers.title: Trending use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools in K–12 school settings
papers.authors: Nicholas Shirlaw, Jihyun Lee
papers.abstract: This study examined AI tool use trends by analysing messages in the Facebook group ‘AI & ChatGPT for Australian School Leaders and Teachers’ using a mixed-methods approach built upon the ‘Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD)’ framework. Results revealed a rapidly evolving landscape with 72 AI tools mentioned across two years, but only 14 referenced in both. While ChatGPT remained popular, tools such as Canva, Curipod, Bing, Turnitin and Bard, mentioned in 2023, were absent in 2024. Teachers consistently used AI tools for generating ideas across both years. The discussion shifted from general topics to specific classroom applications, such as worked examples and lesson hooks/starters. This study offers insights for educators, schools and policymakers, to guide more informed decisions on AI use in K–12 schools.

papers.title: Verification and task performance in teacher-guided AI-supported EMI: an SDT-informed multisection study in Taiwan
papers.authors: Stanley Y. B. Huang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in higher education, but access does not by itself establish educational value. This cross-sectional multisection study examined how teacher-guided AI use was associated with motivation, self-regulation, self-reported verification practice, and performance in Taiwan’s English-medium instruction (EMI) and bilingual higher education. De-identified records came from 684 students in 30 course sections at nine universities. The design combined questionnaire measures with an embedded, independently rated task in which students evaluated and revised an AI-assisted academic response. Standardized regressions used course-section-clustered CR1 standard errors and t(29) inference. Adaptive feedback quality, AI dialogic scaffolding, and student-rated teacher orchestration were positively associated with need satisfaction. Need satisfaction was associated with autonomous motivation, and autonomous motivation was associated with AI-supported self-regulated learning. Self-reported verification practice was associated with self-regulated learning, need satisfaction, and section-level verification climate. In the task-performance model, self-reported verification practice had the largest conditional association (β = .484), followed by AI-supported self-regulated learning (β = .172) and section-level EMI/bilingual task challenge (β = .140); the model explained 38.7% of the variance. The design does not establish temporal mediation or causal effects. The results offer a bounded conceptual distinction between conversational AI support, actionable feedback, and evidence-facing learner regulation in a linguistically demanding context.

papers.title: AI literacy and self-regulated learning: variable- and person-centred evidence from pre-service English language teachers
papers.authors: Meral Şeker, BANU İNAN KARAGÜL
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, making Artificial Intelligence Literacy (AIL) an important competence for critical and responsible engagement with AI technologies. Although previous research has extensively examined how AI-supported environments foster self-regulated learning (SRL), less is known about how learners’ SRL strategies and broader profiles are associated with AIL. The study examined the relationship between SRL and AIL among 301 pre-service English language teachers. Data were collected using the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS) and analysed using correlation analysis, multiple regression, and latent profile analysis with Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars (BCH)-adjusted comparisons. The results showed that the five SRL strategy dimensions were significantly associated with AIL, explaining 21.9% of its variance. Rehearsal, elaboration, and critical thinking made significant unique contributions to AIL, whereas metacognitive self-regulation and organisation did not. LPA identified three profiles characterised by low, moderate, and high SRL. The profiles differed significantly in overall AIL and most dimensions, with higher SRL profiles generally reporting higher AIL. Overall, the findings indicate that AIL is associated with both specific SRL strategies and broader patterns of SRL engagement, highlighting the value of integrating SRL-oriented approaches into AIL education within teacher education.

papers.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 school education through self-determination theory from a longitudinal study: opportunities, challenges, and future direction
papers.authors: Thomas K. F. Chiu
papers.abstract: Successful integration of artificial intelligence into K-12 school education depends on teacher motivation. This motivation can be explained by the three basic psychological needs (i.e. autonomy, competence, and relatedness) proposed by self-determination theory (SDT). This study used SDT to investigate how teachers experience psychological need satisfaction and frustration during AI integration. Using a two-year longitudinal qualitative design, seventy-four K-12 school teachers were interviewed, and data were analyzed via deductive thematic analysis. Findings revealed that the three SDT needs satisfaction fostered pedagogical innovation, efficiency, and professional community. Conversely, needs frustration undermined high-quality integration, which is caused by external control, skill gaps, isolation, and ethical disengagement. These results demonstrate that AI integration is fundamentally a motivational challenge, not merely a technical one. Implications call for needs-supportive environments that honor teacher agency, build genuine AI competence through sustained professional learning, and strengthen collaborative professional communities. Schools must move beyond tool-centric mandates to human-centered implementation strategies that proactively address teacher psychological needs. This transforms AI from a source of resistance into a catalyst for sustainable educational change.

papers.title: Learning effectiveness in AI-supported higher education: examining the roles of AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, self-Directed learning, and digital readiness
papers.authors: Chiao‐Chen Chang
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed higher education by reshaping learning processes, instructional practices, and human-AI interactions. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines associations among AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, self-directed learning, learning performance, learning effectiveness, and digital readiness. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 164 undergraduate students who had prior experience using generative AI tools in university learning activities, and the proposed associations were examined using structural equation modeling. AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, and self-directed learning were positively associated with learning performance, which was positively associated with learning effectiveness. Statistically significant indirect associations through learning performance and interaction effects involving digital readiness were also observed. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because learning performance and learning effectiveness were assessed with highly overlapping self-report items concerning the perceived benefits of AI-supported learning. The direct and indirect associations may therefore partly reflect semantic redundancy and shared method variance rather than distinct educational processes. Moreover, the cross-sectional, single-source design does not establish temporal mediation or causal effects. Subject to these limitations, the findings suggest that technological support, learner agency, and digital readiness are jointly relevant to students’ perceptions of AI-supported learning.

papers.title: How does conversation unfold? analyzing learner–LLM dialogues through multiple analytical lenses
papers.authors: Luciano Hidalgo, Mar Pérez‐Sanagustín, André Câmara Alves do Nascimento, Jorge Muñoz-Gama
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models increasingly permeate educational scenarios, understanding the dynamics of learner-LLM collaboration has become a priority for learning analytics research. Existing approaches, however, tend to rely on surface-level metrics or single perspective coding schemes, limiting insight into the multifaceted nature of these exchanges. This study introduces an analytical framework that combines three theoretically grounded coding schemes with process mining techniques to analyze learner-LLM collaboration in a metacognitive learning task. We applied the framework to 159 conversations from 78 higher education students interacting with a Socratic LLM-based chatbot deployed in a Thermodynamics course, identifying patterns in dialogue structure, epistemic contribution, and conversational balance. For each coding scheme, cluster analysis identified distinct interaction profiles, capturing meaningful variability beneath aggregate patterns. Results reveal that dialogue was structurally dominated by the LLM, yet epistemic contributions were similar in proportion between agents despite pronounced asymmetry in utterance volume. Cross-scheme comparison showed that the three schemes produced related but non-equivalent partitions, each capturing a complementary dimension of the same conversations. Furthermore, learners and the LLM assumed clearly differentiated interactive roles, consistent with a tutor-student dynamic. These findings illustrate the value of multi-perspective, process-oriented frameworks for studying learner-LLM dialogues.

papers.title: Assessing Extraneous and Intrinsic Cognitive Load of Teleoperation: A Physiological-Performance Study with Cognitive Load Theory
papers.authors: Xiaonan Yang, Haonan Fang, Yan Zhao, Yaoguang Hu, Yahui Wang, Chaoran Wang, Hongwei Niu
papers.abstract: Teleoperation is critical in high-risk environments such as space missions, where operators face substantial cognitive demands.Existing studies often assessoverall cognitive load (CL) without distinguishing between intrinsic (ICL) and extraneous (ECL) components. This study examinedphysiological-performance correlates of ICL and ECL during space robotic arm teleoperations. A 2 × 2 experiment manipulated task difficulty (high/low) and operation mode (joystick/key), while measuring CL via subjective scales, attention allocation, electroencephalography (EEG) and pupil diameter. Results revealed that higher task difficulty significantly increased ICL, whereas joystick control elevated ECL. EEG spectral changes in frontal and occipital regions and pupil diameter variations provided complementary physiological evidence, but these measures should be regarded as exploratory correlates rather than validated source-specific biomarkers. These findings suggest that multimodal monitoring may support teleoperation interface design and adaptive assistance, while further validation is needed before physiological measures can reliably distinguish ICL and ECL.

papers.title: AI-Driven Kiosk Support for Older Adults Through Nonverbal Behavior Recognition
papers.authors: Gayoung Kim, Hyun K. Kim
papers.abstract: Older adults experience difficulties using digital kiosks because of low digital literacy, perceived social pressure, and low self-efficacy, and often encounter confusion and negative interactions when errors occur. Additionally, because of the challenges associated with seeking help from nearby individuals, an automated system that detects difficulties and provides support is needed. This study proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) kiosk that automatically detects difficulties experienced by older adults by analyzing their nonverbal behaviors and facial expressions from video data and provides real-time voice and video guidance. Considering that older adults typically require more time to process visual information, a multimodal guidance system combining visual and auditory cues was designed. The concept of “kiosk literacy” was introduced to define five types of guidance: location, task, input, feedback, and screen narration. Furthermore, 16 major pain points experienced by older adults were identified and systematically mapped to their corresponding literacy levels and guidance types to generate appropriate voice and video feedback. A user test with older adults demonstrated that the difficulty detection performance of the proposed AI kiosk achieved 82.35% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 87.5% recall, and an F1 score of 90.32%. Furthermore, the AI kiosk scored significantly higher than conventional kiosks across several user experience dimensions, including ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, satisfaction, and personalization. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides both a technical and practical foundation for improving accessibility and helping bridge the digital divide among older adults.

papers.title: User–AI–Physician Collaboration in Self-Medication: Decision Weight Allocation and Continuance Intention
papers.authors: Guyue Tang
papers.abstract: Self-medication increasingly involves artificial intelligence (AI) and healthcare professionals, yet how users distribute decision authority among AI, physicians, and themselves remains insufficiently understood. This study examined decision-authority allocation and continuance intention in user–AI–physician self-medication systems among 1136 participants. Measures included perceived eHealth literacy, AI use, perceived AI risk, trust, self-medication behavior, and fixed-sum authority allocations. Participants assigned the greatest authority to physicians, followed by AI and themselves, and preferred joint AI–physician systems over either single-agent configuration. Higher eHealth literacy was associated with more frequent AI use, lower perceived risk, greater trust, more authority allocated to AI and users, and less physician-reliant behavior. Trust in AI and physicians showed distinct associations with authority allocation and system preference, while autonomous self-medication behavior was related to authority allocation. These findings conceptualize digital self-medication as a triadic process and support adaptive designs that coordinate roles, preserve user agency, and mitigate AI overreliance.

papers.title: Determinants of Perceived Source Credibility in Generative AI: The Roles of Information Source Type, Information Accuracy, Information Type, and Presentation Modality
papers.authors: Hongjin Shim, Eunyi Kim
papers.abstract: This study examines how information source type, information accuracy, information type, and presentation modality shape perceived source credibility in generative AI settings. A four-way factorial experiment (N = 960) revealed that information accuracy was the dominant determinant of source credibility, while source type (human, AI) and presentation modality (text, video) produced no significant effects. The credibility penalty for factual inaccuracy was nearly four times larger than the penalty for counter-attitudinal opinion content, consistent with Expectancy Violations Theory: higher baseline accuracy expectations in verifiable domains amplify the credibility penalty for error. A significant three-way interaction further showed that human sources incurred larger penalties for factual errors than AI sources, suggesting that individuals apply unequal accuracy standards depending on source identity. The credibility consequences of accuracy violations are thus context-dependent, varying by information type and source identity. These findings offer theoretical and practical insights for AI literacy education and generative AI design.

papers.title: When AI Challenges the Manager: From Technostress and Identity Threat to Leadership Resilience in Design Management
papers.authors: Haoyang Zhang, Zhang Luokuan, Tongxi Ye, Le Yi
papers.abstract: As AI increasingly handles managerial tasks, it undermines some design managers while encouraging others. To explain this divergence, we surveyed 556 Chinese design managers, linking five technostress dimensions to professional identity threat, adaptive learning, and leadership effectiveness. Results show that all technostress dimensions—especially technological invasion and overload—heighten professional identity threat. However, this threat positively drives adaptive learning, which strongly enhances leadership effectiveness. Perceived organizational support and growth mindset strengthen this threat-to-learning conversion, whereas general self-efficacy does not. Machine learning confirmed adaptive learning as the strongest predictor of effectiveness. Ultimately, this study shifts the focus from initial AI adoption to reconstructing human leadership as AI becomes routine, highlighting system explanation, support visibility, learning scaffolds, and boundary-preserving workflows as critical system-design levers.

papers.title: Emotional Comfort at a Cost: The Dynamic Role of Social Chatbot Use in Daily Loneliness, Well-Being, and Interpersonal Interaction
papers.authors: Yun Chen, Yue DING, Linxin Wang, Yu Kou
papers.abstract: As generative AI chatbots increasingly serve as emotional companions, understanding their implications for users’ emotional and social lives is critical. This 14-day diary study involving 97 social chatbot users examined how daily loneliness relates to chatbot engagement and subsequent psychosocial outcomes. Bayesian multilevel models showed that on days when participants felt lonelier than usual, they reported longer chatbot use and stronger emotional engagement. Notably, these two forms of engagement showed distinct associations with daily outcomes. Emotional engagement was associated with higher daily subjective well-being but shorter interpersonal interaction duration, whereas longer usage duration was associated with lower interpersonal interaction pleasure. Mediation analyses reflected the same patterns. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing behavioral from emotional engagement with social chatbots and suggest that emotional benefits and interpersonal costs may coexist in everyday human–AI interaction, informing the responsible design and balanced use of social AI companions.

papers.title: Robot gaze-timing combinations and the uncanny valley
papers.authors: Te-Yi Hsieh, Pai-He Hsiao, Sin-Cheng Ciou, Chia-Hui Pan, Tzu-Chun Chen, Chia-Chun Tsai, Yu Fang, Su‐Ling Yeh
papers.abstract: Anthropomorphic robots are increasingly prominent technologies, yet how variations in robot gaze are associated with human perception and visual engagement remain poorly understood. We examined this with a multi-method design spanning three complementary levels: subjective ratings assessed whether an uncanny-valley pattern was present across the tested gaze combinations, individual-difference measures tested moderation effects by personality and attitudes, and eye movements characterized how the robot's face is visually explored. We presented a virtual robot across nine gaze conditions, systematically varying direct-to-averted gaze ratios and durations within a storytelling scenario. Participants ( N = 61) rated each robot's anthropomorphism, likability, and perceived empathy while their eye movements were recorded, and their personality traits and attitudes toward robots were assessed. Results showed that (1) the relationship between perceived anthropomorphism and likability followed an uncanny-valley pattern (a significant cubic relationship), whereas perceived empathy increased monotonically with anthropomorphism; (2) exploratory analyses showed that extraversion and negative attitudes toward robots moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and likability, while neuroticism moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and perceived empathy; (3) Eye Movement analysis with Hidden Markov Models (EMHMM) identified two viewing patterns (analytic and holistic) and participants higher in openness viewed the highest-rated robot gaze more analytically and the uncanny robot gaze more holistically. These findings indicate that an uncanny valley pattern was observed across the tested gaze-timing combinations and that individual differences may be associated with variation in robot evaluations and visual attention patterns.

papers.title: The invisible signature: Top-down bias in aesthetic evaluation of visual and textual AI-generated art
papers.authors: Cinzia Di Dio, Federico Manzi, Giulia Peretti, Federico Longoni, Vittorio Gallese M. D, Davide Massaro, Gabriella Gilli, Antonella Marchetti
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of generative AI has blurred the boundaries between human and machine art making, raising questions about how authorship information shapes the evaluation of creative products. This study extends previous research by examining how attributed authorship influences the evaluation of genuinely AI-generated art by directly comparing expressive modalities, namely prose (ChatGPT) and images (DALL·E), while also accounting for participant- and stimulus-related characteristics. Participants (N = 121 Italian adults) first evaluated stimuli under a blind baseline condition and then a different, balanced set accompanied by an explicit human- or AI-attribution label. Mixed repeated-measures GLMs examined whether evaluations changed from baseline to disclosure as a function of attributed authorship; educational level and perceived complexity were then entered stepwise as covariates to assess whether the observed pattern was sensitive to participant- and stimulus-related variability, respectively. Across models, evaluations decreased following AI attribution, whereas they remained stable following human attribution. Before covariate adjustment, the baseline-to-disclosure decrease was stronger for texts than for images and varied across evaluative dimensions, with the largest decreases observed for subjective and objective aesthetic judgments, a smaller near-threshold change for emotion, and comparatively stable originality. After educational level and perceived complexity were taken into account, modality- and dimension-related differences were no longer evident in the final model, suggesting that these effects were partly intertwined with characteristics of the participants and stimuli. By contrast, the differential response to attributed authorship persisted after adjustment. These findings confirm that source attribution exerts a robust top-down influence on the appraisal of AI-generated creative products, while differences across expressive modalities and evaluative dimensions provide a more fine-grained account of how this influence is expressed within aesthetic evaluation.

papers.title: Constructing Selves in AI ‐Mediated Apprenticeship Learning: Students of Colour's Narratives of Agency, Recognition and Negotiation
papers.authors: Eugene Kwasi Gyekye
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming computer‐assisted learning, yet little is known about how students of colour engage with AI within authentic educational settings. Existing research has focused primarily on academic integrity, efficiency and technological adoption, with comparatively less attention to students' own experiences of AI‐mediated learning. Objectives This study examined how students of colour in online apprenticeship programs constructed narratives of agency, recognition and negotiation while engaging with generative AI and what these experiences reveal about AI‐mediated learning within apprenticeship education. Methods A qualitative narrative inquiry was conducted over 9 months with five secondary school apprentices participating in online placements across healthcare, government, finance, technology and public service. Data comprised repeated narrative interviews, classroom observations, digital artifacts and field notes, which were analyzed using manual narrative coding. Results Three interconnected patterns emerged. First, students exercised agency by strategically using, refusing, verifying, revising and disclosing AI in ways that maintained authorship and credibility. Second, participants viewed AI as procedurally fair while also recognizing that generic responses often overlooked their cultural and linguistic identities. Third, students negotiated tensions between AI‐generated outputs and institutional expectations through continual verification and adaptation, while proposing design features that would better support transparency, learning and equitable participation. Conclusions The findings suggest that effective AI‐mediated learning extends beyond technical proficiency to include learners' capacity to exercise agency, establish legitimate authorship and experience meaningful recognition within educational contexts. The study introduces Institutional AI Literacy and Recognition Bandwidth as interpretive concepts for understanding how students of colour navigate AI within apprenticeship learning and highlights the importance of designing AI systems that support transparent, equitable and culturally responsive learning experiences.

papers.title: Rethinking Giftedness in the Age of Generative AI: A Relational Epistemic Agency Model for Advanced Learners
papers.authors: Çiğdem Nilüfer Umar
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can enhance the quality and visibility of advanced learners’ work while making it harder to determine what the resulting performance reveals about their independent competence. This theoretical paper develops the Relational Epistemic Agency Model for Advanced Learners (REAM-AL) through a structured database search and an integrative synthesis of scholarship on talent development, extended and distributed cognition, cognitive offloading, metacognition, epistemic agency, intellectual ownership, transfer, and assessment validity. The model organizes five focal constructs across four analytical layers: developmental epistemic readiness, cognitive task distribution, epistemic decision distribution, intellectual ownership, and the relationship among supported performance, independent competence, and transfer. Their configuration may produce relational cognitive extension, in which AI broadens thinking while epistemic authority remains with the learner, or developmental substitution, in which the system performs operations the learner is expected to develop. REAM-AL treats these as interaction patterns rather than fixed student categories. It offers a framework for task design and assessment that distinguishes joint human–AI performance from independently sustained and transferable competence. The proposed constructs and relationships remain theoretical and require direct testing with advanced children and adolescents across varied tasks, developmental periods, and AI conditions.

papers.title: Achievement emotions in AI-assisted learning, academic self-efficacy, and learning engagement and AI dependence among university students in statistics-related programs: a moderated mediation study
papers.authors: Huijuan Qin, Kun Liu
papers.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have become part of everyday coursework for university students, yet the emotional and motivational conditions under which these tools support or undermine learning remain poorly understood. Drawing on the control-value theory of achievement emotions, this study examined whether academic self-efficacy mediates the links of positive achievement emotions in AI-assisted learning with learning engagement and AI dependence, and whether AI literacy moderates the first stage of these pathways. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 700 undergraduate students (386 female; M_age = 19.81 years, SD = 1.27) majoring in applied statistics and related programs at three universities in Shijiazhuang, China. Participants completed measures of positive and negative achievement emotions, academic self-efficacy, learning engagement, AI dependence, and AI literacy. Confirmatory factor analysis preceded a first-stage moderated mediation analysis with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples), controlling for negative emotions, gender, and year of study. Results The six-factor measurement model fitted the data well, χ 2 (50) = 55.62, p = 0.271, CFI = 0.998, RMSEA = 0.013, SRMR = 0.017. Positive achievement emotions predicted higher self-efficacy ( β = 0.374), which in turn predicted stronger engagement ( β = 0.395) and lower AI dependence ( β = −0.176), all p < 0.001, with AI literacy entered in every equation. AI literacy moderated the emotion-efficacy association ( β = 0.152, p < 0.001): the conditional indirect association with engagement rose from 0.088 to 0.208 across ±1 SD of AI literacy, and that with AI dependence fell from −0.039 to −0.093. The direct association with AI dependence was positive ( β = 0.447, p < 0.001), and the conditional total association remained positive (0.355 to 0.408). Both indexes of moderated mediation were significant. Conclusion Positive emotional experiences in AI-assisted coursework show beneficial and costly associations simultaneously, and self-efficacy statistically accounts for opposing parts of each. The total association with dependence remained positive at all literacy levels, so the results describe inconsistent mediation rather than protection. AI literacy marks where the emotion-engagement pathway is strongest.

papers.title: GenAI-supported project-based product design learning: differential changes in multidimensional learning outcomes
papers.authors: Yizhou Chen, Yingqi Zhao, Kenny S L Cheah, Nur Yuhanis Mohd Nasir
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet evidence remains limited on whether its educational value derives from tool access itself or from how human–AI interaction is structured within project work. This quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test study compared a 4-week GenAI-Integrated Project-Based Learning Module (GIPLM) with traditional project-based learning (PjBL) in an undergraduate product design course ( N = 60). Rather than treating GenAI as a stand-alone content-generation tool, GIPLM embedded GenAI as process scaffolding across four stages: product and requirement analysis, user research and knowledge structuring, ideation with multimodal visualization and 3D prototyping, and feedback, validation, and reflective presentation. Learning outcomes were assessed across cognitive, affective, and psychomotor-related domains, together with course performance. According to a mixed-design ANOVA, the GenAI-supported group was associated with significantly greater gains than the control group in cognitive understanding, problem-solving and creativity, fundamental tool operation, advanced design application, and final academic performance. Because advanced design application differed at baseline, ANCOVA was additionally conducted; the post-test group effect remained significant after controlling for pre-test scores, F (1, 57) = 20.519, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.265. Engagement and participation and ethical and user-centered responsibility improved over time but showed no significant Time × Group interactions. These findings suggest that the observed advantages are more consistent with structured, workflow-embedded GenAI scaffolding than with AI access alone, with stronger short-term effects on cognitive, procedural, and performance outcomes than on affective development.

papers.title: Psychological associations between perceived generative AI-supported learning and creative design performance in vocational design education: a within-course correlational study
papers.authors: Xu Xiaoping, Wang Chenhui, 傅双燕, Jiawei Tong, Dian Jin
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design courses, but evidence remains limited on how students’ appraisal of such support co-varies with domain cognition, creative confidence, engagement, and independently assessed creative work. This within-course correlational study examined within-course change and theory-specified contemporaneous associations in a 72-h Furniture Appreciation and Selection course involving 150 vocational design students in China. Sustainable design cognition and creative self-efficacy were measured before and after the course; perceived GenAI-supported learning and learning engagement were measured after it; and final creative design performance was rated independently by three experts. Paired-samples t tests described within-course change. Item-level CFA preceded the score-level association analyses, while standardized composite-score ordinary least squares models and 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap confidence intervals summarized theory-specified post-course associations and coefficient products. Sustainable design cognition increased from 3.326 to 3.792, t (149) = 10.362, p < 0.001, d z = 0.846, and creative self-efficacy increased from 3.509 to 3.877, t (149) = 7.424, p < 0.001, d z = 0.606; these values indicate change during the course as a whole rather than a GenAI-specific intervention effect. Among the direct post-course associations, learning engagement showed the largest coefficient with expert-rated creative design performance (β = 0.515, p < 0.001; f 2 = 0.361). The theory-specified coefficient products were 0.076 for SDC-CSE-LE, 0.204 for CSE-LE-CP, and 0.0080 for AISL-SDC-CSE-LE-CP. The last interval narrowly excluded zero [0.0002, 0.0234], but the product was statistically detectable and negligible in magnitude. Because the study followed one cohort without a comparison condition and most model variables were measured at the same post-course occasion, the findings support within-course change and contemporaneous association, not causal or temporally ordered effects.

papers.title: Can users trust AI doctors? Unpacking the dual credibility pathways linking AI chatbot use to AI health advice adherence intention
papers.authors: Zhanyou Wang, Jingru Wang, Dongmei Han, Liang Ma, Feifei Hao
papers.abstract: With the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare, AI doctor chatbots have emerged as increasingly prevalent tools for health information acquisition and health management. However, existing research has paid insufficient attention to how AI doctor utilization is associated with AI healthcare users' credibility judgments and subsequent AI health advice adherence intention. To address this research gap, this study examines the relationship between AI doctor utilization and AI health advice adherence intention, with a particular focus on the mediating roles of perceived honesty and ability credibility, as well as the moderating role of anxiety sensitivity. A questionnaire survey was conducted among participants from various regions of China, and 224 valid responses were retained after data cleaning. SmartPLS 4.0 was used for data analysis. The results show that AI doctor utilization is significantly and positively associated with both perceived honesty and ability credibility, which, in turn, are positively associated with AI health advice adherence intention. Additionally, perceived honesty and ability credibility play mediating roles in the relationship between AI doctor utilization and AI health advice adherence intention. Regarding the moderating effect, anxiety sensitivity negatively moderates the relationship between perceived honesty and AI health advice adherence intention, while positively moderating the relationship between ability credibility and AI health advice adherence intention. These findings provide nuanced insights for designing anxiety-sensitive AI healthcare services by tailoring credibility cues to users' psychological characteristics and promoting appropriate reliance on AI-generated health advice.

papers.title: When AI translations fall flat: embodied simulation and effort in cross-language reading
papers.authors: Zeli Liu
papers.abstract: Common machine translation evaluation metrics, such as the Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and Crosslingual Optimized Metric for Evaluation of Translation (COMET) are reliable measures of propositional fidelity and surface fluency but systematically ignore the embodied texture of reading, leaving unexplained why high-scoring AI translations still feel flat to readers despite formal accuracy. The Embodied Translation Quality Assessment (E-TQA) framework was developed based on embodied cognition theory to operationalize three key dimensions of cross-language comprehension: sensorimotor simulation, affective-cultural resonance, and processing friction. To validate this framework, a counterbalanced Latin-square design was employed with 192 English-major participants. Six literary and culturally loaded excerpts were each presented in three rigorously matched conditions. Published professional human translations, and translations from DeepSeek and ChatGPT, with all versions controlled for BLEU (±1.2 points) and COMET (±0.04 points) to isolate embodied variation from semantic equivalence. Participants completed the Self-Assessment Manikin and E-TQA scales after each excerpt, and data were analyzed via linear mixed-effects models, reporting partial η 2 as effect size. Human texts were consistently rated higher than both AI conditions in sensorimotor imagery, affective resonance, valence, and arousal, whereas AI texts were rated much higher in phenomenological flatness and cognitive effort. All critical indices showed medium to large effect sizes (η p 2 = 0.15–0.35) and were consistent across educational levels and text genres. These results offer evidence for a dissociation of propositional accuracy and embodied richness, showing that the E-TQA framework accounts for unique variance in reader experience beyond that explained by standard computational metrics. The work advances translation quality assessment by centering embodied cognition, provides a psychometrically sound complement to existing tools, and motivates future multimodal investigations of cross-language processing mechanisms.

papers.title: Toward a cognitive framework of expert singing-voice evaluation in bel canto pedagogy: a longitudinal exploratory study
papers.authors: Kyoko Ikeda, Michiko Yamaguchi, 朱実 小畑, Tomohiro Tani, Yasuki Yamashita, Taisei Terauchi, 隆 永井, Yuko Mesuda, Mizue Kayama
papers.abstract: Classical singing pedagogy relies on expert judgments that integrate auditory-perceptual cues, embodied pedagogical knowledge, and specialized evaluative language. This exploratory, longitudinal study proposes a cognitive framework, centered on Polanyi's concept of tacit knowledge, for describing how experienced bel canto pedagogues perceive singing-voice development from a brief excerpt. Twenty female soprano students (7 music-education, 13 vocal-performance majors) sang the word 'tanto' from Caro mio ben at university entry (Z1) and after 2 years of instruction (Z2). Four professional singers and voice pedagogues, blind to institutional affiliation, rated perceived development on a 0-2 scale and selected evaluative terms from a 27-item Italian pedagogical vocabulary; median ratings, rather than the mean of an even number of raters, served as the primary outcome. Acoustic analysis proceeded in two exploratory, descriptive stages. First, the singer's-formant ratio (SFR) and a Q-value index were compared with a pedagogical reference recording (M2025) using path-length-normalized dynamic time warping. Movement toward M2025 did not correspond consistently with expert ratings: several students whose SFR/Q-value profiles moved toward M2025 received low or zero median ratings (e.g., E06, E07, V07), whereas six students whose profiles moved away from M2025 on both indices received high median ratings of 1.5-2 (E02, E05, V01, V02, V03, V06). Second, changes in alpha ratio, H1-H2, spectral centroid, smoothed cepstral peak prominence (CPPS), and singing power ratio (SPR) were examined descriptively alongside participants' evaluative terms, without regression or machine-learning modeling, given the small, non-random sample. Case-level analysis indicates that experts attended to qualitatively different cues depending on what they heard in a given voice-e.g., basic, mouth-opening- and resonance-related terms (S07, R02) versus depth- and vibrato-related terms (R10, S09)-independent of institutional cohort. We propose a Polanyi-centered interpretive framework in which candidate acoustic correlates, the 27 evaluative terms (understood, after Vygotsky, as mediating cultural-linguistic tools), and Dreyfus-and-Dreyfus-informed developmental sensitivity jointly, but only partially, illuminate the focal judgment that pedagogically meaningful development has occurred. The framework is hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory; no predictive or inferential claims are made about the acoustic determinants of expert judgment.

papers.title: Social cognitive communication mechanism of digital participation in Chinese traditional music in the context of cultural identity and intangible cultural heritage
papers.authors: Tingting Kuai, Jing Qian, Wei Xu
papers.abstract: Digital platforms have reshaped how traditional Chinese music circulates, yet the psychological mechanism linking user participation to cultural identification remains undertheorized. Drawing together social cognitive theory, contemporary cultural psychology, and communication theory, this study develops a four-layer architecture (input, participation, cognitive, and identity) coupled with a staged process model spanning information encoding, symbolic decoding, cognitive reconstruction, and identity internalization. A hybrid specification formalizes the mechanism, pairing structural equation modeling with attention-weighted neural aggregation; both components are estimated and validated on the same data. Empirical testing draws on 2,346 behavioral records from music, short-form video, and social media platforms, paired with 1,128 survey responses from users engaged with the guqin, Kunqu, pipa, and regional opera repertoires. Item loadings, heterotrait-monotrait ratios, collinearity diagnostics, and a common-method check document measurement quality. Results indicate that digital participation (DP) shapes cultural identity (CI) mainly through social cognitive communication (SCC), with the co-creation and dissemination strata showing indirect effects that are more than three times those of passive exposure. As the direct participation-identity path remains significant, the pattern is one of partial rather than full mediation. Cultural identity also looks more like a hinge than a terminal state: a chained specification linking identification to downstream cognitive engagement returns a reliable indirect path, which is consistent with the recursive reading the framework proposes but, on single-wave evidence, cannot establish it. Community climate exerts the strongest moderating influence, exceeding both platform affordance and content polish. Since the design is cross-sectional, all of these patterns are read as associations rather than as causal effects; even so, they suggest that audience cultivation and co-creation tooling deserve at least as much investment as interface refinement in the digitization of traditional music.

papers.title: Teachers’ self-regulated learning profiles in artificial intelligence contexts: implications for differentiated professional development
