papers.authors: Yuhao Su, Mustafa Alpsülün, Müge VURAN, Hasan Celal Balıkçı, M. Barut
papers.abstract: Introduction: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education requires teachers to develop new competencies and manage their own learning. While research has examined teachers' AI attitudes, acceptance, and literacy, less is known about how they regulate their learning in AI contexts. This study examined teachers' self-regulated learning (SRL) profiles and their associations with demographic characteristics and AI-related experience. Methods: In a descriptive survey, 213 in-service teachers completed the Artificial Intelligence Self-Regulated Learning Scale for Teachers (AI-SRLS). Two-Step Cluster Analysis was conducted using five dimensions: task planning, self-monitoring, help seeking, institutional support, and self-evaluation. Results: Two profiles emerged: High Strategic Learners, who scored consistently higher across all five dimensions, and Limited Strategy Users, who reported comparatively lower strategy use. Profile membership was significantly associated with prior AI experience and AI-related training. Gender, age, and professional experience did not significantly differentiate the profiles. Discussion: Teachers' AI-related SRL strategies co-occur in distinct profiles, supporting a differentiated approach to professional development. Teachers with limited strategy use may benefit from structured guidance, scaffolded AI learning opportunities, and stronger institutional support, while highly strategic learners may benefit from more autonomous and advanced learning opportunities.

papers.title: Textbook, multimedia, and generative AI in elementary English learning: usage patterns and family-reported evaluations
papers.authors: Lu Sun, XiaCheng Song, Jing Jin, Min Dai, Huafeng Qu, Xiqiong Yi, Huirong Huang
papers.abstract: Introduction This study examined how often elementary-school learners used textbooks, multimedia resources, and generative AI tools and how these modalities were evaluated by family respondents. Methods A non-probability, teacher-mediated online survey yielded 987 consented responses from multiple sites in mainland China. Respondents rated usage frequency and 15 evaluation items crossing five dimensions with three modalities. Results Textbooks were used most frequently and received the most favorable ratings. After applying a single-step multivariate-t adjustment to each family of three within-dimension contrasts, multimedia and AI differed reliably only for enjoyment in the full sample. The original three-modality confirmatory model had poor absolute fit (RMSEA = 0.151). A crossed dimension-by-modality model improved fit (RMSEA = 0.067) but produced a negative residual variance and was therefore inadmissible; latent achievement regression was not retained. In the primary proportional-odds model using observed modality scores and categorical controls, textbook evaluation was positively associated with family-reported achievement band ( b = 0.343, OR = 1.409, p < 0.001), whereas multimedia ( p = 0.085) and AI ( p = 0.808) were not. Discussion These cross-sectional associations describe this teacher-mediated convenience sample and do not establish modality effects on achievement.

papers.title: Deep brain stimulation and spinal cord stimulation for chronic disorders of consciousness: a decade of clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and critical appraisal
papers.authors: Dongsheng Liu, Kai Yang, Jianlei An, Sipeng Zhu, Yitong Jia, Yichen Zhou, Yong Wang, Weihua Cheng, Kaihan Jiang, Yi Yang, Shaoya Yin, Lei Liu
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) have been investigated for over four decades as neuromodulatory treatments for chronic disorders of consciousness (DOC), including the vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS), for which no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy exists. This narrative review synthesizes literature published between 2016 and 2026 on the neurobiological rationale, clinical evidence, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety of DBS and SCS for chronic DOC. The 'mesocircuit hypothesis', supported by human intraoperative electrophysiology and nonhuman primate causal manipulation, provides a coherent rationale for central thalamic and centromedian-parafascicular targeting. Across case series, cohort studies, and individual patient data meta-analyses, both DBS and SCS produce clinically meaningful improvement in a minority of patients, consistently more often in MCS (63-74% response) than in VS/UWS (26-30% response), with younger age and shorter injury-to-treatment interval predicting better outcomes. However, the two largest individual patient data meta-analyses of DBS concur that current evidence is insufficient to conclude that stimulation alters the natural history of neurological recovery beyond what would be expected from patient selection and spontaneous recovery, and adverse event rates (8.1% for SCS, 18.2% for DBS) indicate non-trivial surgical risk in this vulnerable population. Neurophysiological and neuroimaging biomarkers derived from EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, functional MRI, and FDG-PET show promise for objective outcome prediction but await prospective validation. We conclude that DBS and SCS remain experimental, mechanistically motivated but not yet definitively proven therapies for chronic DOC, and that adequately powered randomized controlled trials, biomarker-guided patient selection, and dedicated ethical frameworks are needed before either modality can be recommended outside of research settings.

papers.title: Graded multisensory neurofeedback via the iNems system for comprehensive upper limb recovery after stroke: a multiple baseline study
papers.authors: Takayuki Kodama, Ken Kitai, Yasuhisa Mizomoto, Kaichi Nishigaya, Shoutarou Hashimoto, Riona Hiraga, Satomi Shimizu, Miki Kawabata, Yuumi Hirabayashi, Keita Ikesue, Hazime Kako, Syouta Yasui, Hiroki Ito, Kazuhei Nishimoto, Osamu Katayama, Hideaki Yamaguchi, Hikaru Nagano, Mari Inoue, Shin Murata, Kiichiro Morita
papers.abstract: Introduction: Post-stroke upper-limb recovery remains challenging, especially in the presence of sensory impairments. Conventional brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are constrained by binary feedback, single-modality stimulation, and exclusion of patients with sensory deficits. We developed the Imagery Neurofeedback-based Multi-sensory System (iNems), a neurofeedback system that provides graded multisensory (visual and electrical) feedback based on ERD magnitude. This study validated iNems' efficacy in motor function, self-reported numbness, and cognitive functions using a multiple-baseline design (MBD). Methods: Four participants with post-stroke upper-limb motor and sensory impairments underwent a multiple baseline design. The baseline phase (phase A) used random feedback; the intervention (phase B) used adaptive iNems. iNems quantified motor intention via sensorimotor EEG event-related desynchronization (ERD) and delivered graded visual and electrical feedback. Primary outcomes were the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) and Box and Block Test (BBT). Secondary outcomes included body cognition, numbness, and neurophysiological (ERD/ERS) changes. Results: All participants demonstrated significant improvement during the intervention. FMA-UE increased by 6-16 points. The BBT showed large effects (integrated Tau-U = 0.75). Body cognition improved significantly in both sense of agency (Tau-U = 0.80) and ownership (Tau-U = 0.89). Numbness was reduced in affected cases (Tau-U = -0.85). Neurophysiological changes correlated with functional gains, with some patterns suggesting increased neural efficiency. Conclusion: This first MBD-validated demonstration shows that graded, multisensory graded neurofeedback based on ERD magnitude can improve motor, self-reported numbness, and cognitive domains after stroke. These findings support adaptive closed-loop therapy as a promising, multifaceted rehabilitation strategy.

papers.title: Reward positivity and affective functioning in early childhood: evidence from temporospatial principal components analysis
papers.authors: Yu Sun Chung, Armen Bagdasarov, Michael Santo Gaffrey
papers.abstract: Reward-related Positivity (RewP) indexes neural sensitivity to reward feedback and has been widely studied in adolescents and adults. However, little is known about how individual differences in RewP are associated with emotional functioning during early childhood, a critical period for affective development. Interpretation of feedback-related ERPs in children is further complicated by temporally overlapping components. This study examined whether a principal component analysis (PCA)-derived RewP is associated with affective functioning in children aged 4-7 years. Electroencephalography was recorded from 140 children during an age-appropriate reward task. Temporospatial PCA was performed on the full EEG sample ( n = 140), and primary regression analyses were conducted in the subset with complete covariate data ( n = 48). Temporospatial PCA was applied to isolate a RewP component differentiating gain from loss feedback. Positive and negative affect were assessed using the child version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Regression analyses examined whether PCA-derived RewP- and gain-related P200 amplitudes were associated with affective functioning while controlling for age, sex, ethnicity, income-to-need ratio, child depressive symptoms, and parental depressive symptoms. At the group level, boys showed greater PCA-derived gain-related P200 amplitudes than girls. At the individual level, higher child positive affect was associated with larger PCA-derived RewP amplitudes in the primary covariate-adjusted regression model. In sensitivity analyses conducted in the larger sample without the income-to-needs covariate, negative affect, rather than positive affect, was significantly associated with PCA-derived RewP amplitude. These findings provide novel evidence that RewP may serve as an early neural marker of affective functioning. By extending RewP research to an understudied developmental period and emphasizing normative emotional functioning, this study advances understanding of early reward processing and highlights the utility of PCA for isolating meaningful ERP components in children.

papers.title: Finding Love in the Black Box: Algorithm Awareness on Dating Apps
papers.authors: Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans
papers.abstract: Most dating apps use algorithms to match users to one another, but are not fully transparent about how their recommender systems work. In turn, users have varying degrees of awareness of matching algorithms. Unfortunately, little is known about how awareness of algorithmic functioning relates to online dating. This research examined the relationship between algorithm awareness, trust in algorithms, and satisfaction with the quality of matches. A survey was conducted among 500 users of the Dutch dating app Breeze, presented to respondents within the app itself. Relationships were estimated with structural equation modeling. Higher algorithm awareness was associated with more trust in algorithms, which positively related to satisfaction with the quality of matches. This mediated association between awareness and satisfaction with matches suggested that awareness of matching algorithms is associated with better outcomes of dating app use. This research contributes to the limited literature on human-algorithm interaction on dating apps. Overall, the results suggest that algorithm awareness may be a relevant part of the online dating experience.

papers.title: The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation
papers.authors: PAOLO BARBIERI, Jacopo Frascaroli, Greta Varesio, Francesca Piovesan, Ludovico Bechis, Pietro Sarasso, Irene Ronga
papers.abstract: A century-old tradition characterizes aesthetic experiences as intense contemplative moments in which we suspend practical concerns and devote our full attention to the object at hand. In line with this tradition, recent theories suggest that aesthetic experiences involve heightened sensory processing accompanied by a suppression of motor activity. Yet, while the link between aesthetic appreciation and perceptual enhancement has received considerable attention, the role of motor inhibition remains largely unexplored. The present study addressed this gap by investigating whether the aesthetic appreciation of images can modulate behavioral and electrophysiological markers of motor inhibition. In Experiment 1, significantly slower reaction times following the observation of preferred images were found. In Experiment 2, EEG responses associated with motor preparation and execution were significantly reduced in trials involving preferred compared with non-preferred images. Time-frequency analysis revealed significantly decreased alpha power (associated with attentional engagement toward visual perception) and increased beta power (associated with inhibited motor preparation) for preferred than non-preferred images. Overall, our results provide new evidence for the existence of a relationship between aesthetic appreciation and motor inhibition and position aesthetic experience as a valuable case study for exploring the adaptive coordination of sensory and motor systems in response to environmental demands.

papers.title: Different forms of interaction with generative AI in higher education: a latent profile analysis
papers.authors: Marcos Pascual‐Soler, Luca Delbello, Alejandro de Vega de Unceta, María Dolores Frías Navarro
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how students interact with digital systems in learning contexts, although students differ substantially in how and why they use these technologies. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and adopting a person-centered approach, this study examined latent profiles of students’ interaction with generative AI based on autonomous motivation, amotivation, AI self-efficacy, and academic self-concept, and their associations with behavioral and attitudinal variables. A sample of 422 undergraduate students completed the study measures. Latent profile analysis identified four distinct user profiles: moderate functional users, self-determined and competent users, low-motivation users, and active competent users. Multinomial logistic regression indicated that AI user identity consistently differentiated the more adaptive profiles, whereas perceiving AI as a form of academic plagiarism was associated with the low-motivation profile. Positive expectations regarding the professional impact of AI were also associated with the self-determined and competent profile. Overall, the findings suggest that students’ relationships with generative AI reflect heterogeneous configurations of motivational regulation, perceived competence, and academic self-perceptions, associated with differences in AI-related identity, ethical beliefs, and professional expectations. These results highlight the importance of motivational heterogeneity in students’ use of generative AI.

papers.title: Examining measurement properties of AI literacy instruments in the era of generative artificial intelligence: a review study
papers.authors: Zhenghong Du, Tianle Dong, Bing Wei
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes embedded in interactive learning environments, measurement of AI literacy is central to instructional design and policy. Valid and reliable instruments are essential for capturing what AI literacy entails in the GenAI era, yet existing reviews have not systematically evaluated the quality of evidence for their measurement properties. This review applied the COSMIN methodology to assess the methodological quality and measurement properties of AI literacy instruments developed in the GenAI context. A search across five databases yielded 37 eligible empirical studies covering four populations, including students, teachers, employees, and the general public. Instrument development was concentrated in East Asian and Western regions and predominantly targeted university students. Self-report scales outnumbered performance-based assessments, with Likert-type formats dominating. The included instruments drew on a range of theoretical sources, with earlier AI literacy concepts often reframed, reorganized, or extended to fit different contexts and emerging assessment needs. Structural validity and internal consistency were the best-supported measurement properties, whereas evidence for several other applicable properties was limited or uncertain. Based on these findings, this review provides guidance for instrument selection according to assessment purpose while considering population and context.

papers.title: Teaching English language learners to prompt effectively: examining effects on prompt literacy, AI self-efficacy, and self-directed English learning readiness
papers.authors: Rahavi Murugesan, P Madhumathi
papers.abstract: Prompt literacy, Artificial Intelligence (AI) self-efficacy and self-directed learning (SDL) are increasingly recognized as essential skills and competencies for learners in the AI era, regardless of discipline. However, developing these key competencies in AI-assisted language learning contexts has received limited scholarly attention. This study examined whether structured instruction in prompt literacy could enhance learners’ prompt literacy, AI self-efficacy (AISE), and self-directed English learning readiness (SDELR) in GenAI-assisted learning contexts. 82 undergraduate English as a Second Language (ESL) learners were randomly assigned to a control group (CG), which received AI-assisted language instruction and an experimental group (EG) that additionally incorporated structured prompt literacy instruction. The results revealed that structured prompt literacy instruction significantly enhanced students’ prompt literacy and AISE. However, there were no marked differences between the two groups in SDELR. The study highlights the value of prompt literacy instruction in AI-based language learning contexts to promote equitable development of digital competencies essential for the AI era alongside language instruction. The findings have important implications for language learners, language educators, teacher educators and researchers.

papers.title: The AI-Provided Social Support Scale: Development, Psychometric Properties, and Its Relationship to Mental Health
papers.authors: Xinglu Shen, Sufen Chen, Sang Min Lee
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly functions as a source of social and emotional support, yet existing measureswere developed for human-human interactions.This study introduces the AI-Provided Social Support Scale (AISS), providing initial validation evidence. Using a split-sample of 684 adults, we examined its psychometric properties through exploratoryand confirmatory factor analysis. Results suggested a three-factor, 11-item structure comprising emotional support, social companionship, and functional support, reflectingAI’s blend of informational and instrumental assistance. The AISS showed moderate positive correlations with human-provided online social support. However, unlike human support being negatively associated with psychological distress, AI-provided support was not significantly related to depression, anxiety, or stress in this sample. These findings suggest that although users perceive AI as supportive, such interactions may function as a functional supplement or emotional companion in this sample, rather than showing the same associations with psychological distress typically associated with human-provided online support.

papers.title: How Agent-Driven Creative Trace Mining Reshapes Design Behavior in a Deployment Study of Intent-Aligned Multimodal Design
papers.authors: Seung Won Lee, Jiin Choi, Yejin Yun, Semin Jin, Yugyeong Jang, Geunmin Hwang, Sang Woon Park, Seonghoon Ban, Kyung Hoon Hyun
papers.abstract: Designers continuously capture inspirations across media, yet these creative traces remain underutilized in computational design support. We present DesignJournal, an agent-driven system that mines multimodal creative traces and transforms them into intent-aligned image generation. The system consolidates artifacts into a unified workspace and employs an agentic pipeline for structured grouping, belief-guided prompt refinement, and iterative intent updates. We developed a framework that classifies sequential design actions, deriving a hierarchical action taxonomy from interaction logs. We used it to examine how agent affordances reshape design behavior. A 10-day deployment study with eight professional designers compared baseline and agent-supported conditions across 5838 classified actions. Agent support significantly reduced the frequency of spatial repositioning actions, particularly small-distance movements, while sequential transition structures shifted from extended repositioning chains toward relational encoding sequences. Awareness of agent interpretation shaped upstream recording behavior, and agent-mediated collaboration extended designers’ creative reach beyond independent exploration.

papers.title: Activating Social Responses in Human–AI Interaction: The Effects of Reciprocal Self-Disclosure and Social Role Framing
papers.authors: Xuejiao Chen, Shuining Wang, Chen Chen, Yiming Zhao, Guoming Yu
papers.abstract: As chatbots become increasingly embedded in everyday communication, understanding when they elicit social responses is important. We conducted an experiment in which 169 participants interacted with LLM-based chatbots in a 2 (reciprocal self-disclosure: yes vs. no) × 3 (social role: mentor, companion, or assistant) between-subjects design. Self-esteem was measured before the interaction as an individual-difference factor. Factorial analyses showed that reciprocal self-disclosure increased users’ disclosure but did not significantly increase trust or perceived support; enjoyment was lower in the reciprocal-disclosure condition. Social role interacted with self-esteem in predicting self-disclosure quality, with favorable responses to the mentor role among participants with higher self-esteem. These findings suggest that chatbot social cues elicit different behavioral and evaluative responses and that role framing should account for user characteristics. The study offers a conditional account of social responding in human–AI interaction and implications for chatbot design in relational contexts.

papers.title: Different lenses on human-AI collaboration: towards a comprehensive view on hybrid intelligence in education
papers.authors: Anne Horvers, Inge Molenaar, Karcie Snoeijen, Oana Costache, Joep van der Graaf, Anne‐Wil Kramer, Susanne M. M. de Mooij, Paraskevi Topali, Zowi Vermeire, Peter J. C. Sleegers
papers.abstract: This paper aims to deepen our understanding of hybrid intelligence in education by investigating human-AI collaboration in four real-world educational use cases. We argue against the simple view of automation and augmentation as distinct processes and foreground the automation-augmentation paradox. This paradox proposes a comprehensive view of automation and augmentation as co-occurrent processes that drive task allocation between humans and AI. We use this paradox as an analytical lens to examine patterns of task changes in human-AI collaboration across four educational use cases. This study approaches teacher-AI collaboration as emerging from task-level changes when AI tools are implemented in educational settings, and these task-level changes are conceptualised as replacement, complementation, and transformation. Across cases, the analysis suggests that automation and augmentation are distributed across different stages in the instructional process. Replacement was primarily situated in bounded analytical subtasks, whereas complementation emerged when teachers interpret, validate and enact AI-generated output. Transformation was most visible in the planning and reflection phases. The cases illustrate how AI may redistribute tasks between teachers and AI systems without displacing teachers’ pedagogical judgement. These findings suggest that the automation-augmentation paradox can serve as a useful analytical lens for analysing meaningful patterns of human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Beyond think-aloud: Toward a representational–recursive agenda for multimodal process-tracing research in learning and instruction
papers.authors: Anthony John Onwuegbuzie
papers.abstract: Background Think-aloud traditionally has been conceptualized as a means of accessing cognitive processes through verbal report. The nine studies in this special issue reveal a broader methodological transition in which verbal protocols increasingly are combined with eye tracking, retrospective cueing, classroom observation, qualitative and quantitative coding, process mining, and epistemic network analysis. Purpose This meta-commentary synthesizes the nine studies together with Hu and Gao's commentary on culturally aware think-aloud research and considers what they collectively imply for the future of process-tracing research in learning and instruction. Results The special issue demonstrates that contemporary process tracing is becoming multimodal, transformational, and implicitly mixed methodological. However, greater methodological sophistication also creates new inferential problems: different traces represent different aspects of cognition; transformations can alter what is represented; integration often remains implicit; ecological validity is relational rather than merely situational; and verbalization itself is culturally situated. Building on these observations, I propose a representational–recursive perspective in which process-tracing research is organized around the design, transformation, integration, and recursive interrogation of multiple representations. I extend this framework further to cultural legitimation, representational equity, and human–AI inquiry. Conclusions The future of think-aloud research lies not in replacing verbal protocols, but in repositioning them within theoretically coherent multimodal systems. Progress will depend on making representational choices explicit, integrating evidence recursively, evaluating meta-inferences across traces, embedding cultural and equity considerations throughout the research process, and using artificial intelligence transparently and accountably.

papers.title: From emotional inhibition to memory suppression: Acute exercise modulates electrophysiological dynamics associated with inhibitory control during suppression of negative memories
papers.authors: Yifan Zhang, Haiting Zhu
papers.abstract: Failures in inhibitory control over negative emotional memories can lead to intrusive recollections that interfere with cognitive functioning and well-being. The present study examined whether acute exercise modulates the electrophysiological dynamics underlying inhibitory control during the suppression of negative emotional memories. Seventy healthy participants were randomly assigned to an acute exercise group or a seated-rest control group. The exercise group completed 30 min of moderate-intensity exercise, whereas the control group remained seated at rest. Participants completed the emotional Think/No-Think paradigm both before and after the intervention, while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Event-related potentials (ERPs), time-frequency analyses, and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) were used to characterize neural processes associated with inhibitory control. Results showed that acute exercise selectively modulated late-stage neural activity during negative memory suppression, particularly within the 2400-3000 ms time window. This modulation was most evident over central site and left parietal site, and was accompanied by changes in alpha- and beta-band power at the left parieto-occipital junction. Overall, these findings suggest that acute exercise modulates late-stage neural dynamics during the suppression of negative memories. The observed neural changes were accompanied by a reduction in intrusion frequency during suppression attempts, consistent with the possibility that acute exercise facilitates late-stage sustained inhibition.

papers.title: Learn AI with AI: Designing conversational agents to support older adults in learning about AI
papers.authors: Eugene Tang KangJie, Tianqi Song, Mengqi Shi, Yi‐Chieh Lee

papers.title: Trust, ethical exposure, and AI adoption intention among accounting professionals: Incremental explanatory evidence beyond UTAUT
papers.authors: Mahfoudh Hussein Mgammal
papers.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in accounting and auditing increasingly considers trust, ethics, and organizational conditions, but less often asks whether such appraisals add explanatory value after a conventional technology-acceptance baseline is already entered. This study conducts a composite-score nested-model comparison using 362 accounting professionals in Saudi Arabia, of whom 285 (78.7%) are external auditors. The UTAUT-aligned baseline contains performance expectancy (ETB), effort expectancy (EOP), social influence (PSE), and facilitating conditions (ERC); the added block contains perceived trust in AI (CTR) and ethical exposure appraisal (EEA). The baseline explains 25.2% of adoption-intention variance and the extended model explains 45.0% (ΔR 2 = .198; HC3 Wald χ 2 (2) =76.68, p < .001; f 2 = .36; 95% CI for ΔR 2 [.126, .283] from a 5,000-resample bootstrap). The increment remains positive after removal of the EEA item overlapping with willingness to use AI, alternative ETB/EOP baselines, demographic and occupational controls, conservative repeated-pattern rules, both chronological waves, and external-auditor subgroup analysis. CTR is positively associated with adoption intention, whereas EEA is also positive, contrary to its negative directional hypotheses; these individual coefficients are treated as secondary descriptive associations. Measurement evidence limits stronger interpretation: ETB and EOP are nearly indistinguishable (HTMT = .977), ordinal dimensionality analyses recover fewer dimensions than specified, and reliability deteriorates sharply in the later recruitment wave. The conclusion supported by the available evidence is therefore sample-bounded and model-comparative: the added score block contributes incremental in-sample explanatory information, but the study does not validate a new latent extension of UTAUT, establish stable mechanisms or causality, or measure actual AI use or audit quality.

papers.title: Recall of overlearned speech in noise: Developmental ERP findings and an episodic buffer frame for culturally situated brain activity
papers.authors: Amedeo D’Angiulli, Matthew Sheculski, Aaron Morrow
papers.abstract: How does extensively practiced speech memory remain dependent on momentary sensory input, and how does this interaction shape brain activity during development? This perspective integrates exploratory behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) findings from a culturally situated spoken-sequence recognition paradigm with a working memory episodic-buffer account. We reanalyzed data from children and young adults who had memorized Quranic passages despite limited Arabic comprehension. Participants heard incomplete passages with or without static noise and selected the missing final word from phonologically plausible alternatives. Noise reduced recognition accuracy, and children generally responded more slowly. Descriptive ERP patterns revealed larger, more spatially distributed responses in children, spanning early auditory processing, mid-latency positivity, and later negative activity. We propose that recognition requires temporary binding of acoustic input, serial and rhythmic expectations, visual response cues, and consolidated sequence knowledge within an episodic buffer under executive control. Noise may impair perceptual fidelity and matching between transient input and stored representations. Developmental ERP differences may reflect representational coordination rather than neural efficiency. These preliminary findings motivate testable predictions concerning cross-modal congruence, familiarity, comprehension, and independently measured expertise. Culturally embedded learning practices provide informative contexts for examining interactions among working memory, long-term knowledge, and developing neural systems supporting cognition.

papers.title: Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners’ Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Yijia Yuan, Yiran Du
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the growing use of educational technologies, including AI and generative AI, how these technologies support learners’ metacognition remains insufficiently understood. The present study synthesised 33 studies using a three-level meta-analysis. Technology-supported interventions were associated with higher metacognitive outcomes on average, Hedges’ g = 0.653, 95% CI [0.520, 0.786], although heterogeneity was substantial. Technology type did not significantly moderate effects. Exploratory analyses showed descriptively larger estimates for interventions with technology-use guidance, immediate feedback, and system-directed learner control, but none remained significant after BH-FDR adjustment (adjusted p = .095 for each). Because these features overlapped, the patterns are hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of independent moderator effects. Interventions most frequently supported evaluation/reflection, monitoring, and strategic control, whereas planning was less consistently represented. Importantly, 77 of 94 effects (81.9%) concerned metacognitive regulation, and 90 (95.7%) relied on self-report measures, indicating that the pooled association primarily reflects self-reported metacognitive regulation. Overall, the findings suggest that technology-supported interventions can support metacognitive outcomes, while these effects should be interpreted in light of the specific regulatory processes targeted and how metacognitive outcomes are measured.

papers.title: Collaborating in the age of GenAI: a mixed-methods study of model preferences
papers.authors: Maria A. Perifanou, Anastasios A. Economides

papers.title: AI interventions as hypothesis cues: rethinking overreliance in human-AI decision-making
papers.authors: Mai Phuong Pham, David Anthony Illingworth, Rickey P. Thomas
papers.abstract: The proliferation of human-AI systems has intensified concerns about the misuse of AI technologies (Parasuraman and Riley, 1997;Amershi et al., 2019). A growing literature has examined cases of misuse with a keen interest in miscalibrated use, specifically overreliance. Currently, numerous interventional methods have emerged to mitigate the improper integration of AI recommendations in decision-making processes. These interventions have had mixed results, as some appear to exacerbate the issue by implying AI technologies are better calibrated to an operator's task than they truly are. We argue that such results may be a consequence of hyper-fixation on behavioral outcomes and tool escalation, while failing to advance theoretical accounts for how AI outputs are integrated into cognitive processes.Here, we use explainable AI (XAI) as an example intervention for illustrating the influence of AI interventions on overreliance. Specifically, we propose that AI interventions prematurely cue and privilege one interpretation of the decision space before competing alternatives have been sufficiently activated.In this view, what is typically characterized as blind acceptance of an AI recommendation may instead reflect an inadequately populated comparison set, in which plausible alternatives were never retrieved, maintained, or activated strongly enough to compete with the AI-supported interpretation. Thus, the acceptance of AI recommendations may reflect a constrained decision-making process rather than poorly calibrated trust.Figure 1 illustrates the proposed XAI-as-hypothesis-cue framework, in which AI recommendations and explanations influence trust and reliance by shaping the hypotheses available for comparison. Task cues and AI outputs activate candidate hypotheses, while explanations can either strengthen the AI-supported interpretation (focal hypothesis) or activate plausible alternatives. These effects depend on cognitive and task constraints. When multiple alternatives remain active, operators are more likely to engage in diagnostic search and exhibit calibrated reliance. When the AI-supported hypothesis becomes dominant, search is more likely to become confirmatory, increasing the risk of overreliance.Many accounts frame overreliance as a problem of excessive trust, insufficient monitoring, or opacity in AI output (Endsley and Kiris, 1995;Hoff and Bashir, 2015). XAI addresses this problem by making model recommendations more interpretable, with the expectation that operators can better evaluate why an output was produced (Lee and Moray, 1992;Ribeiro et al., 2016). This approach can be effective in relatively simple or well-structured tasks, especially when AI recommendations are accurate and explanations clarify task-relevant cues (Bansal et al., 2021). However, calibrating reliance becomes more difficult in complex or uncertain decision environments, where model outputs may reflect epistemic uncertainty, aleatory uncertainty, or hallucinations (Parmar et al., 2021;Ashktorab et al., 2025).Consistent with this limitation, richer explanations can increase trust and overreliance even when incorrect (Bussone et al., 2015;Bansal et al., 2021). By compressing task cues and model reasoning into digestible chunks, explanations may encourage model-consistent search (Payne et al., 1993;Pirolli and Card, 1999).Under time pressure or cognitive load, this can anchor operators to the model's characterization of the problem, impair error detection, and increase acceptance without improving complementary performance (Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2021).Process-level interventions, such as cognitive forcing, provide further evidence that the sequence of reasoning matters. Requiring operators to form an independent judgment before viewing AI advice can reduce overreliance (Buc ¸inca et al., 2021). Yet, such interventions are often interpreted as improving posthoc evaluation of AI advice through greater effort or more cautious trust calibration. This interpretation leaves open another possibility that delaying AI input may preserve the opportunity to retrieve and consider competing hypotheses before an AI-supported interpretation becomes focal.From a memory-theoretic perspective, judgment and decision-making behaviors are grounded in the hypotheses retrieved from and maintained within memory systems. Available task information acts as a set of retrieval cues that activate candidate hypotheses (Thomas et al., 2008). These processes are constrained by information search costs, restricted by cognitive load (Sprenger et al., 2011), working memory capacity (Dougherty and Hunter, 2003), time pressure (Dougherty and Hunter, 2003), and other resources (Böckenholt and Weber, 1993;Weber et al., 1993;Thomas et al., 2014;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022;Payne et al., 1993;Pirolli and Card, 1999). Specifically, under time pressure or cognitive load, people can maintain only a limited set of active alternatives (Dougherty and Hunter, 2003). Early cues shape which hypotheses are retrieved, maintained, used to form confidence, and used to guide further search (Dougherty et al., 2010;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022;Lange et al., 2013).Research in diagnostic reasoning suggests that the precursors of overreliance emerge well before belief evaluation, at the point of hypothesis generation. Work on the temporal dynamics of hypothesis generation has shown that early cues, data serial order, and the first hypotheses generated can exert a primacy-like influence on subsequent diagnostic reasoning (Böckenholt and Weber, 1993;Lange et al., 2012). Initial hypotheses shape which evidence is sought, how subsequent information is interpreted, and whether the decision-maker ultimately arrives at the correct diagnosis (Böckenholt and Weber, 1993;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022). Related work on counterfactual forecasting suggests that better decisions may require increasing the number and diversity of generated hypotheses, not only improving explanations (Illingworth et al., 2023). Model-blindness findings similarly show that cueing effects are conditional when feedback and explanations reveal model limitations, providing operators with opportunities to recalibrate which model's output they treat as diagnostic, preventing the model's recommendations from dominating the hypothesis space (Parmar et al., 2023). Together, these findings motivate the idea that the set of alternatives available for comparison may be determinative of whether the subsequent AI output is appropriately evaluated.The hypothesis-cue account overlaps with, but is not reducible to, neighboring concepts of AI overreliance.Automation-bias and authority accounts emphasize excessive deference to automated recommendations (Skitka et al., 1999;Hoff and Bashir, 2015;Lee and Moray, 1992); anchoring invokes the heuristic mechanism of insufficient adjustment from the initially presented conclusions (Epley and Gilovich, 2006); effort-reduction accounts emphasize the switch to less demanding strategies (Payne et al., 1993;Buc ¸inca et al., 2021); and confirmation bias accounts emphasize the preferential testing of an already focal belief (Klayman and Ha, 1987). Our distinct claim concerns a change in the alternatives available for evaluation at an earlier stage where AI output can alter the number, diversity, accessibility, and activation strength of the hypotheses in the operator's active comparison set (Dougherty and Hunter, 2003;Thomas et al., 2008;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022). Accordingly, two operators may report equal trust in an AI system, but rely on it differently because different alternatives are available for comparison. Thus, the framework predicts that the timing and content of explanations will affect alternative generation and information search even after perceived trust, authority, and effort are controlled.The findings reviewed in the previous section point to a broader account of overreliance in which XAI interventions shape not only how operators evaluate a recommendation but also how recommendations are integrated into reasoning processes and influence the construction of the alternative hypothesis set. We next consider how this process varies with the presence, content, and timing of an AI explanation.AI output without explanation. Our claim is not that AI interventions inevitably narrow the hypothesis space. Even an AI output without an explanation attached can cue one hypothesis by making it focal (Skitka et al., 1999;Epley and Gilovich, 2006). Because a stripped-down recommendation often provides little supporting structure, its effect will likely depend on perceived model competence and whether alternative hypotheses are already active (Hoff and Bashir, 2015). Even so, early presentation can give an AI-prompted hypothesis temporal and retrieval advantages that shape the interpretation of later evidence (Böckenholt and Weber, 1993).AI output with a supportive explanation. Adding a supportive explanation can do more than increase credibility. By supplying model-consistent cues and compressing the model's reasoning into a fluent rationale, the explanation may elaborate the recommended hypothesis, increase its accessibility, and reinforce model-consistent search or undermine the perceived usefulness of disconfirmatory search (Bansal et al., 2019;Dougherty et al., 2010;Payne et al., 1993;Pirolli and Card, 1999). Subsequent reasoning may appear careful even though it occurs within an impoverished comparison set. That is, operators may inspect evidence and articulate a coherent rationale without retrieving viable alternatives. The explanation can then guide confirmatory rather than discriminating search (Klayman and Ha, 1987;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022), increasing reliance without improving complementary performance (Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2021).AI output with a contrastive or uncertainty-focused explanation. An explanation that identifies plausible alternatives, specifies why the recommendation was favored over them, or indicates what evidence would discriminate among them can broaden the active comparison set (Miller, 2019;Illingworth et al., 2023).These explanations should have qualitatively different effects because expanding the hypothesis space can support calibration and orient information search toward evidence to discriminate among alternatives.However, explanations that display uncertainty alone may calibrate perceived reliability (e.g., through a confidence percentage display) without helping operators determine what alternative to consider. Therefore, the effectiveness of such interventions may depend on how well the uncertainty signal is calibrated to the model's actual reliability (Lemus et al., 2023). Accordingly, uncertainty should be linked to model error, misspecifications, missing information, and competing hypotheses if it is to influence hypothesis generation and evaluation rather than trust alone (Zhang et al., 2020;Parmar and Thomas, 2020;Parmar et al., 2023).Intervention before versus after independent judgment. Sequencing should determine whether the intervention helps construct the initial hypothesis set or is evaluated against alternatives already generated.When presented before independent judgment, a supportive intervention may give one hypothesis both primacy and greater elaboration. Presented after an initial judgment or explicit alternative-generation step, the same explanation is more likely to encounter an already populated comparison set. Cognitive forcing may therefore reduce overreliance not simply by lowering trust or increasing effort, but by preserving an opportunity to retrieve alternatives before AI guidance becomes dominant (Buc ¸inca et al., 2021). Thus, the framework predicts an interaction where early supportive explanations should narrow consideration of alternative hypotheses most strongly, whereas contrastive explanations and delayed presentation should promote alternative hypothesis generation and diagnostic comparisons.The practical implication of the proposed frameowrk is straightforward in that operators should form an independent judgment and generate at least one plausible alternative before viewing an AI recommendation or its explanation. Operators should be prompted to ask what evidence would distinguish the AI-supported hypothesis from its strongest competitor and what observation would indicate that the AI is in error. When feasible, recording an initial assessment before consulting AI can separate hypothesis generation from AI evaluation. The purpose is not to discourage trust, but to ensure that reliance follows comparison among plausible alternatives rather than the fluency of a single AI-supported interpretation (Klayman and Ha, 1987;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022).For designers, the framework shifts intervention downstream. Systems should delay recommendations when early outputs are likely to dominate, prompt operators to generate alternatives, present explanations that compare hypotheses, and identify potentially discriminating evidence, rather than merely justify the model's answer. Interfaces can highlight missing evidence and diagnostic task information to discriminate among competing hypotheses, as well as alert operators when they fall prey to confirmation bias (when their search is focused on a single option). In this role, AI facilitates the mapping of the decision space before promoting a preferred conclusion. Moreover, probabilistic support may externalize uncertainty, although its value will likely depend on whether it expands what operators attend and consider rather than simply making recommendations appear more precise and trustworthy.For researchers, we believe that they should consider that reliance, trust, and accuracy are insufficient outcome measures. Studies should also address the number and diversity of hypotheses generated, their rank or relative activation, the information operators select, and whether search is confirmatory or diagnostic (Dougherty and Hunter, 2003;Thomas et al., 2008;Illingworth and Thomas, 2022). The presence of the recommendation, the type of explanation, and the timing should be manipulated separately to determine whether an intervention changes trust, the set of active hypotheses, or both. A key prediction is that reliance can change without a corresponding change in reported trust when AI output alters the alternatives available for comparison. Thus, the central design challenge is therefore not only to make AI recommendations comprehensible, but to prevent a single AI-consistent interpretation from becoming the only option seriously considered by the operators. Explanations should be most useful when they support comparison, review model limitations, and preserve access to viable alternatives before commitment.

papers.title: The layer of lesson preparation delegated to AI predicts classroom discourse quality: a four-wave video study of 90 junior secondary mathematics teachers
papers.authors: Hongyu Chen, Na Wang, 陈冲, Dirong Zhang, Xin Dang
papers.abstract: Research on teachers and generative artificial intelligence has largely measured how much they use these tools, leaving open which cognitive operations they hand over. We asked whether the layer of processing delegated during lesson preparation predicts what happens in the classroom. Ninety junior secondary mathematics teachers in 18 public schools in eastern China were followed across four waves of video-recorded lessons over one school year, yielding 897 coded lessons, 4,640 unplanned student contributions, 1,518 preparation sessions, and 556 stimulated-recall interviews. For each lesson, the final plan was compared against the interaction logs segment by segment, producing two ratios that index offloading by provenance: generative-layer offloading, the share of questioning and variation segments originating in model output, and formulation-layer offloading, the share of context and wording segments. Three-level models decomposing within- and between-teacher variation showed that the two layers behaved differently. Within teachers, generative-layer offloading was associated with less higher-order questioning, less substantive uptake of student talk, weaker maintenance of high cognitive demand, and lower recognition and substantive use of unplanned student contributions, with standardized coefficients between 0.08 and 0.18. Formulation-layer offloading was unrelated to four of those indicators, positively associated with the length and variety of designed variation sequences, and positively associated with recognition of unplanned contributions, the single indicator on which the two layers cross in opposite directions. Total preparation time with AI predicted discourse outcomes on its own and lost that value for the lesson-level indicators once layer composition was entered. An embedded micro-randomized comparison, in which teachers drafted their own questioning and variation sequence before consulting the model, lowered generative-layer offloading and raised substantive uptake. Professional attention to student thinking, coded from stimulated-recall interviews conducted after the lesson by a separate team, followed the same within-teacher pattern and carried the association with the substantive use of unplanned contributions. However, the retrospective measurement leaves its direction open. Teachers' post-preparation confidence rose with generative-layer offloading by 0.23 standard deviations per within-teacher standard deviation. It carried no positive information about the lesson that followed, a confidence-performance dissociation. What predicted classroom discourse was which layer was delegated, not how much.

papers.title: Generative AI acceptance in study-travel contexts: an integrative model of affective and utilitarian pathways with mediation and grade-level moderation
papers.authors: Yuan Li, Dexin Li
papers.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence is progressively reshaping study-travel-a curriculum-embedded educational practice. Yet, the psychological processes governing upper-primary and middle-school students' adoption of such technology in this context remain underexplored. Prior technology acceptance inquiries have predominantly centered on adult populations, leaving adolescent cognitive-developmental contingencies unaddressed. Objective: This investigation aimed to elucidate the differential roles of affective versus utilitarian drivers in shaping study-travel participants' anticipated intentions to adopt GenAI, and to determine whether these pathways differ by grade level. Method: We constructed an integrative model grounded in the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), supplemented by Piaget's developmental framework. The model incorporated perceived enjoyment as a mediator and perceived risk as a direct negative antecedent, with grade level specified as a moderator of selected pathways. Survey data from 741 students in grades 4-9, drawn from twelve schools across six Chinese cities, were analyzed using structural equation modeling, multi-group comparisons, and cluster-robust standard errors to account for the nested sampling structure. Measurement invariance across grade groups was established prior to structural comparisons. Results: < 0.001), with primary students exhibiting approximately twice the inhibitory magnitude of middle-school counterparts. Grade significantly moderated the performance expectancy-intention relationship, and provided borderline evidence for moderation of the risk-intention relationship, indicating systematic grade-related differences in how these pathways operate. Conclusion: These findings advance technology acceptance theory by introducing grade-related contingency and establishing an "affective-efficacy" dual-channel model. Practical implications for designing grade-differentiated educational AI products are discussed.

papers.title: Generative AI-assisted learning and perceived academic performance in higher education: the indirect role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of AI literacy
papers.authors: Shen Xiaotong, Geumchul Um
papers.abstract: Introduction: Generative AI is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, yet the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and students' perceived academic performance, as well as the conditions under which this association varies, remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and AI literacy research, this study tested whether generative AI-assisted learning use was indirectly associated with perceived academic performance through self-efficacy and whether AI literacy conditioned the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy. Methods: Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 376 undergraduates at universities in China. An item-level latent interaction structural equation was estimated using a matched-pair product-indicator approach. Results: = 0.068, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.012, 0.123]), indicating that the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy was stronger at higher levels of AI literacy. The conditional indirect association was not statistically significant at low AI literacy but was positive and statistically significant at the mean and high levels. The index of moderated mediation was 0.011 (95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.002, 0.026]), indicating that the indirect association varied across levels of AI literacy. Discussion: These findings describe a theory-consistent conditional pattern of cross-sectional associations but do not establish temporal or causal ordering.

papers.title: AI-contextualized self-efficacy and exercise engagement among vocational college students in China: a cross-sectional serial mediation analysis of exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations
papers.authors: Guoliang Hou, Lintong Gan
papers.abstract: Background It remains unclear whether artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy, reflecting general efficacy beliefs about coping with difficulties and achieving goals with artificial intelligence support, is associated with exercise engagement. This study examined this association and specific and serial statistical indirect effects involving exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations. Methods A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among 2,279 students recruited by convenience sampling from one vocational college in China. Participants completed self-report measures of artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy, exercise self-efficacy, exercise outcome expectations, and exercise engagement. Confirmatory factor analysis examined the measurement model. PROCESS Models 4 (preliminary) and 6 (primary) evaluated indirect effects using 5,000 bootstrap resamples and percentile 95% confidence intervals. Supplementary latent-variable structural equation models examined the theory-specified mediator ordering and its reversal. All regression and structural models adjusted for gender, age, and grade. Results In the main PROCESS analyses, artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy was positively associated with exercise engagement in the total-association model ( β = 0.427, p < 0.001). After including exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations, the direct association remained significant ( β = 0.246, p < 0.001). The specific indirect effects through exercise self-efficacy ( B = 0.047, 95% confidence interval [0.0352, 0.0598]) and exercise outcome expectations ( B = 0.048, 95% confidence interval [0.0378, 0.0586]) were significant. The serial indirect effect through exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations in the theory-specified order was also significant ( B = 0.016, 95% confidence interval [0.0116, 0.0198]). Supplementary models yielded identical fit for the two mediator orderings. Conclusion In this convenience sample, artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy was associated with self-reported exercise engagement, with statistical indirect effects involving exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations. These minimally adjusted cross-sectional findings do not establish temporal ordering, causal mechanisms, or effects of actual artificial intelligence use.

papers.title: Multimodal data processing for affective perception in AI-supported developmental bibliotherapy: a mixed-methods feasibility study in university libraries
papers.authors: Chenyang Zhou, Wei Kang
papers.abstract: Introduction: Multimodal data processing is increasingly important for understanding human affective experience in naturalistic settings. In this study, "multimodal" refers to the integration of heterogeneous human-centered evidence streams rather than synchronized perceptual or physiological sensing. We evaluated a low-threshold university-library support model integrating developmental bibliotherapy salons with AI chatbot-supported emotional expression. Methods: A convergent mixed-methods feasibility and acceptability design was conducted at a Chinese university. Of 180 baseline respondents, 45 voluntarily registered for a three-week intervention and 38 completed all sessions and post-intervention assessments; 68 non-participating students with complete baseline and follow-up assessments served as a descriptive comparison group. Evidence sources included psychological self-report data, participation records, AI-use feedback, participant evaluations, and semi-structured interviews with nine intervention participants. Quantitative indicators assessed recruitment, retention, acceptability, and exploratory SCL-90 change, while thematic analysis examined participants' affective experiences and perceived mechanisms. Results: All available intervention places were filled within two days, retention reached 84.4%, and 94.7% of completers reported moderate or considerable benefit. The intervention-group mean SCL-90 change was -0.12 points, with an approximate 95% confidence interval of [-0.23, -0.01]. Because allocation was voluntary and non-randomized, no causal group-by-time intervention effect is claimed. Qualitative findings suggested that bibliotherapy salons supported interpersonal resonance, cognitive reframing, and shared reflection, whereas the AI chatbot provided a private and non-judgmental channel for emotional disclosure. Discussion: AI-supported developmental bibliotherapy appears feasible and acceptable as a low-threshold university-library wellbeing service. The findings support feasibility, acceptability, and perceived mechanisms only; they do not establish treatment efficacy, clinical effectiveness, or a neuroscience mechanism. More broadly, the study illustrates how heterogeneous psychological, behavioral, and experiential evidence can be integrated in a naturalistic educational setting.

papers.title: Translating AI and peer feedback in sustainability-oriented STEM teacher education: pre-service mathematics teachers’ uptake, revision, and modeling task-design quality
papers.authors: Sejun Oh
papers.abstract: Introduction: As generative AI becomes increasingly available in teacher education, a central question is how pre-service teachers interpret, evaluate, and translate different feedback sources into coherent design decisions. This study examined how 22 South Korean pre-service mathematics teachers used AI and peer feedback while revising sustainability-oriented mathematical modeling tasks on school cafeteria food waste, a context aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 12. Methods: Using an exploratory, comparative mixed-methods sequence-comparison design embedded in an authentic teacher-education course, participants received two rounds of feedback in different sequences: AI followed by peer feedback or peer feedback followed by AI. Framed within cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions of feedback engagement, the analysis combined double-coded ratings of initial and final task designs, feedback-response records, revision-depth coding, validation-focused revision indicators, and post-activity reflections. Results: Participants rarely copied feedback passively: 20 selectively accepted feedback in at least one round, and 17 made at least one structural or reconceptual revision. Five participants showed a positive composite gain in rated task-design quality. Participants valued AI feedback for its specificity, new perspectives, and speed, and more often made validation-focused revisions after it, whereas they valued peer feedback for mutual communication, classroom realism, and student perspective. Descriptive comparisons showed different engagement trajectories across the sequence conditions alongside similar composite-quality changes. Discussion: Feedback translation provides an analytic perspective on the divergence between revision activity and artifact quality. Within this course context, the findings show how feedback evaluation, revision decisions, and artifact quality can diverge and suggest that teacher educators should scaffold evaluative judgment, source comparison, and post-revision coherence checking.

papers.title: Pedagogical GenAI use and self-reported creative cognition in art education: a three-wave time-lagged correlational study among design students
papers.authors: Jingyi Zhang, Da Xing
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, yet the psychological pathways associated with students' self-reported creative cognition remain unclear. In this three-wave time-lagged correlational study, 389 design students at a South Korean university reported pedagogical GenAI use at Wave 1, creative self-efficacy and AI-related learning anxiety at Wave 2, and creative engagement and self-reported creative cognition at Wave 3. Pedagogical GenAI use referred to coursework-related use for ideation, style exploration, revision, comparison of alternatives, and feedback seeking. Covariance-based structural equation modeling showed good fit [comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.983, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) = 0.026]. Higher GenAI use was associated with higher self-efficacy (β = 0.489) and lower anxiety (β = -0.191). The total modeled association with self-reported creative cognition was β = 0.456 [95% CI [0.314, 0.604]]; its indirect components constituted approximately 59%. The GenAI-origin serial indirect association through self-efficacy and engagement was β = 0.122, whereas the corresponding anxiety-engagement association was β = 0.015. Separately, self-efficacy was indirectly associated with creative cognition through engagement (β = 0.249); this quantity does not include the preceding GenAI-use path. Because the study was observational and engagement and cognition were measured concurrently at Wave 3, the findings do not identify causal mediation. They are consistent with an appraisal-to-engagement account in which competence beliefs have a larger modeled role than anxiety reduction.

papers.title: Experiential avoidance and smartphone addiction in adolescents: a study using multi-model machine learning and mediation analysis
papers.authors: Xinyao Zhang, Weixin Zhang
papers.abstract: Background: Smartphone addiction is closely associated with adolescents' mental health and educational outcomes. Current research lacks comprehensive machine learning studies for predicting smartphone addiction factors, and studies examining relationships between various factors including mediation effects are also insufficient. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 3,405 adolescents in China (1,853 boys, 54.4%; 1,552 girls, 45.6%; mean age = 14.50 years, SD = 1.18). Eight machine learning algorithms (Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Support Vector Regression, Bayesian Ridge Regression) were employed with SHAP analysis for interpretability. Predictive variables included demographic characteristics, social support, experiential avoidance, self-efficacy, and emotional symptoms. Baron and Kenny's method was used for mediation effect analysis. Results: = 0.478, RMSE = 8.66). SHAP analysis identified experiential avoidance as the strongest predictor (SHAP value = 5.472), followed by depressive symptoms (1.723), BMI category (1.438), age (1.394), and anxiety symptoms (1.337). Mediation analysis revealed that social support's negative association with smartphone addiction (total effect = -0.231) was almost indirect (-0.252), with experiential avoidance mediating the majority of the total effect. The final model explained 49.4% of variance in smartphone addiction. Conclusion: Experiential avoidance is a strong correlate of adolescent smartphone addiction and plays a mediating role in the association between social support and smartphone addiction. This finding is consistent with the "reality deficit-virtual compensation" theoretical framework. Additionally, depressive symptoms, BMI category, age, and anxiety symptoms were also independently associated with smartphone addiction.

papers.title: Behavioural expression of ictal embarrassment: a stereo-EEG case report
papers.authors: Anna Scarabello, Veronica Pelliccia, Francesca Bisulli, M. Revay, Francesca Gozzo, A. Mingarelli, Chiara Peretto, R. Mai, C. Pizzanelli, F. Pizzo, Fabrice Bartoloméi, L. Tassi
papers.abstract: Embarrassment is a rare ictal manifestation whose neurophysiological basis remains poorly understood. We describe the case of a 40-year-old woman with drug-resistant focal epilepsy characterized by an unusual ictal semiology combining an intense positive emotional experience with behavioral manifestations of embarrassment. Stereo-EEG demonstrated seizure onset within the middle frontal gyrus bank of the superior frontal sulcus (F2sb), with rapid propagation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and superior anterior insula (sAI). Electrical stimulation of the F2sb reliably reproduced the habitual electroclinical seizure. While identical stimulation parameters elicited the subjective and autonomic manifestations in both supine and upright postures, the complete behavioral repertoire of embarrassment emerged only when stimulation was delivered in the standing position. Exploratory functional connectivity analyses revealed that overt embarrassment was associated with reduced node strength within a network encompassing the dACC, sAI, mesial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). More restricted network changes were associated with only mild sensations, whereas asymptomatic stimulation produced a distinct and partly reversed connectivity pattern. This case suggests that the behavioral expression of ictal embarrassment arises from the transient reconfiguration of a frontal-cingulo-insular network and is critically shaped by bodily context.

papers.title: The domain-specific bias in creativity evaluation: human evaluators favor human-created art, but prefer AI outputs for divergent thinking
papers.authors: Yanming Hou, Yingying Zhang, Bin Wang, Yuxi Zhu, Xiaofei Wu
papers.abstract: Abstract How do humans perceive and evaluate creativity when it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI)? This research examined how labeling a source as “AI” versus “human” systematically biases creativity evaluations across different domains. In experiment 1 (painting and poetry), outputs labeled as human-created were rated as more creative than identical AI-labeled outputs in artistic creation. Experiment 2, which manipulated the attribution of co-created works, revealed that the “human ideation with AI assistance” label enhanced perceived originality in poetry, whereas those attributed primarily to humans remained dominant in evaluations of painting. Experiment 3 utilized a divergent thinking task (Alternative Uses Test), found a reversal: the same output received higher creativity ratings when bearing an AI label. The findings reveal a domain-specific pattern in attitudes toward AI creativity: viewing collaboration positively yet maintaining a persistent bias in valuing AI’s creative contributions.

papers.title: Neural Representations of Perceptual Reorganization in the Musical Scale Illusion
papers.authors: Ahyeon Choi, Jusung Ham, Kyogu Lee, Inyong Choi
papers.abstract: The auditory system organizes complex acoustic input into coherent perceptual streams, yet how neural responses relate to physical stimulus structure and reported perception when the two diverge remains unclear. We investigated perceptual reorganization using the scale illusion, in which interleaved tone sequences presented separately to the two ears are typically heard as continuous melodic streams.Thirty participants listened to illusory, zigzag, and continuous sequences during EEG recording and reported whether each sequence sounded continuous or zigzag. Temporal response function models characterized neural encoding and reconstruction of amplitude-envelope (envelope) and pitch-change magnitude features. We tested whether neural responses during illusory listening corresponded more closely to reference patterns associated with the physical zigzag structure or reported continuous organization. Illusory sequences were predominantly categorized as Continuous and elicited longer RTs than non-illusory sequences. Encoding models revealed delayed pitch-change magnitude responses in the illusory condition, whereas envelope latencies remained comparatively stable. For pitch-change magnitude, reconstruction correlations computed over the full sequence exceeded chance levels estimated separately for each reference, with higher correlations for the continuous reference. Envelope correlations exceeded neither chance level, despite a small relative preference for the zigzag reference. These findings show that neural response timing and relative correspondence with the tested reference patterns depend on the modeled feature during the scale illusion. The reconstruction result concerns correlations across complete sequences and does not establish continuous tracking of the perceived melody.

papers.title: The User Agency Trap in Media Literacy Chatbots: Interactive Evaluation Format, Imperfection Disclosure, and Visual Misinformation Discernment
papers.authors: Jiyoung Lee, Suhyun Kim, Hakjun Lee, Jiwon Hwang
papers.abstract: Although media literacy interventions are increasingly used to counter misinformation, many remain text-centered and non-interactive, limiting engagement during real-time evaluation. This limitation is particularly consequential for visual misinformation, where realistic synthetic images can encourage intuitive judgments. This study examines how two chatbot design features—interactive evaluation format and chatbot (im)perfection disclosure—shape perceived user and AI agency and, in turn, truth discernment. In an online experiment (N = 348), participants evaluated visual misinformation in a chatbot-supported task varying these two features. Interactive evaluation increased perceived user agency but decreased perceived AI agency, whereas imperfection disclosure modestly increased user agency without affecting AI agency. Critically, interactive evaluation indirectly reduced truth discernment through increased perceived user agency. These findings reveal a potential user agency trap: chatbot interactivity can make users feel more empowered while paradoxically undermining their ability to discern visual misinformation.

papers.title: No added benefit of VR and neurofeedback-enhanced VR for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training
papers.authors: Yuqin Liu, Weitao Zhang, Yilin Wang, Chen Wu, Sha Zhao, Gang Pan, 胡宇正
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) and neurofeedback (NF) are increasingly promoted to enhance mindfulness meditation, yet it remains unknown whether these externally engaging technologies confer lasting benefits for trait mindfulness over sustained practice. This longitudinal randomized controlled trial compared three conditions over a 4-week program (eight sessions) with a three-month follow-up: screen-based audio-guided mindfulness (Non-VR), mindfulness in an immersive VR environment (VR), and mindfulness in VR with real-time EEG neurofeedback (VR-NF). Ninety-four meditation-naïve participants completed the study. Trait mindfulness (Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire, FFMQ) was assessed at six time points, EEG signal was recorded during all sessions, and subjective presence (Igroup Presence Questionnaire, IPQ) in VR was measured. Linear mixed models and Bayesian analysis revealed comparable FFMQ increases across all three groups, indicating that VR and VR-NF did not confer added behavioral benefit for trait mindfulness development. Higher IPQ presence scores showed a modest negative correlation with long-term FFMQ gains at three-month follow-up. Exploratory EEG analyses described a numerically steeper theta trajectory in the Non-VR group relative to the VR and VR-NF groups, whereas alpha trajectories were comparable across groups. However, because the two EEG systems were not equivalent across conditions and recordings were obtained from frontopolar sites, these patterns are descriptive only and cannot be interpreted as evidence of group differences. Taken together, these findings suggest that VR and VR-NF did not confer added benefit for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training.

papers.title: Human–AI interaction in cybersecurity: An SOR model approach to users' intention to adopt AI-based authentication systems
papers.authors: Md. Solaiman Chowdhury, Shafiyatur Maria, Md. Rabiul Awal, Raiyan Jannat Sohana
papers.abstract: Cyber-attack poses potential threats and challenges for both individuals and organizations. Although strong security systems can protect against the destructive outcomes of cybercrime victimization, this is comparatively feasible in the current era of Artificial Intelligence. Therefore, the current study aims to unlock users’ intention to adopt AI-based authentication systems (AAI), prioritizing the role of attitude toward AI (AT) as a key direct predictor, while investigating prior cybercrime victimization experience (CVE), perceived severity (PS), and fear of cybercrime victimization (FCV) as antecedent psychological factors determining users’ adoption-related perceptions. Employing a cross-sectional research design, the current study uses convenience sampling with a quantitative method to examine the inner, outer, and structural models. PLS-SEM was applied to conduct both descriptive and inferential statistics by using a total of 453 screened responses. The findings explore that users’ AT, compared to CVE, FCV, and PS, has the strongest impact on users’ AAI. The outcomes also indicate that CVE, FCV, and PS have a positive association with AAI, but all the paths are statistically insignificant. Moreover, FCV has a positive and statistically significant relationship with users’ PS, while CVE has a positive interaction with FCV. By integrating the SOR model into AI-based technology adoption for cybersecurity, this empirical study offers a robust understanding of how AT shapes individuals’ AAI through human-AI interaction. This study uniquely identifies users’ AAI as a key factor in promoting cybersecurity, whereas previous studies emphasized traditional authentication systems.

papers.title: Exploring AI literacy in elementary classrooms: students’ perspectives on generative AI, fairness, and ethical use
papers.authors: Panagiotis Kosmas, Andria Agesilaou

papers.title: Generative AI in the Global South: a PLS-SEM analysis of student perceptions and intentions
papers.authors: Anthony Aapia Korku Dzidzornu, Xukan Xu

papers.title: Problematic reliance on generative AI among university students: an I-PACE-informed PLS-SEM and fsQCA study
papers.authors: Guoqing Liu, Caisang Hou
papers.abstract: Generative AI has become increasingly embedded in university students' academic learning, offering immediate feedback, content generation, and problem-solving support. Alongside these benefits, repeated reliance has raised concerns about problematic dependence on AI-mediated academic support. Drawing on an I-PACE-informed framework, this cross-sectional study examined psychological and academic factors associated with learning-related problematic reliance on generative AI, defined as a non-clinical, self-reported pattern rather than a clinical diagnosis. Data were obtained from a non-probability online sample of 242 university students who had used generative AI for learning-related purposes.
